lessons.title: Start here · How this pack works
lessons.summary: Exam facts, the 20 published topics, the six mock papers and what was verified.

blocks.text: The SAFe Agilist exam for Leading SAFe has 45 multiple-choice, single-select questions and a 90-minute timer. The pass mark is 80%, which means 36 correct answers. It is web-based and closed book; the timer starts when the questions appear, the exam submits itself when time runs out, and unanswered questions count as wrong. The first two attempts are included when taken within 60 days of finishing the course or buying the exam; a retake costs $50 unproctored. A third attempt is available straight after a second failure, the next one 10 days later, then 30 days apart. These facts come from the exam study guide as it stood on 16 November 2026, and the guide says details can change, so check it again before you sit the exam.
blocks.title: The exam

blocks.text: Exam share is the study guide's range. The course page shows different ranges for three domains (mindset 18-21%, team and technical agility 7-9%, LPM 25-28%) and lists two extra LPM topics; the pack follows the study guide.
rows: Build a Foundation with Mindset, Value, and Principles
blocks.title: The six domains and this pack

blocks.text:
Each domain is split into the topics the study guide lists, 20 in all, numbered 1.1 to 6.3. Every question and flashcard belongs to one topic, so the mastery view shows which topic is weak. Every topic lesson follows the same shape: the idea, a worked example, the usual exam trap, a self-check, more detail, a worked case, an exercise with its solution, the facts to learn, and a note on what was verified. Two labs give extended practice on WSJF and on PI Planning risks and objectives.

Short mocks draw 20 questions at random, weighted by domain. The six full papers, A to F, each have 45 fixed single-select questions weighted like the exam and spread across the topics. Practice never shows you a question from a paper you have not opened, so each paper stays a fresh test until you sit it.

blocks.title: Suggested way through

blocks.text:
Most wrong options are not nonsense. They are good practice put in the wrong place.

1. A generic Scrum or project answer where SAFe has a specific one. Example: 'the sprint review' where SAFe means the System Demo of the whole train.
2. A manager deciding where the team or the role should. Example: a manager reordering the team backlog, which belongs to the Product Owner.
3. The right practice given to the wrong role, event or level. Example: the Release Train Engineer prioritising features, which is Product Management's job.

Every lesson ends with a callout that applies these traps to its topic.
blocks.title: Three traps this exam uses

lessons.title: 1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption
lessons.summary: The age of software and digital, Business Agility and the Business Agility Value Stream.

blocks.text:
SAFe starts from a claim about the present: we live in the age of software and digital, and every business is a software business. A bank, a freight company and a hospital all compete on how quickly they can turn an idea into a digitally enabled solution. Enterprises that cannot do this lose to those that can.

Business Agility is SAFe's name for the answer. It is the ability to compete and thrive in the digital age by quickly responding to market changes and emerging opportunities with digitally enabled business solutions. Note what it is not: it is not a team practice and it is not an IT programme. It involves everyone who helps deliver solutions, including leaders, finance, legal and operations.
blocks.title: Thriving in the age of disruption

blocks.text: SAFe draws on Carlota Perez's account of five technological revolutions: the industrial revolution, the age of steam and railways, the age of steel and heavy engineering, the age of oil and mass production, and today's age of software and digital. Each revolution starts with a period in which a new technology is installed, followed by a turning point and a period in which it is deployed across the whole economy. Companies that learn to use the new technology take markets from those that do not, whatever their size. That is why SAFe treats digital disruption as structural, not as a passing trend.
blocks.title: Why now: technological revolutions

blocks.text: Lean-Agile leadership enables the whole stream.
rows: Market and customer signals reveal a possibility
Lean Portfolio Management funds a minimum viable product
People are organised around the work, in value streams
Teams learn what the customer really needs
The smallest solution that can test the idea is delivered
Evidence decides whether to continue, change or stop
The Continuous Delivery Pipeline delivers on demand
blocks.title: Business Agility Value Stream

blocks.text: A regional insurer issues policies on paper. A newcomer sells cover in two minutes on a phone and takes the insurer's younger customers. Cutting costs in the paper process or upgrading servers makes the old model cheaper, not faster. The SAFe question is how quickly the insurer can sense the opportunity, fund an MVP, organise people around that value and learn from real customers.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Business Agility is an enterprise capability, not a team practice and not an IT programme. The option that says "our teams use sprints" or "IT works faster" is the generic answer. SAFe's answer involves everyone who helps deliver solutions: leaders, finance, legal, marketing, operations and IT.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What is the first step of the Business Agility Value Stream, and what comes straight after Fund MVP? Sense Opportunity is first. Organize Around Value follows Fund MVP, before Connect to Customer.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A business unit wants to enter a new market but is unsure about demand. Instead of a five-year business case or a full budget up front, it funds a small MVP, learns from customers, and lets the evidence decide whether to pivot or persevere. After the launch it reviews what it learned about customers and about its own process, the Learn and Adapt step, which feeds the next opportunity.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: A firm's teams are Agile, but funding, approvals and planning follow an annual project cycle, and launches still take years. Name the missing idea and two parts of the enterprise that must change.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Business Agility needs the whole system to change, not just the teams. Funding must move from projects to value streams, and governance and planning must work on a short cadence. Fast teams inside slow annual processes still deliver slowly.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Business Agility: competing and thriving in the digital age by responding quickly to market changes and emerging opportunities with digitally enabled business solutions. Every business is a software business. Five technological revolutions; today is the age of software and digital. BAVS: Sense Opportunity, Fund MVP, Organize Around Value, Connect to Customer, Deliver MVP, Pivot or Persevere, Deliver Value Continuously, Learn and Adapt.

lessons.title: 1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization
lessons.summary: The dual operating system, the seven core competencies, the configurations and the three measurement domains.

blocks.text:
Why do successful companies become slow? SAFe borrows the explanation from John Kotter. A company begins as an entrepreneurial network of people working directly for customers. As it grows it adds a hierarchy for efficiency and stability: departments, reporting lines, budgets, policies. The hierarchy is useful, but over time its needs crowd out the network, and the company loses the speed it started with.

SAFe does not ask a company to dismantle its hierarchy. It asks for a second operating system beside it: a network organised around value streams, which gives back speed and adaptability, while the hierarchy keeps providing efficiency and stability. In SAFe the network is made of development value streams, each containing one or more Agile Release Trains.
blocks.title: The dual operating system

blocks.text:
A Lean-Agile organisation is built on seven core competencies: Lean-Agile Leadership, Team and Technical Agility, Agile Product Delivery, Enterprise Solution Delivery, Lean Portfolio Management, Organizational Agility and Continuous Learning Culture. The current glossary renames two of them: Agile Product Delivery is now Product Development Flow, and Enterprise Solution Delivery is now Large Solution Integration and Delivery. Recognise both sets of names.

Progress is measured in three domains. Flow shows how efficiently value moves through the system. Outcomes show whether the solutions deliver business benefit. Competency shows how well the organisation practises what enables agility.
blocks.title: Seven core competencies and three measures

blocks.text: Dimensions are from the author's knowledge of SAFe 6; the competency names were checked.
rows: Mindset, values and principles; leading by example; leading change
Agile teams; teams of Agile teams; built-in quality
Product Development Flow (formerly Agile Product Delivery)
Customer centricity and design thinking; develop on cadence, release on demand; DevOps and the Continuous Delivery Pipeline
Large Solution Integration and Delivery (formerly Enterprise Solution Delivery)
Lean system and solution engineering; coordinating trains and suppliers; continually evolving live systems
Strategy and investment funding; Agile portfolio operations; Lean governance
Lean-thinking people and Agile teams; Lean business operations; strategy agility
Learning organization; innovation culture; relentless improvement
blocks.title: The seven core competencies and their dimensions

rows: The starting point: teams, ARTs, the core roles and events
One or more ARTs on one solution
Solution trains coordinating several ARTs and suppliers
Very big systems such as aircraft
Lean Portfolio Management, strategic themes, the portfolio backlog
Several value streams under one budget
blocks.title: Configurations

blocks.text:
Marrow Retail has 9,000 staff and a three-year queue for new digital products. A consultant proposes removing two layers of management. The chief executive instead keeps the hierarchy for pay, compliance and store operations, and forms a network beside it: one development value stream for online ordering, with two trains. Funding moves from 40 small projects to that value stream. The first MVP, kerbside pickup in ten stores, shows customers want one-hour slots, not same-day delivery, and the portfolio pivots.

The SAFe reading: the hierarchy stayed, the network was added, and evidence from an MVP steered the money.
blocks.title: Worked example: Marrow Retail

blocks.text: "Flatten the hierarchy" is the wrong answer: SAFe keeps it for efficiency and stability and adds a value stream network for speed. "Team SAFe" and "Enterprise SAFe" are not configurations. And the three measurement domains are outcomes, flow and competency; velocity and utilisation are not among them.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A train ships features fast, but customers stop using them. Which measurement domain needs attention? Outcomes: flow is healthy, but the solutions do not deliver the intended benefit.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

rows: The share of features, enablers, defects and risks in the work
How many items are completed in a period
How long items take from start to finish
How many items are in progress
Active time as a share of total time
blocks.title: The six flow metrics

blocks.text: Finance, HR and legal still work in annual cycles and large batches while the ARTs deliver every two weeks. The competency that addresses this is Organizational Agility, which extends Lean thinking and Agile teams into business functions. An enterprise that builds aircraft with several ARTs and suppliers, but needs no portfolio management yet, would choose Large Solution SAFe.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Match each to a competency: (a) a company wants people to keep learning and innovating; (b) stakeholders decide how funds are split across value streams; (c) teams build quality into every increment.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Continuous Learning Culture. (b) Lean Portfolio Management. (c) Team and Technical Agility.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Dual operating system: hierarchy for efficiency and stability, value stream network for speed. Seven core competencies, with Lean-Agile Leadership as the foundation; recognise both old and new names for two of them. Four configurations: Essential, Large Solution, Portfolio, Full. Three measurement domains: outcomes, flow, competency. Six flow metrics.

lessons.title: 2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values
lessons.summary: What the mindset combines, Lean thinking, the Agile Manifesto and the four Core Values.

blocks.text:
SAFe says agility is a change of mindset before it is a change of practice. The Lean-Agile mindset is the combination of beliefs, assumptions, attitudes and actions of leaders and practitioners who embrace two bodies of thought: Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto. It also needs a growth mindset, the belief that abilities can be developed, because people have to unlearn habits that once made them successful.

A company can run every event in the framework and still fail if its leaders think in the old way: fixed scope, fixed dates, maximum utilisation, decisions at the top.
blocks.title: The Lean-Agile mindset

rows: Value is defined by the customer, for a specific product
Identify the value stream for each product
See every step needed to deliver it
Build in response to demand, not to keep people busy
Keep improving; there is no finished state
blocks.title: Lean thinking in five ideas

blocks.text: The manifesto states four values. It values individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, and responding to change over following a plan. The items on the right still have value; the items on the left have more. Exam distractors often reverse a pair.
blocks.title: The Agile Manifesto

blocks.text: Paraphrased from the twelve principles of the Agile Manifesto.
rows: Early and continuous delivery of valuable software
Changing requirements are welcome, even late
From a couple of weeks to a couple of months
Business people and developers work together daily
Give them the environment and support, and trust them
The most efficient way to convey information
Sponsors, developers and users keep a constant pace indefinitely
The art of maximising the amount of work not done
At regular intervals the team reflects and tunes its behaviour
blocks.title: Manifesto principles the exam draws on

blocks.text: Earlier versions listed built-in quality and program execution. The current four are the ones above.
rows: Everyone works toward the same vision and objectives
Connecting strategy to backlogs and stating priorities clearly
Facts are visible, including bad news
Making it safe to report problems and sharing their own
People are valued, developed and trusted
Growing people and involving those who do the work in decisions
Giving time to improve and acting on what Inspect and Adapt finds
blocks.title: The four SAFe Core Values

blocks.text:
At Kestrel Foods every feature is reported green until release week. Two years ago a team lead who reported a delay was removed from the project. The trains have all the events, but the status board is fiction.

Which Core Value is missing? Transparency. Alignment may be fine: everyone may agree on the goal. Respect for people is damaged too, but the direct gap is that reality is not visible. The repair starts with leaders, who have to show that bad news is welcome, for example by reporting their own missed commitments first.
blocks.title: Worked example: Kestrel Foods

blocks.text:
Generic answer: 'The Scrum values are commitment, courage, focus, openness and respect.' True for Scrum. The SAFe Core Values are alignment, transparency, respect for people and relentless improvement.

Outdated answer: 'alignment, built-in quality, transparency, program execution.' That is the earlier set.

Wrong fix: 'Roll the practices out more strictly.' SAFe answer: practices without the mindset give mechanical agility. Change the thinking, starting with leaders.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: A team shows a running product to its customer every two weeks instead of sending specifications. Which Manifesto value is that? Working software over comprehensive documentation.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Respect for people starts from the idea that people do all the work. It covers employees, customers, suppliers and partners, with long-term, trust-based relationships rather than squeezing the next party in the chain. Relentless improvement means a constant sense of danger about complacency, regular reflection and structured problem solving, and it needs protected time, such as the Inspect and Adapt event and the IP iteration, because delivery pressure otherwise crowds it out. A growth mindset, the belief that abilities develop with effort and learning, underpins both.
blocks.title: Respect for people and relentless improvement

blocks.text: Name the Core Value: (a) leaders repeat the mission so every team sees how its work contributes; (b) a team reports a delay the day it becomes likely; (c) a supplier is treated as a partner, not a cost to squeeze; (d) a train runs a problem-solving workshop every PI.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Alignment. (b) Transparency. (c) Respect for people. (d) Relentless improvement.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: The mindset combines Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto, with a growth mindset. Lean thinking: specify value, identify the value stream, make value flow, let the customer pull, pursue perfection. Four Manifesto values; the right-hand items still have value. Core Values: alignment, transparency, respect for people, relentless improvement.

lessons.title: 2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5
lessons.summary: Each principle with its number, then the economic view, systems thinking, options, learning cycles and milestones.

blocks.text: SAFe rests on ten Lean-Agile principles, which it calls immutable and underlying. Practices can be adapted to context; the principles are what the adaptation must honour. The exam refers to principles by number and by name, so learn both.
blocks.title: Why the principles matter

rows: Decisions weigh cost, value and Cost of Delay inside an economic framework
Optimise the whole value stream, not one department
Keep design options open until evidence allows a choice
Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
Integrate often so that feedback arrives early
Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
Judge progress by a working system, not by documents
Limit work in process, shrink batches, shorten queues
Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
A shared rhythm and joint planning manage uncertainty
Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
Autonomy, mastery and purpose beat individual incentives
Decide locally what is frequent and time-critical
Structure people around value streams, not functions
blocks.title: The ten principles

blocks.text:
#1 Take an economic view. Deliver early and often, and understand the trade-offs between development expense, lead time, product cost, value and risk; changing one moves the others. Operate within Lean budgets and guardrails, and sequence work by Cost of Delay, which is the basis of WSJF.

#2 Apply systems thinking. The solution is a system, the enterprise building it is a system too, and the full value stream is what should be optimised. Speeding up one department can build queues elsewhere.

#3 Assume variability; preserve options. Set-based design keeps several design options open and narrows them as knowledge grows, instead of committing early to one point design.

#4 Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles. Short Plan, Do, Check, Adjust cycles end in integration points that give objective evidence and reduce risk; problems surface while they are cheap to fix.

#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems. Progress is judged by demonstrations of the integrated solution, such as the System Demo and the PI System Demo, not by signed-off documents or phase gates.
blocks.title: Principles 1 to 5 in more depth

blocks.text:
Principles 1 and 9 work together. Principle 9 says who decides; principle 1 gives them the economic framework to decide well. Without the framework, decentralised decisions are guesses.

Principles 3 and 5 are swapped most often. Link 3 with options, through set-based design, and 5 with milestones, through demonstrations of a working system.

Principles 4 and 7 both involve integration. Principle 4 is about learning from integrated increments. Principle 7 is about the rhythm that lets many teams plan and integrate at the same moment: cadence makes events predictable, and synchronisation brings perspectives together.

For principle 9, keep a decision central when it is infrequent, long-lasting and has significant economies of scale, such as a common technology platform. Decentralise everything else: decisions that are frequent, time-critical and need local information.
blocks.title: The pairs that are easy to confuse

blocks.text: A steering committee approves each phase when its documents are signed off, and the first integration of a new tariff engine is planned for month nine. Principle #5 would replace document sign-offs with demonstrations of the working system, and principle #4 would integrate every iteration so that learning starts in week two, not month nine.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Principles 3 and 5 are the pair most often swapped: 3 is options and set-based design, 5 is milestones and working systems. And principle 1 is not "minimise cost"; it is weighing all the economic trade-offs, including the cost of delay.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A team spends a month gathering data for a small, reversible decision that costs little either way. Which principle says to decide sooner? #1 Take an economic view: a month of delay costs more than a wrong first choice that can be undone.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Name the principle: (a) architects keep three messaging options open until load tests are run; (b) a test department optimises its own throughput while lead time grows; (c) the board asks for a demo of the integrated system instead of a design document.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) #3 Assume variability; preserve options. (b) #2 Apply systems thinking. (c) #5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Learn all ten names with their numbers. #1 economic trade-offs and Cost of Delay; #2 optimise the whole; #3 set-based design; #4 PDCA and integration points; #5 working systems as milestones. The principles are immutable; practices adapt to them.

lessons.title: 2.2b · Principles #6 to #10: flow, cadence, motivation, decisions and value
lessons.summary: Flow accelerators and Little's Law, cadence and synchronisation, intrinsic motivation, decentralisation and organising around value.

blocks.text: Principles 6 to 10 describe how work flows and how people are organised and led. #6 Make value flow without interruptions: limit work in process, shrink batches, shorten queues and remove the policies that cause delay. #7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning: a shared rhythm makes routine events predictable, and synchronisation lets many perspectives be resolved and integrated at the same time, with PI Planning as the main example. #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers: autonomy, mastery and purpose, as Daniel Pink describes, matter more than individual incentives. #9 Decentralize decision-making. #10 Organize around value.
blocks.title: Understand

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge of SAFe 6; the public principle #6 article shows only its introduction.
rows: A Kanban board with a WIP limit on each column
Add capacity or cross-train where work piles up
Release a feature in small slices
Keep the backlog short enough to act on
Protect long stretches of focused work
Replace a monthly change board for low-risk fixes
blocks.title: The eight flow accelerators

blocks.text: Little's Law says that average wait time equals the length of the queue divided by the rate at which it is processed. If a team finishes five items a week and forty are waiting, a new item waits about eight weeks. A longer queue at the same rate means a proportionally longer wait, which is why reducing queue length, not working harder, shortens lead time.
blocks.title: Little's Law and queues

blocks.text: A train has thirty features in progress and finishes two per PI, and every design change waits a week for one architecture manager. Principle #6 says limit WIP and finish before starting. Principle #9 says the architecture manager should define a decision framework and let teams decide inside it, because design changes are frequent, time-critical and need local knowledge.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Keeping everyone fully busy is not flow; high utilisation lengthens queues. A bonus for the developer who closes the most stories breaks principle #8. And centralising a frequent, local decision "for quality" breaks principle #9: keep central only what is infrequent, long-lasting and has significant economies of scale.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which decision belongs at the centre: choosing a common technology platform for all trains, or how a team sequences the stories in its iteration? The platform choice: it is infrequent, long-lasting and has economies of scale.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Analysts, developers and testers sit in separate departments, and each feature crosses five handoffs. Principle #10 says organise around value: form cross-functional teams and trains around the flow of value to customers, and reorganise when that flow changes. Spreading new work across departments recreates the handoffs.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Name the accelerator: (a) developers are interrupted all day; (b) a shared database team has a three-week queue; (c) every small fix waits for a monthly approval board.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Optimize time 'in the zone'. (b) Address bottlenecks. (c) Remediate legacy policies and practices.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: #6 flow: eight accelerators, Little's Law. #7 cadence for predictability, synchronisation for integration; PI Planning is cross-domain planning. #8 autonomy, mastery, purpose; avoid individual incentives. #9 centralise decisions that are infrequent, long-lasting and with economies of scale, decentralise the rest. #10 organise around value, not functions.

lessons.title: 2.3 · Empowering agility with AI
lessons.summary: Where AI fits in SAFe, how roles use it, and the human-in-the-loop rule.

blocks.text:
SAFe's public guidance describes AI as a wide range of smart machines performing tasks that normally need human intelligence, and says it can be applied at all levels of SAFe: to build intelligent customer solutions, to automate value stream activities and to improve customer insight. It contrasts AI with conventional rule-based software for situations that predefined rules cannot cover.

The Leading SAFe course page lists three AI points for an Agilist: AI fundamentals and prompting for the role's duties, the SAFe CoPilot assistant, and human-in-the-loop evaluation of AI output. The practical rule is simple. Give the assistant the source material, the audience and the format you need, and have a person check the output before it informs a decision.
blocks.title: Empower agility with AI

rows: Drafting acceptance criteria and story splits
Refining them with the team and accepting stories
Finding patterns in thousands of reviews and tickets
Turning them into hypotheses to test with customers
Clustering anonymous retrospective comments into themes
The team's discussion and its decisions
Analysing flow metrics across the train
Judging the advice against principles and evidence
blocks.title: AI across the roles

blocks.text: AI helps a team write code twice as fast, but stories now wait longer in testing. Systems thinking, principle #2, says the bottleneck has moved: improve the whole flow, for example by using AI to help with testing too, rather than generating code even faster. The right measure of whether AI helped is shorter flow time, not tokens used or tools licensed.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: The principles still apply to AI-enabled work, and they guide where AI helps. Options that let AI deploy without checks, remove code review because "AI wrote it", or adopt AI-drafted PI objectives wholesale are wrong: teams must own their objectives and code.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What does human-in-the-loop mean? A person evaluates AI output before it informs a decision or an action.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Confidential company data goes only into tools approved for it. AI summaries are checked against the source before they inform decisions. Generated code must be understandable and maintainable by the team, because passing tests is not enough for built-in quality. Start adoption with small, measured experiments that show where AI improves the flow of value, and share what works.
blocks.title: Responsible use on a train

blocks.text: A Product Manager analyses customer reviews with AI and finds that delivery tracking is the top complaint. Rather than treating that as a final feature list, the train writes a benefit hypothesis for better tracking, builds a minimum marketable feature and measures its effect.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: An AI assistant drafts PI objectives for every team before PI Planning. What is the risk, and what is a better use?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Teams would commit to objectives they did not create or believe in, which weakens the commitment. A better use is to let AI prepare inputs, such as summaries of the features and their dependencies, while teams write their own objectives.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: AI can be applied at all levels of SAFe: intelligent customer solutions, automating value stream activities and improving customer insight. AI suits problems that predefined rules cannot cover. Human-in-the-loop. Approved tools for confidential data. Measure AI's impact with flow and outcomes.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams
lessons.summary: What an Agile Team is, its two roles, SAFe Scrum and Team Kanban, and the team events.

blocks.text:
Team and Technical Agility has three dimensions: Agile Teams, Teams of Agile Teams, and Built-In Quality.

An Agile Team is a cross-functional group of typically ten or fewer people with all the skills needed to define, build, test and deliver value. It can be a technical team or a business team. Teams use SAFe Scrum, SAFe Team Kanban or a hybrid. Each team has two specific roles. The Product Owner maximises the value the team delivers by keeping the team backlog aligned with customer and stakeholder needs, and decides its order. The Scrum Master/Team Coach is a servant leader and coach who facilitates team events and helps the team improve; this person is usually not a people manager and does not assign tasks.
blocks.title: Agile Teams

rows: Agree iteration goals and the stories to work on
Show what the team completed and get feedback
blocks.title: Team events

blocks.text: A new team expects its Scrum Master/Team Coach to hand out tasks and chase individuals for status. In SAFe the coach is a servant leader who facilitates events, helps the team improve flow and removes impediments; the team organises its own work, and the Product Owner orders the backlog and accepts stories.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: The Scrum Master/Team Coach does not assign tasks or prioritise the backlog, and a development manager does not order the team backlog. Iteration goals are a short summary of what the team aims to achieve, not task lists or velocity targets.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A team's work is mostly unpredictable, interrupt-driven maintenance. Which way of working suits it? SAFe Team Kanban, which pulls work continuously within WIP limits while still planning with the train.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A cross-functional team has the skills to define, build and test an increment itself, so work does not queue between departments. People split across several teams lose time switching and make each team wait for them, so SAFe prefers dedicated, stable members. When the Product Owner is absent for weeks, stories stall or drift, because nobody is answering the questions that arise as they are built.
blocks.title: Why cross-functional and dedicated

blocks.text: Assign each responsibility to the Product Owner or the Scrum Master/Team Coach: (a) accepting stories; (b) facilitating the retrospective; (c) ordering the team backlog; (d) helping remove an impediment.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) and (c) Product Owner. (b) and (d) Scrum Master/Team Coach.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Agile Team: cross-functional, ten or fewer, defines, builds, tests and delivers. Two roles: Product Owner and Scrum Master/Team Coach. SAFe Scrum or SAFe Team Kanban. Team events: planning, sync, refinement, review, retrospective. Iteration goals summarise intent.

lessons.title: 3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains
lessons.summary: The ART, its roles, team topologies and why trains are long-lived and capped in size.

blocks.text: An Agile Release Train, or ART, is a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers and often operates one or more solutions in a development value stream. It typically has 50 to 125 people. It is not a project: it is not formed for one release and disbanded afterwards.
blocks.title: The Agile Release Train

blocks.text: The System Team supports the train by building the development environment and helping with integration.
rows: Servant leader and coach for the train; facilitates ART events
Defines features, owns and prioritises the ART backlog
Defines the architecture, identifies nonfunctional requirements, designs interfaces
Key stakeholders responsible for governance, fitness for use and return on investment
blocks.title: Roles on the train

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge; the ART article shows only its introduction.
rows: Delivers a continuous flow of value in one area
Owns a part that needs deep specialist knowledge
Provides self-service services to other teams
Helps other teams build new capabilities
blocks.title: Four team topologies

blocks.text: A train has a front-end team, a back-end team and a database team, and every feature needs all three. SAFe favours stream-aligned teams that can work end to end, with a platform or complicated subsystem team only where the work truly needs it. A single thirty-person team would be too large to work as one.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: An ART is long-lived; it is not formed for one release and disbanded. The RTE is the chief Scrum Master for the train, not the person who prioritises features. Business Owners hold primary responsibility for governance, compliance and return on investment.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Two teams wait every iteration for an environment team. What reduces the dependency? A platform team that offers environments as self-service.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: An ART typically has 50 to 125 people in around five to twelve teams. SAFe cites Dunbar's number: beyond about 150 people, personal relationships and trust are hard to keep, and a team of teams depends on them. A development value stream larger than one train is split into several ARTs.
blocks.title: Size and trust

blocks.text: Choose the topology: (a) shared build tools every team uses; (b) coaching teams new to BDD; (c) a payments engine needing rare cryptography skills.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Platform. (b) Enabling. (c) Complicated subsystem.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: ART: 50 to 125 people, long-lived, in a development value stream. RTE, Product Management, System Architect, Business Owners, System Team. Four topologies: stream-aligned, complicated subsystem, platform, enabling. Dunbar's number limits train size.

lessons.title: 3.3 · Built-in Quality practices
lessons.summary: Why quality is built in, the basic practices for every team, and why it makes delivery faster.

blocks.text: Built-In Quality is a set of practices that help the outputs of Agile teams meet quality standards throughout the creation of customer value. Quality is built in at every step; it is not inspected in by a test phase at the end. SAFe ties this to principle 6 and to shifting learning left, so problems are found when they are cheap to fix. The listed benefits include higher customer satisfaction, better velocity and delivery predictability, and better system performance. Cutting quality to go faster therefore makes a train slower.
blocks.title: Built-in quality

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge of SAFe 6; the built-in quality article shows only its introduction.
rows: Moves testing, review and feedback earlier, where fixes are cheap
Catches problems early and spreads knowledge
Several people can change any part, so nobody is a bottleneck
Artifact standards and definition of done
A shared standard for when work is finished
Removes manual steps from the path to production
blocks.title: Basic built-in quality practices for all teams

blocks.text: A team finds most defects in the last week before release, and its manager proposes a hardening iteration. SAFe's concern is that this treats quality as a phase. The fix is to shift learning left with test-first practices, peer review and a definition of done, so each increment is releasable as it is built.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Dropping automated tests to finish more stories makes a train slower, because rework and unpredictability grow. Built-in quality applies to business teams too, through practices that suit their work, not just to software teams.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Only one developer understands a critical module. Which practice addresses this? Collective ownership with T-shaped skills, often built through pairing.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: For software, built-in quality includes test-first development such as TDD and BDD, continuous integration and automated tests, alongside the basic practices. Code generated by AI is held to the same standard: the team must understand and be able to change it. For business teams, such as marketing, the same ideas appear as standards, peer review and checks suited to the work.
blocks.title: Quality for software and beyond

blocks.text: Name the practice: (a) a checklist that every story must meet before it counts as done; (b) a script that builds, tests and deploys every commit; (c) two people writing code together.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Artifact standards and definition of done. (b) Workflow automation. (c) Pairing.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Quality is built in at every step, not inspected in at the end. Five basic practices: shift learning left, pairing and peer review, collective ownership and T-shaped skills, artifact standards and definition of done, workflow automation. Built-in quality speeds delivery by cutting rework.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps
lessons.summary: The four aspects of the pipeline, separating deployment from release, and CALMR.

blocks.text: Deployment and release are separate: functionality can sit in production, hidden, until the business releases it.
rows: Explore the market and customer needs; define vision, roadmap and features
Make it available when the business chooses
Release in one event or in waves, by market need
blocks.title: The Continuous Delivery Pipeline

blocks.text: DevOps in SAFe is a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that support the integration, automation and collaboration needed to develop and operate a solution. It is not a team and not a toolset. SAFe's approach is CALMR: Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement and Recovery. The general industry acronym is CALMS, ending in sharing; SAFe treats sharing as part of culture and adds recovery.
blocks.title: DevOps and CALMR

blocks.text:
Halden Freight's tracking train deploys a new route-pricing feature to production on Tuesday behind a feature switch. Customers see nothing. Product Management and the Business Owners decide to release it to ten large customers on the first of the month, when the new contracts start, and to everyone a month later.

Deployment was a technical event on Tuesday. Release was a business decision on a different date, in waves. The developers did not decide the release date, and neither did the RTE.
blocks.title: Worked example: Halden Freight

blocks.text: A separate DevOps team between development and operations recreates the handoff DevOps removes. Release is a business decision; developers and the RTE do not set the release date. And CALMR ends in Recovery, not in Sharing as the industry acronym CALMS does.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Code is merged, built and tested in staging several times a day. Which aspect is that? Continuous Integration. Moving it to production is Continuous Deployment.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Progressive releases, such as canary releases to a small group first, expose a change to a few users, watch the results and widen or roll back. Recovery means designing for quick restoration, for example automated rollback or fixing forward. Lead time from idea to value in production, with quality and recovery measures, shows whether the pipeline is improving.
blocks.title: Lowering release risk

blocks.text: Place each activity in an aspect: (a) researching the market and defining features; (b) verifying a change in production behind a toggle; (c) turning the feature on for ten customers.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Continuous Exploration. (b) Continuous Deployment. (c) Release on Demand.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Four aspects in order: Continuous Exploration, Continuous Integration, Continuous Deployment, Release on Demand. Deployment and release are separate. DevOps is a mindset, culture and set of practices. CALMR: Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement, Recovery.

lessons.title: 4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking
lessons.summary: Building the right thing: customers, the design thinking tools, and desirable, viable, feasible, sustainable.

blocks.text:
Customer Centricity is a mindset focused on creating positive customer experiences through the full set of products and services an enterprise offers. SAFe recognises internal customers, people inside the company who use what a train builds, and external customers, who buy or use the products. A platform train has customers too.

Design thinking is a customer-centric development process for creating desirable products that are profitable and sustainable over their life. Where a waterfall approach starts from requirements, design thinking starts from understanding the problem and the context of use. It alternates divergent thinking, which widens the set of possibilities, with convergent thinking, which narrows it to a choice. Its tools include personas, which are representative characterisations of users, and story maps.

Product Management is responsible for solutions that are desirable, viable, feasible and sustainable.
blocks.title: Customer centricity and design thinking

rows: A fictional but realistic user, to keep real needs in view
What a user says, thinks, does and feels
Each step of the customer's experience, with feelings and pain points
User activities in order, with stories beneath, sliced into releases
A cheap model to test a design with users before building
blocks.title: Design thinking tools

rows: Do customers want it, and will they use it?
Will it create enough value for the business?
Can we build it with our technology and skills?
Can we support and evolve it over its life?
blocks.title: Four qualities of a good solution

blocks.text: A team building a hospital supply app watches nurses order supplies during a real shift and finds they order on a phone with gloves on. A persona, "a night-shift nurse who orders supplies on a phone", keeps that need in view. A clickable prototype tested with five nurses shows that the order button is too small, and the design changes before any code is written.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Design thinking starts from understanding the problem, not from a signed-off specification. Internal teams have customers too. And customer insight from AI analysis or surveys is a source of hypotheses, not a substitute for testing with real users.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: What does SAFe's Lean UX approach start with? A benefit hypothesis, then collaborative design, a minimum marketable feature and evaluation against the hypothesis.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Customer-centric teams go where the work happens, the gemba, rather than relying on second-hand reports. They segment the market and learn each segment's needs, think in terms of customer lifetime value rather than a single sale, and validate assumptions before investing, because even an experienced Product Manager's view of customers is a hypothesis until tested.
blocks.title: Customer-centric habits

blocks.text: Name the tool: (a) a one-page profile of 'Dana, who orders supplies at night'; (b) a diagram of every step of a policy renewal, with frustrations marked; (c) what a user says, thinks, does and feels.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) A persona. (b) A customer journey map. (c) An empathy map.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Customer centricity is a mindset focused on positive customer experiences. Design thinking: understand the problem, then design the right solution, diverging and converging. Tools: persona, empathy map, journey map, story map, prototype. Desirable, viable, feasible, sustainable. Lean UX starts with a benefit hypothesis.

lessons.title: 4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog
lessons.summary: Features, enablers and capabilities, benefit hypotheses, WSJF and capacity allocation.

blocks.text:
The ART backlog holds the features and enablers that enhance the solution and extend its architectural runway, and it is managed as a Kanban system. A feature is solution functionality that delivers business value and is sized to be delivered by one ART within one PI. Product Management defines features and prioritises the backlog. The System Architect defines enablers. Teams split features into stories for their own team backlogs, which the Product Owners own.

Nonfunctional requirements, such as security and performance, are system qualities that constrain the design across the backlogs. Capacity allocation reserves a share of capacity for each type of work, so enablers and maintenance are not always outranked by features.
blocks.title: The ART backlog

rows: Research, prototypes and spikes to build knowledge
Large solution behaviour spanning several ARTs
Split into features for each train
blocks.title: Enablers and capabilities

blocks.text:
Weighted Shortest Job First sequences jobs to produce the best economic outcome. WSJF equals Cost of Delay divided by job duration, and job size is used as a proxy for duration.

Cost of Delay has three components: user-business value, time criticality, and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. All values are relative: jobs are compared with each other, usually with a modified Fibonacci scale, not priced in money. WSJF ignores sunk costs; only the remaining work counts. The job with the highest WSJF goes first.
blocks.title: Prioritising with WSJF

blocks.text: Refund status goes first. Loyalty tiers has the highest Cost of Delay but is so large that it scores lowest.
blocks.title: Worked example: a WSJF table at Verano Travel

blocks.text:
Wrong role: 'The RTE prioritises the ART backlog.' SAFe answer: Product Management does; the RTE facilitates.

Wrong level: 'A feature needs a Lean business case and an MVP.' Those belong to epics. A feature has a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria.

Generic answer: 'Finish what we have spent the most on' or 'do the most valuable first.' SAFe answer: WSJF ignores sunk cost and divides value by size, so a small, urgent job beats a large, valuable one.
blocks.title: SAFe answer versus generic answer

blocks.text: Two features have equal Cost of Delay, but one is half the size. Which goes first? The smaller one, because WSJF divides Cost of Delay by job size.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: A feature has a short name, a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria. The benefit hypothesis states the measurable outcome expected, for example "we believe one-click reorder will lift repeat orders by 10%", so it can be tested after release. Acceptance criteria are observable and testable, such as "location updates appear within two minutes". A feature too large for one PI is split into smaller valuable slices. Cost of Delay is estimated by Product Management with Business Owners; teams help with job size. The ranking is refreshed before each PI Planning, because Cost of Delay and size change over time.
blocks.title: Features that can be tested

blocks.text: Which Cost of Delay component is highest: a regulatory change that brings fines if missed in three months? And what is 'job size' in WSJF?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Time criticality. Job size is the denominator, a proxy for duration; it is not part of Cost of Delay.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: ART backlog: features and enablers, owned by Product Management. Four enabler types: exploration, architectural, infrastructure, compliance. Feature: benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria, fits one PI. WSJF = Cost of Delay / job size; Cost of Delay = user-business value + time criticality + risk reduction or opportunity enablement; relative, modified Fibonacci; ignore sunk cost. Capacity allocation protects enablers and maintenance.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: Lab · WSJF and backlog decisions
lessons.summary: Five scored exercises in Weighted Shortest Job First and capacity allocation.

blocks.text: Work each exercise on paper before reading the solution. WSJF questions in the exam usually give the scores and ask for the order, or test one rule: relative estimates, sunk cost, job size as a proxy for duration, or what Cost of Delay is made of.
blocks.title: How to use this lab

blocks.text: Calculate Cost of Delay and WSJF for each feature and rank them.
blocks.title: Exercise 1

blocks.text: Cost of Delay: Ash 16, Birch 13, Cedar 21, Dune 8. WSJF: Ash 2.0, Birch 6.5, Cedar about 1.6, Dune 8.0. Order: Dune, Birch, Ash, Cedar. Cedar has the highest Cost of Delay but is the largest job, so it goes last.
blocks.title: Solution 1

blocks.text: A stakeholder says feature Elm must be finished first because two PIs of effort have already gone into it. Its remaining WSJF is 1.2; another feature scores 3.0. What does WSJF say?
blocks.title: Exercise 2

blocks.text: Do the feature scoring 3.0 first. WSJF ignores sunk cost: only the remaining work and its Cost of Delay count.
blocks.title: Solution 2

blocks.text: Finance asks for each feature's Cost of Delay in dollars before ranking. What does SAFe suggest?
blocks.title: Exercise 3

blocks.text: Estimate relatively, comparing the features with each other on a modified Fibonacci scale with the smallest set to 1. Relative estimates are fast and good enough for sequencing.
blocks.title: Solution 3

blocks.text: Enablers keep losing to features in WSJF, and technical debt grows each PI. What fixes this?
blocks.title: Exercise 4

blocks.text: Capacity allocation: reserve a share of each PI for enablers and maintenance, for example 20% and 10%, then rank within each share. Flow distribution later shows whether the split held.
blocks.title: Solution 4

blocks.text: A feature cannot fit in one PI. Product Management wants to plan it across three PIs. What is the better move?
blocks.title: Exercise 5

blocks.text: Split it into smaller features that each deliver value and can be delivered, demonstrated and measured within a PI, then rank the pieces.
blocks.title: Solution 5

blocks.text: Highest value is not highest priority. Divide by size, ignore what has been spent, compare relatively, and protect enablers with capacity allocation.

lessons.title: 4.3 · Participating in PI Planning
lessons.summary: Readiness, the two-day agenda, PI objectives and business value, ROAM and the confidence vote.

blocks.text:
PI Planning is a cadence-based event for the whole train that aligns teams and stakeholders to a shared mission and vision. It is typically a two-day event, facilitated by the Release Train Engineer, and everyone who does the work takes part.

Before the event the train prepares three kinds of readiness: organizational, content and logistics. The two primary outputs are committed PI objectives from each team and the ART planning board, which shows feature delivery dates and the dependencies between teams.

PI objectives summarise the business and technical goals a team intends to achieve. Each is committed or uncommitted. Uncommitted objectives cover planned work with significant uncertainty; they are left out of the commitment so that the commitment stays reliable.
blocks.title: PI Planning

blocks.text: This agenda is from author knowledge of SAFe 6; the public article shows only its introduction.
rows: Business context, product vision, architecture vision and planning context
Business Owner or executive, Product Management, System Architect, RTE
Team breakouts: draft plans, capacity, risks and dependencies
Draft plan review, then management review and problem-solving
RTE; managers adjust scope or resources
Planning adjustments, then team breakouts; Business Owners assign business value
Final plan review, ART risks, confidence vote, plan rework if needed, retrospective
blocks.title: How the two days usually run

blocks.text:
Risks that affect the train are discussed in front of everyone and placed in one of four categories, known as ROAM. Resolved: no longer a concern. Owned: someone takes responsibility for it after the event. Accepted: nothing more can be done, and the risk is understood. Mitigated: a plan exists to reduce its impact.

Each team, and then the whole train, holds a confidence vote, usually by showing one to five fingers. A low vote means the plan is not yet a commitment, and it is reworked. Business Owners assign business value from 1 to 10 to each team's objectives; that value is later compared with what was achieved.
blocks.title: Risks and the confidence vote

blocks.text: At Odell Health's PI Planning, the scheduling team depends on an interface a vendor may deliver late. The team writes that objective as uncommitted. At the end of day one the draft plans exceed capacity by a third, so the management review removes two features. On day two a risk about a data centre move cannot be settled; the infrastructure director takes it, so it is Owned. One team votes two fingers. The RTE does not close the event: the team explains its concern, a dependency is moved, and the second vote is four.
blocks.title: Worked example: Odell Health

blocks.text: Product Owners do not assign business value; Business Owners do, from 1 to 10. Product Management does not facilitate; the RTE does. Only team leads attending is wrong: the whole train plans together. And a lone low vote is heard, not overridden.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A team will build a fallback that reduces a risk's impact if it happens. How is the risk ROAMed? Mitigated. If a director took responsibility for it after the event, it would be Owned.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: In team breakouts each team estimates its capacity, plans features into iterations, drafts PI objectives and identifies risks and dependencies; its Scrum Master/Team Coach facilitates. Dependencies between teams go on the ART planning board for everyone to see. The System Architect presents the architecture vision and advises teams. Content readiness means the vision and the top features, with acceptance criteria, are ready. When draft plans exceed capacity, the management review adjusts scope rather than forcing more in. Distributed trains plan together online with the same agenda.
blocks.title: During the event

blocks.text: Put these day-2 items in order: confidence vote, planning adjustments, final plan review, planning retrospective, team breakouts.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Planning adjustments, team breakouts, final plan review, confidence vote, planning retrospective. ART risks are ROAMed after the final plan review and before the vote.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Two days, the whole train, facilitated by the RTE. Readiness: organizational, content, logistics. Outputs: committed PI objectives and the ART planning board. Committed and uncommitted objectives. Business value 1 to 10 from Business Owners. ROAM: Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated. Fist-of-five confidence vote; rework if low.

lessons.summary: Practice placing risks, writing objectives and handling a low vote.

blocks.text: For each item, decide before reading the answer. These are the situations the exam turns into scenario questions.
blocks.title: How to use this lab

blocks.text: Fill the second column, then check below.
rows: A vendor API may arrive late; the vendor manager will chase it weekly
The test lab was double-booked; it was rebooked during the event
A key specialist may leave; nothing more can be done this PI
A data migration may fail; the team will rehearse it twice and keep a rollback
blocks.title: Exercise 1: ROAM these risks

blocks.text: Owned (someone takes responsibility after the event), Resolved (no longer a concern), Accepted (understood, nothing more to do), Mitigated (a plan reduces its impact).
blocks.title: Solution 1

blocks.text: A team will deliver the new booking screen, and it would also like to integrate a partner's loyalty API, which depends on the partner's unconfirmed release date. How should it write these?
blocks.title: Exercise 2: committed or uncommitted?

blocks.text: The booking screen is a committed objective. The loyalty integration is uncommitted: it is planned and counts toward capacity and business value, but it is not part of the commitment, so the uncertainty does not damage predictability.
blocks.title: Solution 2

blocks.text: Who scores the objectives, on what scale, and what happens to the scores at the end of the PI?
blocks.title: Exercise 3: business value

blocks.text: Business Owners score each objective from 1 to 10 during PI Planning. At the end of the PI they score the value actually achieved, and the ART predictability measure compares the two; 80 to 100 percent is considered predictable.
blocks.title: Solution 3

blocks.text: The train's average vote is three fingers, but one team votes two and a single engineer in another team votes one. What happens?
blocks.title: Exercise 4: a low vote

blocks.text: The low votes are heard. The team and the engineer explain their concerns, and the plan is reworked until people can commit. Overriding a lone voice wastes the purpose of the vote.
blocks.title: Solution 4

blocks.text: The people who do the work make and own the plan. Business Owners score value, the RTE facilitates, teams commit, and uncertainty is written down, not hidden.
blocks.title: Pattern to remember

lessons.title: 4.4 · Executing the PI
lessons.summary: The PI cadence, ART sync, System Demo, the IP iteration and Inspect and Adapt with its problem-solving workshop.

blocks.text: A Planning Interval, or PI, is a cadence-based timebox in which a train delivers continuous value aligned with its PI objectives. It typically lasts 8 to 12 weeks, most often as four or five development iterations followed by one Innovation and Planning iteration. SAFe plans on this cadence but releases on demand: the PI is a planning rhythm, not a release schedule.
blocks.title: The Planning Interval

rows: Visibility into progress toward PI objectives, with scope adjustments
Combines the PO Sync and the Coach Sync
Integrated view of new features from all teams
Demonstrate, measure, and solve systemic problems
blocks.title: Events while the PI runs

blocks.text:
The Innovation and Planning iteration gives an estimating buffer for meeting PI objectives and dedicated time for innovation, continuing education, PI Planning and Inspect and Adapt. No feature work is planned into it. It is not a hardening or bug-fixing iteration.

Inspect and Adapt has three parts, in this order: the PI System Demo, a quantitative and qualitative measurement review, and a retrospective and problem-solving workshop. The workshop looks for root causes of systemic problems, and the improvement items it produces go into the ART backlog for the next PI Planning. The ART Predictability Measure compares the business value achieved with the business value planned.
blocks.title: The IP iteration and Inspect and Adapt

blocks.text: Steps from the author's knowledge of SAFe 6; the public I&A article shows only its introduction.
rows: 1 Agree on the problem to solve
A clear statement of what, where, when and impact
They go into the ART backlog for PI Planning
blocks.title: The problem-solving workshop

blocks.text: Mid-PI, a team finds a dependency that will delay another team. It raises it in the coach sync, where Scrum Masters/Team Coaches and the RTE address impediments and dependencies across the train; the PO sync handles any scope changes. Waiting for the next PI Planning would let the delay land.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: The IP iteration is not for finishing slipped features or hardening. The System Demo shows the integrated work of the whole train each iteration, not each team's stories separately. And the PI is a planning cadence: releases happen on demand.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which two meetings make up the ART sync? The coach sync and the PO sync.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The ART predictability measure compares the business value achieved with the value planned; 80 to 100 percent is considered predictable. In the quantitative and qualitative part of Inspect and Adapt the train reviews this and other metrics, such as flow, to choose what to work on in the problem-solving workshop. Teams that finish their committed objectives early pull uncommitted work or other backlog items.
blocks.title: Measuring the PI

blocks.text: A train meets its PI objectives, but customers see nothing new until a year-end release. What should it improve, and which aspect of the pipeline is that?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Its ability to release on demand: develop on cadence, release when the business and customers need it. That is the Release on Demand aspect.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: PI: 8 to 12 weeks, often four or five iterations plus the IP iteration. ART sync = coach sync + PO sync. System Demo every iteration, often run by Product Management with the System Team's help. IP iteration: innovation, planning, I&A, learning, estimating buffer, no features. I&A: PI System Demo, measurement review, retrospective and problem-solving workshop.

lessons.title: 5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio
lessons.summary: What a portfolio is, operational and development value streams, the LPM function and the portfolio canvas.

blocks.text:
Lean Portfolio Management, or LPM, aligns strategy and execution by applying Lean and systems thinking to three areas: strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations, and Lean governance.

A SAFe portfolio is a set of value streams that deliver solutions within common funding and governance. It is not a list of projects. The Enterprise is the business entity the portfolio belongs to; a small enterprise may have one portfolio and a large one several.
blocks.title: What Lean Portfolio Management is

blocks.text: Development value streams build the solutions that operational value streams use. Each development value stream has one or more ARTs.
rows: The activities that deliver a product or service to a customer
Taking a mortgage from application to payout
The activities that turn a business hypothesis into a digitally enabled solution
The trains that build the mortgage systems
blocks.title: Two kinds of value stream

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge of SAFe 6.
rows: A claim from report to payment
A product from order to delivery
blocks.title: Types of operational value stream

rows: Highest decision-making and financial accountability; approves epics
Coordinates an epic through the portfolio Kanban
Sets the portfolio's technology vision, strategy and roadmap
Supports LPM with governance and operations
Carry business responsibility on the trains
blocks.title: Roles at the portfolio level

blocks.text: A bank maps its loan operational value stream, from application to payout, and lists the systems each step uses. Systems that change together become candidate development value streams, each with one or more ARTs. Starting from departments or projects would recreate the silos SAFe tries to remove.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: A portfolio is not a list of projects; it is a set of development value streams under common funding and governance. Operational value streams serve customers; development value streams build the systems they use. Distractors swap them.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: An enterprise has three business units, each with its own strategy, budget and customers. How many portfolios might it have? Three, one per unit.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The portfolio canvas adapts the Business Model Canvas to describe a portfolio on one page: its value streams and solutions, customer segments, channels, customer relationships, value propositions, key partners, activities and resources, budget, cost structure, revenue and key metrics. LPM is carried out by business executives, Enterprise Architects and the Agile PMO or Value Management Office, which supports it with metrics, budgeting and governance. Shared services used by every train are usually organised as platform teams or shared services.
blocks.title: The portfolio canvas

blocks.text: Classify each operational value stream: (a) an insurer's claim from report to payment; (b) internal procurement; (c) an app customers subscribe to.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Fulfillment. (b) Supporting. (c) Software product.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: LPM: strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations, Lean governance. Portfolio: value streams with common funding and governance. Enterprise: the business entity that owns one or more portfolios. Operational versus development value streams. Portfolio canvas from the Business Model Canvas. VMO.

lessons.title: 5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy
lessons.summary: Enterprise strategy, Strategic Themes as OKRs, SWOT and TOWS, and how themes reach the trains.

blocks.text:
The enterprise strategy answers four questions: which customers and markets are served, which products and solutions are provided, what unique value and resources the enterprise brings, and how these will be extended in future.

Strategic Themes carry that strategy into the portfolio. They are portfolio-level business objectives that provide competitive differentiation and business context for decisions. SAFe recommends writing them as Objectives and Key Results, in plain business language. Portfolio leaders use them to steer, and trains refer to them when defining epics and features. An epic with no link to a theme should prompt a hard question.
blocks.title: Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy

rows: Strategic themes and a portfolio budget
Mission and vision, business drivers, distinctive competence, financial goals, competitive environment
Portfolio context, such as performance and solution status
blocks.title: Between enterprise and portfolio

blocks.text:
Quarry Insurance has one portfolio for personal lines. Its enterprise strategy is to grow among drivers under thirty. LPM writes a Strategic Theme as an objective, 'Become the easiest insurer for young drivers to join', with key results on quote completion rate and time to first policy.

An Epic Owner proposes rebuilding the agent commission system. It may be worthwhile, but it serves no theme, so Portfolio Leadership asks which objective it supports before spending analysis effort. A second epic, a five-minute mobile quote, maps directly to the theme and moves forward.
blocks.title: Worked example: Quarry Insurance

blocks.text: Key results measure outcomes, not outputs: "cut claim time from 12 days to 5" is an outcome; "launch the portal in March" is an output. Strategic themes are not just for executives: they shape the vision, backlogs and PI objectives of trains.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: In a SWOT analysis, which factors are internal? Strengths and weaknesses. Opportunities and threats come from the environment.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: After a SWOT analysis, a TOWS matrix pairs internal and external factors into strategic options. SO strategies use strengths to seize opportunities, ST strategies use strengths to counter threats, WO strategies overcome weaknesses to take opportunities, and WT strategies minimise weaknesses and avoid threats. Strategy is formulated continuously and collaboratively, with portfolio stakeholders, because markets change faster than an annual cycle.
blocks.title: From analysis to options

blocks.text: At a Strategic Portfolio Review, leaders find that one value stream no longer serves any strategic theme. They may move its funding to higher-priority areas or plan its retirement. A team whose PI objectives relate to no theme checks whether the work is still the right priority; it does not rewrite the themes to fit its work.
blocks.title: Worked case

blocks.text: Write one key result for the objective "Delight our mobile customers".
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: For example: "Raise the app store rating from 3.6 to 4.4 by Q3." It is measurable, time-bound and an outcome for customers.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Strategic Themes: portfolio-level business objectives, written as OKRs. Enterprise passes themes and a budget; the portfolio returns its context. SWOT then TOWS. Themes give business context for decentralised decisions and shape epics, budgets and PI objectives.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow
lessons.summary: The portfolio vision and canvas, epics and their hypotheses, the portfolio Kanban and its WIP limits.

blocks.text:
The Portfolio Vision describes the future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions. It should be aspirational yet realistic, and motivating. It is a key input for identifying epics, and Business Owners or senior leaders typically present it at PI Planning.

The portfolio canvas, adapted from the Business Model Canvas, captures on one page the portfolio's development value streams, solutions, customers, revenue streams and other key elements. A canvas of the current state and a canvas of the future state show the gap, and epics are how the gap is closed. To generate options for the future state, SAFe uses a SWOT analysis followed by a TOWS analysis, which combines strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats into strategic options.
blocks.title: Vision and canvas

blocks.text:
An epic is a significant solution development initiative. SAFe is explicit that an epic is not a project. Business epics deliver value directly to customers; enabler epics extend the architectural runway for future business or technical needs.

Because of its size, every epic needs a Lean business case and a minimum viable product, and it must be approved by Portfolio Leadership. An Epic Owner coordinates it through the portfolio Kanban. The MVP is an early, minimal version of the solution whose job is to prove or disprove the epic's hypothesis. After the MVP comes the decision SAFe takes from the Lean Startup cycle: pivot, persevere or stop. Approval of an epic is approval to test a hypothesis, not a promise to build the full scope.
blocks.title: Epics

blocks.text: The state names are from author knowledge of SAFe 6; the public article confirms the Kanban but not its states.
rows: All large ideas are captured; no analysis yet
The idea is shaped into an epic hypothesis statement and roughly sized
Lean business case and MVP are defined; go or no-go decision
Approved epics wait until a train has capacity to pull them
The MVP is built and evaluated; then persevere, pivot or stop
The epic is finished because the hypothesis was proven or abandoned
blocks.title: The portfolio Kanban

blocks.text: An epic hypothesis statement describes the value proposition, the business outcomes expected if the hypothesis is true, the leading indicators that will give early evidence, and any nonfunctional requirements. Leading indicators move early, during the MVP, such as weekly sign-ups to a new checkout; lagging outcomes such as annual revenue arrive too late to steer the epic. Enabler epics, such as a compliance change to where data is stored, go through the same Kanban.
blocks.title: The epic hypothesis statement

blocks.text:
Larkspur's depot-automation value stream has a budget for the year. An Epic Owner proposes self-service returns kiosks. In Analyzing, the Lean business case states the hypothesis, 'kiosks cut returns handling time by half', and an MVP of three kiosks in one depot. Portfolio Leadership approves it, although the value stream is already funded, because the initiative is above the portfolio's epic threshold.

The MVP shows a 15 percent saving, not 50. The sponsor argues for the full rollout because the epic was approved. LPM instead pivots to kiosks for business customers only, where the saving was largest. Nothing was re-approved by finance: the value stream budget did not change.
blocks.title: Worked example: Larkspur Logistics

blocks.text: An epic is not a project, and approving it does not approve its full scope. After a successful MVP an epic stays in Implementing while trains build more features; it reaches Done when it no longer needs portfolio attention. Twenty epics in Implementing with few finishing is a WIP problem, not a reason to add more.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: In which state is the Lean business case developed and the MVP defined? Analyzing.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Place each epic: (a) a new idea just captured; (b) an epic with a hypothesis statement being ranked with WSJF; (c) an approved epic waiting for a train to have capacity.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Funnel. (b) Reviewing. (c) Ready.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Portfolio vision: the future state; current and future canvases show the gap; epics close it. Epics: business or enabler, with a Lean business case and an MVP; pivot, persevere or stop. Kanban: Funnel, Reviewing, Analyzing, Ready, Implementing, Done, with WIP limits. Epics are pulled from Ready by WSJF within capacity. Portfolio roadmap shows timing across PIs.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text: Epics, the MVP, the Lean business case, the portfolio vision and the canvas were checked against public pages. The Kanban state names, the epic hypothesis statement parts and the leading indicator examples are from the author's knowledge.
