lessons.title: 5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails
lessons.summary: Funding value streams, the four guardrails, investment horizons, participatory budgeting and portfolio events.

blocks.text:
Lean Budgets are a financial governance approach that funds value streams instead of projects. Traditional project funding creates overhead: each project needs its own approval, people are moved to the work, and any change triggers re-approval. With a funded value stream, stable teams stay in place and the work comes to them. When a feature takes longer than expected, priorities are adjusted locally inside the budget; no change request is needed.

Each portfolio operates within a budget that comes from the enterprise's strategic planning, and LPM allocates it to value streams. Stakeholders decide the allocation together in a participatory budgeting event, which the current glossary also calls Strategic Investment Planning.
blocks.title: Lean budgets

blocks.text: Investment horizons run from Horizon 0, solutions being retired, to Horizon 3, early evaluation of new opportunities.
rows: The balance of spending between today's solutions and future ones
Applying capacity allocation to optimize value and solution integrity
The mix of features, enablers and maintenance
Portfolio review of epics above a threshold
Ongoing business involvement in priorities and results
blocks.title: The four Lean budget guardrails

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge of SAFe 6.
rows: New ideas tested with small, time-boxed investments
Today's solutions that earn the returns
blocks.title: Investment horizons

blocks.text: The cadence of participatory budgeting is from author knowledge.
rows: Quarterly, at least a month before the next PI Planning
Strategy, budget and progress toward the vision
Allocating the portfolio budget to value streams
blocks.title: Portfolio events

blocks.text: A value stream's budget is set for six months. Within it, Product Management ranks the backlog and the trains plan in PI Planning; finance does not approve each feature. When a feature takes longer than expected, priorities are adjusted inside the budget. An epic above the portfolio's cost threshold still goes to LPM for approval.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Lean budgets do not mean no control: the guardrails govern spending. Requiring a business case for every feature reintroduces project funding's delays. And investment horizons balance today's and tomorrow's solutions; they are not a fixed five-year plan.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A train spends nearly all its time on new features while technical debt grows. Which guardrail applies? Applying capacity allocation to optimize value and solution integrity.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: LPM and Business Owners use the PI System Demo and other objective evidence to see real progress and adjust spending. Budgets are reviewed periodically, for example through participatory budgeting at portfolio reviews, so money can follow changing priorities without waiting a year. Portfolios forecast epics with relative sizing compared against the trains' known capacity rather than detailed plans.
blocks.title: Governing with evidence

blocks.text: Place each solution in a horizon: (a) a product that earns most of today's revenue; (b) a new idea with a two-month experiment budget; (c) a legacy system being switched off.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Horizon 1. (b) Horizon 3. (c) Horizon 0.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Lean budgets fund value streams, not projects. Four guardrails: guiding investments by horizon; applying capacity allocation to optimize value and solution integrity; approving significant initiatives; continuous Business Owner engagement. Horizons 3 to 0. Participatory budgeting, also called Strategic Investment Planning. Strategic Portfolio Review quarterly; Portfolio Sync monthly.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 6.1 · Leading by example
lessons.summary: Lean-Agile leadership, the behaviours of leading by example, and the leader's role as coach.

blocks.text:
Lean-Agile Leadership describes how leaders drive and sustain organisational change and operational excellence by empowering individuals and teams to reach their highest potential. They do this by leading by example, by learning and modelling the Lean-Agile mindset, values, principles and practices, and by leading the change to the new way of working.

The core argument is that only managers, executives and other leaders can change the systems that govern how work is done: budgeting, incentives, approval boards, organisational structure. Teams cannot change those. A transformation that is delegated therefore stalls at exactly the points where it matters.
blocks.title: Lean-Agile leadership

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge of SAFe 6; the leadership article shows only its introduction.
rows: Admitting a mistake openly and sharing the lesson
Recognising a tense team and acknowledging the pressure
Taking courses and asking for feedback on one's own leadership
Coaching and mentoring, with room to try and learn
Letting teams decide what is local and time-critical
blocks.title: Leading by example

blocks.text: A director asks teams for full transparency about problems but never admits mistakes of their own, and a Business Owner overrides a team's estimates to fit a promised date. Both fail to lead by example: the first lacks authenticity, the second ignores decentralised decision-making, since teams own their estimates.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: Sponsoring the change is not enough; leaders model it, because people copy what leaders do more than what they say. Close task control, daily reviews of each person's work and forced ranking are the old habits SAFe asks leaders to drop.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Why does SAFe ask leaders to go and see where the work happens? To understand the real problems first-hand before deciding, the Lean idea of the gemba.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: Name the behaviour: (a) a leader regularly asks for feedback on their own leadership; (b) a manager gives a junior engineer a stretch assignment with coaching; (c) a director explains a mistake in a planning decision to the team.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) Lifelong learning. (b) Growing others. (c) Authenticity.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Three dimensions of Lean-Agile Leadership: mindset, values and principles; leading by example; leading change. Only leaders can change the system. Leading by example: authenticity, emotional intelligence, lifelong learning, growing others, decentralised decision-making. Go and see. Growth mindset.
blocks.title: Details to know

lessons.title: 6.2 · Leading the change
lessons.summary: The tipping point, the vision for change, the guiding coalition, Kotter and the thirteen-step roadmap.

blocks.text:
The SAFe Implementation Roadmap starts with reaching the tipping point: the moment when the overriding organisational imperative is to achieve the change, not to resist it. SAFe names two ways to get there. A burning platform is an obvious failure to compete. Proactive leadership is leaders who see the need before a crisis and set out a compelling vision.

A vision for change provides three things: purpose, motivation and alignment. A vision alone is not enough. Following John Kotter, whose work the roadmap draws on, SAFe calls for a sufficiently powerful guiding coalition: influential, respected people who can secure resources and overcome resistance. SAFe Practice Consultants act as change agents, and a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence, a small Agile team dedicated to implementing the new way of working, usually supports the effort. SAFe recommends that senior leaders attend Leading SAFe themselves.
blocks.title: Reaching the tipping point

blocks.text: SAFe notes that in practice the steps are not perfectly sequential.
rows: Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
Launch More ARTs and Value Streams
blocks.title: The SAFe Implementation Roadmap

blocks.text: From the author's knowledge of Kotter's model, which the roadmap draws on.
blocks.title: Kotter's eight steps

blocks.text:
Pinecrest's teams run iterations well, yet the annual budget cycle, individual performance rankings and a weekly change approval board are untouched. The head of delivery has asked an Agile coach to 'finish the transformation'.

The coach cannot change any of those three systems. The SAFe reading is that the tipping point was never reached at leadership level and there is no guiding coalition. The next steps are for executives to attend Leading SAFe, form the coalition with a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence, and take ownership of the budgeting and approval changes themselves.
blocks.title: Worked example: Pinecrest Telecom

blocks.text: The current roadmap has thirteen steps; older versions had twelve and used names such as Identify Value Streams and ARTs and Extend to the Portfolio. Kotter has eight. Teams are trained when their ART launches, not before leaders, and the LACE keeps driving the change after the first ART launches.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: A company has reached the tipping point and trained its change agents. Which step comes next? Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: The first ART is launched by training its teams together, close to its first PI Planning, so everyone learns the same way of working at once. After launch come Coach ART Execution and Launch More ARTs and Value Streams; Enhance the Portfolio and Accelerate follow. A profitable company with no crisis can still reach the tipping point through proactive leadership.
blocks.title: Launching and growing

blocks.text: Name the route to the tipping point: (a) market share is collapsing and the old way is failing; (b) leaders foresee disruption while results are strong.
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: (a) A burning platform. (b) Proactive leadership.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: Tipping point: burning platform or proactive leadership. A vision gives purpose, motivation and alignment. Guiding coalition, SPCs as change agents, the LACE. Thirteen roadmap steps from Reaching the Tipping Point to Accelerate, not perfectly sequential. Kotter's eight steps.

lessons.title: 6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI
lessons.summary: AI as an accelerant, the SAFe CoPilot, and why leaders stay accountable.

blocks.text: The Leading SAFe course adds AI to the leader's toolkit: fundamentals and prompting for the role, the SAFe CoPilot assistant, and human-in-the-loop evaluation of output. For a leader the principle is that AI prepares and people decide. An assistant can summarise Inspect and Adapt findings, compare options or draft a communication. The leader evaluates what it produced, checks it against reality and stays accountable for the decision. AI output does not replace the objective evidence of a working system, and confidential data goes only into approved tools.
blocks.title: Empower leaders with AI

blocks.text: The Leading SAFe course page describes AI as a powerful accelerant for organisational value and flow and names the SAFe CoPilot assistant for navigating framework guidance, synthesising complex data and drafting strategic artifacts. An accelerant speeds up what is already there, good or bad, so AI amplifies Lean-Agile leadership rather than replacing it.
blocks.title: AI as an accelerant

blocks.text: An AI tool recommends removing the IP iteration to gain capacity. A Lean-Agile leader tests the advice against principles and evidence: removing it would remove the estimating buffer and the time for innovation and planning, so the advice is rejected with reasons. Blind acceptance and blanket rejection both skip the leader's judgement.
blocks.title: Worked example

blocks.text: "The AI recommended it, so we did it" abdicates accountability. A leader who drafts a vision with AI still owns the message. Banning AI until a full policy exists stalls learning; letting teams use any public tool with company data creates risk.
blocks.title: Common exam trap

blocks.text: Which leadership task is AI best placed to accelerate: taking a decision, building trust, or synthesising large volumes of data into options? Synthesising data into options.
blocks.title: Self-check and solution

blocks.text: AI use on a train is very uneven: a few experts, many who never try. What should a leader do?
blocks.title: Exercise

blocks.text: Create time, training and safe ways for everyone to experiment, use AI openly in their own work and share what they learn. Prompt quotas measure activity, not value.
blocks.title: Worked solution

blocks.text: AI prepares, people decide. Leaders model responsible AI use. SAFe CoPilot. AI as an accelerant for value and flow. Check AI summaries against the source; approved tools for confidential data.
blocks.title: Details to know

blocks.text: The accelerant wording, the SAFe CoPilot and the human-in-the-loop points come from the Leading SAFe course page, rechecked on 16 November 2026. The cases are the author's.

blocks.text: When two options both look right, check whether they are one of these pairs or roles. The third column is usually what the question tests.
blocks.title: How to use this lesson

lessons.title: Exam technique
lessons.summary: Pacing, reading the question, and the patterns that separate SAFe's answer from a generic one.

blocks.text: 45 questions in 90 minutes is two minutes each. Answer everything you know in a first pass, flag the rest, and keep ten minutes for flagged questions. Never leave a blank: unanswered questions count as wrong.
blocks.title: Pacing

blocks.text: Find what is asked: a role, an event, a principle number, a Kanban state, a first step. Note qualifiers such as "best", "first" and "most likely". In scenarios, underline who is acting and at what level: team, train or portfolio. Many wrong options are good practice at the wrong level or by the wrong role.
blocks.title: Read the question

rows: The role SAFe names, or the team for local decisions
A manager deciding for the team
The SAFe artifact at the right level
Epic practices applied to features, or the reverse
The plain Scrum or project answer
Coaches, the PMO or the RTE run the transformation
Cost of Delay over size, ignoring sunk cost
Highest value first, or finish what is paid for
blocks.title: Patterns that usually point to the key

blocks.text: The study guide names this exam "AI-Empowered". Expect a few questions on using AI responsibly as an Agilist and as a leader; the answer is almost always that AI prepares and people evaluate and decide.
blocks.title: Exam trap

blocks.text: Sit papers A to F under exam conditions. After each, review every question you got wrong or guessed, read its lesson section and add the idea to your flashcards. Leave at least a day between papers.
blocks.title: Using the papers

lessons.title: Final revision
lessons.summary: The night-before list for each of the six domains.

blocks.text: Business Agility; age of software and digital; BAVS. Dual operating system. Seven competencies, old and new names. Four configurations. Outcomes, flow, competency; six flow metrics.
blocks.title: Adapt and thrive (7-9%)

blocks.text: Lean thinking plus the Agile Manifesto, with a growth mindset. Four Core Values. Ten principles by number; #3 options, #5 milestones; eight flow accelerators; centralise infrequent, long-lasting, scale decisions. AI applies at all levels, under human judgement.
blocks.title: Mindset, value and principles (21-23%)

blocks.text: Teams of ten or fewer with a PO and a Scrum Master/Team Coach. ARTs of 50 to 125, long-lived; RTE, Product Management, System Architect, Business Owners; four topologies. Built-in quality throughout; five basic practices. Pipeline aspects; deployment versus release; CALMR.
blocks.title: Team and technical agility (10-12%)

blocks.text: Customer centricity; design thinking tools; desirable, viable, feasible, sustainable. ART backlog; enabler types; features with benefit hypothesis and AC; WSJF and its three Cost of Delay parts; capacity allocation. PI Planning: two days, RTE facilitates, three readiness areas, objectives and planning board, business value 1 to 10, ROAM, fist of five. Execute: ART sync, System Demo, IP iteration, I&A and its workshop, predictability 80 to 100 percent.
blocks.title: Product development flow (25-28%)

blocks.text: Three LPM areas. Portfolio of value streams; operational versus development. Strategic themes as OKRs; SWOT then TOWS. Vision and canvas; epics with Lean business case and MVP; Kanban states and WIP. Lean budgets, four guardrails, horizons 3 to 0, participatory budgeting, Strategic Portfolio Review and Portfolio Sync.
blocks.title: Lean portfolio management (21-23%)

blocks.text: Three dimensions of leadership; only leaders change the system; leading-by-example behaviours. Tipping point: burning platform or proactive leadership. Vision, guiding coalition, LACE. Thirteen roadmap steps. AI as an accelerant; leaders stay accountable.
blocks.title: Lead the change (7-9%)

blocks.text: Two minutes a question. Right role, right level, SAFe's term over the generic one. Leaders change the system; teams own their plans.
blocks.title: On the day

questions.prompt: How does SAFe define Business Agility?

options.text: Giving every team the freedom to choose its own goals, tools and release dates
Reducing the cost of IT delivery by moving development work to the lowest-cost locations
Running all projects in two-week sprints so that scope can be changed at any moment by the sponsor
Competing and thriving in the digital age by responding quickly with digitally enabled solutions

questions.explanation: SAFe defines Business Agility as the ability to compete and thrive in the digital age by responding quickly to market changes and opportunities with digitally enabled business solutions. Sprints alone are the generic Agile answer: they describe a team practice, not an enterprise capability. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Marrow Retail has grown a deep hierarchy, and new digital products now take years to launch. Which response matches SAFe's dual operating system?

options.text: Add project managers to speed up each handoff
Dissolve the hierarchy and let teams self-assign
Create a new innovation department under the CIO
Add a value stream network beside the hierarchy

questions.explanation: SAFe follows Kotter: keep the hierarchy for stability and efficiency, and add a network organised around value streams for speed and adaptability. Dissolving the hierarchy is the tempting radical answer, but SAFe keeps both operating systems. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility; SAFe · Principle #10.

questions.prompt: In SAFe's dual operating system, what is each side optimised for?

options.text: The network for long-term strategy, the hierarchy for daily delivery
The network for governance and compliance, the hierarchy for innovation and learning
The network for speed and adaptability, the hierarchy for efficiency and stability
The network for cost reduction, the hierarchy for customer experience

questions.explanation: The value stream network gives speed and adaptability while the hierarchy keeps efficiency and stability. The first distractor reverses the roles: compliance and governance functions live in the hierarchy. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe · Principle #10.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of SAFe's seven core competencies?

options.text: Lean Portfolio Management
Project Portfolio Control
Scrum of Scrums Governance
Agile Maturity Auditing

questions.explanation: Lean Portfolio Management is one of the seven core competencies of Business Agility. Project portfolio control sounds close, but SAFe replaces project-based control with Lean portfolio practices. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: A portfolio funds a minimum viable product, and the evidence shows that customers do not want it. In the Business Agility Value Stream, what comes next?

options.text: A full business case for the next phase
A pivot-or-persevere decision
Delivery of the remaining planned scope
A handover to operations

questions.explanation: After the MVP is delivered, the value stream reaches Pivot or Persevere, where evidence decides what happens to the investment. Continuing with the planned scope is the traditional project answer, which ignores what the MVP has just taught. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: Arrange these steps of the Business Agility Value Stream in order.

options.text: Connect to Customer
Pivot or Persevere
Organize Around Value
Sense Opportunity
Deliver MVP
Fund MVP

questions.explanation: The value stream starts by sensing an opportunity and funding an MVP, then organises around value, connects to the customer, delivers the MVP and decides to pivot or persevere. Funding comes before organising: the MVP is funded first and people are then organised around it. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: Which three measurement domains does SAFe use to assess progress toward Business Agility?

options.text: Velocity, utilisation and defects
Strategy, structure and culture
Scope, schedule and budget
Flow, outcomes and competency

questions.explanation: SAFe measures flow, outcomes and competency. Scope, schedule and budget is the traditional project triangle, which measures conformance to a plan, not agility. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: Tessel Bank's leaders say that every business is now a software business. What does this mean for the bank?

options.text: Its competitiveness depends on digitally enabled solutions
Its products should all be rebuilt as cloud services
Its branches should be closed in favour of a mobile app
Its IT department should report directly to marketing

questions.explanation: SAFe places enterprises in the age of software and digital, where the ability to deliver digitally enabled solutions decides who thrives. The statement is about capability, not about a particular channel or architecture choice. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: According to the view SAFe borrows from Kotter, what happens as a successful startup grows?

options.text: Its hierarchy disappears once the teams have become self-managing
Its growing hierarchy starts to crowd out the entrepreneurial network
Its hierarchy and its network merge into one matrix organisation
Its entrepreneurial network naturally takes over from the hierarchy

questions.explanation: Organisations start as a network, add hierarchy to scale, and over time the hierarchy's demands overtake the network. A matrix is a common real-world response, but it is not the dual operating system SAFe describes. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility; SAFe · Principle #10.

questions.prompt: An enterprise wants the simplest starting point for implementing SAFe with one Agile Release Train. Which configuration fits?

options.text: Portfolio SAFe
Essential SAFe
Large Solution SAFe
Full SAFe

questions.explanation: Essential SAFe holds the minimal elements an ART needs and is the simplest place to start. Full SAFe is the most comprehensive configuration, for portfolios of large and complex solutions. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Executives at Halden Freight want Business Agility and ask the PMO to run the transformation while they focus on operations. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: Leaders must lead the change themselves
Agile coaches should own the transformation
The PMO is the right owner of the change
Each team should transform at its own pace

questions.explanation: SAFe holds that only leaders can change the system, so they must lead by example and lead the change. Handing the transformation to coaches is the tempting answer, but coaches support the change; they cannot alter the system that governs how work is done. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility; SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership.

questions.prompt: A portfolio wants to know whether its solutions are achieving the intended business benefits. Which measurement domain answers this?

options.text: Predictability
Outcomes
Flow
Competency

questions.explanation: Outcomes, measured with value stream KPIs, show whether solutions deliver business benefit. Flow shows how efficiently value moves through the system, which says nothing about whether it was worth delivering. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: Drawing on Carlota Perez's work on technological revolutions, which age does SAFe say enterprises are in now?

options.text: The age of steam and railways
The age of steel and electricity
The age of oil and mass production
The age of software and digital

questions.explanation: SAFe uses Perez's account of five technological revolutions and places today's enterprises in the age of software and digital. Earlier ages reshaped industries in the same way, which is why SAFe treats digital disruption as structural rather than a passing trend. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A regional insurer still issues policies on paper while a newcomer sells cover in two minutes on a phone. In SAFe's view of business agility, what matters most for the insurer?

options.text: How quickly its IT department can upgrade all its servers
How large its customer base is compared with the newcomer's
How soon it can cut costs in its paper-based processes
How fast it can respond with digitally enabled solutions

questions.explanation: Business agility is the ability to respond quickly to market changes with digitally enabled solutions. Cost cutting and infrastructure upgrades improve the old model; size is no protection when a competitor responds faster. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe say that business agility involves the whole enterprise rather than IT alone?

options.text: IT departments are too small to deliver the solutions on their own
Digital solutions need business and technology working together
Only business staff are able to talk directly to customers
Agile methods were first invented by business leaders

questions.explanation: SAFe says business agility requires everyone involved in delivering solutions, from business and technology leaders to legal, finance, marketing and support, to use Lean and Agile practices. A fast IT function inside a slow business still delivers slowly. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of the Business Agility Value Stream?

options.text: Connect to customer
Sense opportunity
Organize around value
Fund MVP

questions.explanation: The Business Agility Value Stream starts by sensing an opportunity, then funds an MVP, organises around value, connects to the customer, delivers the MVP, decides to pivot or persevere, delivers value continuously, and learns and adapts. The other options are later steps, so they cannot start the stream. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company spots a market change and funds a minimum viable product to test it. Which Business Agility Value Stream step comes right after funding the MVP?

options.text: Pivot or persevere
Deliver value continuously
Organize around value
Learn and adapt

questions.explanation: After Fund MVP comes Organize around value, which forms or adjusts the teams and trains that will build it, then Connect to customer. Pivot or persevere comes only after the MVP has been delivered and its evidence is in. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does SAFe's Business Agility Value Stream aim to improve?

options.text: Departmental control, by giving each step a separate plan
The care of decisions about value, by making each step take longer
Certainty, by requiring a full business case before any step
The time from sensing an opportunity to delivering value

questions.explanation: Framing business agility as a value stream puts the focus on lead time: shortening the path from a sensed opportunity to delivered value through small funded experiments and teams organised around value. Separate plans and up-front business cases lengthen it. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: After a new product launch, a company reviews what it learned about customers and about its own process, and changes how it senses opportunities. Which Business Agility Value Stream step is this?

options.text: Deliver MVP
Sense opportunity
Fund MVP
Learn and adapt

questions.explanation: Learn and adapt is the last step: the enterprise reflects on results and improves how it runs the whole value stream, which feeds the next cycle of sensing. Sense opportunity is where the next cycle starts, not where lessons are captured. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe argue that a traditional hierarchy alone struggles in the digital age?

options.text: Its leaders lack the technical skills to manage software teams
It is built for efficiency and stability, not for speed
It has too few employees to cover each new market
It cannot legally fund projects that last more than a year

questions.explanation: Hierarchies are good at running a known business efficiently, but decisions travel slowly through layers, so they respond slowly to new opportunities. SAFe keeps the hierarchy and adds a value stream network for speed. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A firm's teams are Agile, but funding, approvals and planning still follow an annual, project-based cycle, and launches still take years. What is SAFe's diagnosis?

options.text: Agility stops at the teams; the business must change too
The firm should add more teams to each of its projects
The annual cycle is fine; the products are simply too complex
The teams need to work faster within the current system

questions.explanation: Business agility needs the whole system to change, including funding, governance and planning. Fast teams inside annual, project-based processes still deliver slowly, because the work waits on the slowest part of the system. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which outcome best shows that an enterprise has achieved business agility?

options.text: It has trained its staff in Scrum and holds daily stand-ups
It has bought the latest software tools for each of its departments
It turns new opportunities into value quickly and repeatedly
It has replaced its managers with self-organizing teams

questions.explanation: Business agility is judged by results: responding to opportunities with value, quickly and repeatedly. Training, tools and structures are means to that end, and adopting them is no proof that it has been reached. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A business unit wants to enter a new market but is very unsure about customer demand. Which approach does SAFe's business agility guidance favour?

options.text: Commit the full budget up front to show confidence
Fund a small MVP and let evidence decide what comes next
Write a five-year business case before any work begins
Wait until a competitor has proved that the market exists

questions.explanation: Under uncertainty SAFe favours small, funded experiments whose results drive a pivot-or-persevere decision. A five-year business case or a full up-front budget commits money before anything has been learned. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe, who must use Lean and Agile practices for an enterprise to achieve business agility?

options.text: Software developers and testers in the IT department
Agile coaches and Scrum Masters across the company
Everyone who helps deliver solutions, in every function
The leadership team and the project management office staff

questions.explanation: SAFe lists business and technology leaders, development, IT operations, legal, marketing, finance, support, compliance, security and others. Limiting Lean and Agile to IT or to coaches leaves the rest of the value stream working the old way. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Source: SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: Which statement about disruption reflects SAFe's position?

options.text: It mostly affects technology firms, not traditional industries
Large enterprises are protected by their great scale and their brands
It favours whoever learns and responds fastest, whatever their size
It can be avoided by investing heavily in today's products

questions.explanation: SAFe's argument is that digital disruption reaches every industry and rewards speed of learning and response, which newcomers often have and incumbents must build. Scale, brands and investment in current products do not protect against a faster competitor. Topic 1.1, lesson “1.1 · Thriving in the age of disruption”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each SAFe core competency to one of its dimensions.

options.text: Relentless improvement
Release train budgeting
Customer centricity and design thinking
Built-in quality
Strategy and investment funding

questions.explanation: Each competency has three dimensions. Lean Portfolio Management includes strategy and investment funding; Product Development Flow, formerly Agile Product Delivery, includes customer centricity and design thinking; Team and Technical Agility includes built-in quality; Continuous Learning Culture includes relentless improvement. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An enterprise wants to measure how proficient it is in the practices that enable business agility. Which measurement domain fits?

options.text: Flow
Productivity
Outcomes
Competency

questions.explanation: SAFe measures progress in three domains: outcomes, whether solutions achieve the intended benefits; flow, how efficiently value is delivered; and competency, how proficient the organisation is in the practices that enable business agility. Velocity is a team measure, not a domain. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measurement domain answers 'How efficiently is the organisation delivering value to customers?'

options.text: Outcomes
Flow
Capacity
Competency

questions.explanation: Flow measures the efficiency of value delivery, using metrics such as flow time, velocity and efficiency. Outcomes asks whether the delivered solutions achieve the intended benefits, which is a different question. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of SAFe's six flow metrics?

options.text: Flow budget
Flow utilisation rate
Flow predictability
Flow capacity

questions.explanation: The six flow metrics are flow distribution, flow velocity, flow time, flow load, flow efficiency and flow predictability. Capacity, budget and quality matter, but they are not among the six. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train wants to see how its work splits between features, enablers, defects and risks. Which flow metric shows this?

options.text: Flow load
Flow efficiency
Flow predictability
Flow distribution

questions.explanation: Flow distribution shows the proportion of each type of work in the system, which helps balance new value against enablers and debt. Flow load counts the amount of work in progress, and velocity counts items completed. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which SAFe configuration adds strategy, investment funding and Lean governance to Essential SAFe?

options.text: Portfolio SAFe
Large Solution SAFe
Enterprise SAFe
Team SAFe

questions.explanation: The four configurations are Essential, Large Solution, Portfolio and Full SAFe. Portfolio SAFe adds Lean Portfolio Management, strategic themes and the portfolio backlog to Essential SAFe; Team SAFe and Enterprise SAFe are not configurations. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An enterprise builds aircraft that need several ARTs and suppliers to cooperate on one system, but it has no need for portfolio management yet. Which configuration fits?

options.text: Portfolio SAFe
Full SAFe
Large Solution SAFe
Essential SAFe

questions.explanation: Large Solution SAFe coordinates multiple ARTs and suppliers in a solution train for big, complex systems, without adding the portfolio level. Full SAFe would combine it with portfolio management, which this enterprise does not need yet. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the Large Solution Integration and Delivery competency, formerly called Enterprise Solution Delivery, cover?

options.text: Building customer-centric products and releasing on demand
Coordinating several ARTs and suppliers on very big systems
Extending Lean thinking into finance, HR and legal teams
Funding value streams and governing the portfolio's spending

questions.explanation: This competency covers Lean system and solution engineering, coordinating trains and suppliers, and continually evolving live systems. The current glossary renamed it, along with Agile Product Delivery, now Product Development Flow; recognise both sets of names. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Finance, HR and legal at a company still work in annual cycles and large batches while its ARTs deliver every two weeks. Which core competency addresses this?

options.text: Product Development Flow
Organizational Agility
Team and Technical Agility
Large Solution Integration and Delivery

questions.explanation: Organizational Agility extends Lean thinking and Agile teams beyond development into business functions, along with Lean business operations and strategy agility. The other competencies concern how solutions are built and delivered. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company wants its people to keep growing their skills, innovating and improving as part of everyday work. Which core competency is this?

options.text: Lean Portfolio Management
Continuous Learning Culture
Product Development Flow
Lean-Agile Leadership

questions.explanation: Continuous Learning Culture has three dimensions: a learning organisation, an innovation culture and relentless improvement. Lean-Agile Leadership enables it, but the competency itself is about the culture. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe place Lean-Agile Leadership at the foundation of the other core competencies?

options.text: Leaders create the environment in which the others can grow
Leaders are the only people trained in all the other competencies
Leaders must approve each team's daily work before it starts
Leadership is the competency that costs the least to put in place

questions.explanation: Leaders own the system, including structures, funding, policies and culture, so the other competencies depend on them changing it. SAFe's leaders enable and model; they do not approve daily work. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A leader asks whether adopting SAFe means removing the existing management hierarchy. Which answer reflects SAFe?

options.text: No: the hierarchy stays, and a value stream network is added
Yes: hierarchy and agility cannot exist together in one firm
Yes, but only after the first Agile Release Train launches
No: the hierarchy simply takes over running the ARTs

questions.explanation: SAFe's dual operating system keeps the hierarchy for efficiency and stability and adds a value stream network, of ARTs organised around value, for speed. The network is not run through the hierarchy's reporting lines. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which SAFe configuration is the most comprehensive, supporting enterprises that build large, integrated solutions and also manage a portfolio?

options.text: Essential SAFe
Full SAFe
Portfolio SAFe
Large Solution SAFe

questions.explanation: Full SAFe combines the Large Solution and Portfolio configurations. Essential SAFe is the starting point with one or more ARTs, and each of the other two adds only one of the two extensions. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company's measures show high flow velocity, but customer adoption of new features is falling. What does SAFe's measurement model suggest?

options.text: Competency is the problem, so teams need retraining
Delivery is efficient, but the outcomes need attention
The company is fully business-agile, since flow is high
Flow velocity should rise further to win customers back

questions.explanation: SAFe measures outcomes, flow and competency together because one can look healthy while another fails. Fast delivery of features customers do not value points to outcomes, for example by validating benefit hypotheses before building more. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the SAFe Big Picture?

options.text: A five-year roadmap that each enterprise must follow step by step
A contract template for agreeing scope with suppliers
A dashboard that tracks each team's progress every day
An overview of the framework's roles, practices and competencies

questions.explanation: The Big Picture is the framework's map: an interactive overview of its configurations, roles, events, artifacts and competencies. The step-by-step guidance for adopting SAFe is the Implementation Roadmap, a different thing. Topic 1.2, lesson “1.2 · Building a Lean-Agile organization”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the Lean-Agile Mindset combine?

options.text: Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto
Six Sigma and the PMBOK Guide
DevOps tooling and design sprint workshops
Agile ceremonies and Kanban boards

questions.explanation: SAFe describes the mindset as the beliefs and actions of people who embrace Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto. Scrum and Kanban are practices that express the mindset; they are not the mindset. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Mindset; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the four SAFe Core Values?

options.text: Commitment, courage, focus, openness, and respect for other team members
Autonomy, mastery, purpose, psychological safety at work
Alignment, transparency, respect for people, relentless improvement
Alignment, built-in quality, transparency, program execution

questions.explanation: The current core values are alignment, transparency, respect for people and relentless improvement. The set with built-in quality and program execution is the earlier version of the values, which makes it the trap. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Source: SAFe · Core Values; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Match each SAFe Core Value to a leader behaviour that expresses it.

options.text: Growing people and valuing different viewpoints
Reflecting at milestones and acting on what is learned
Making progress and problems visible without blame
Connecting strategy to backlogs through a shared vision
Rewarding the individual who works the longest hours

questions.explanation: Alignment connects strategy to execution, transparency makes reality visible, respect for people develops and values them, and relentless improvement turns reflection into action. Alignment and transparency are the pair most often confused: one is about direction, the other about visibility. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Teams at Kestrel Foods report every feature as on track until the week of the release, so leaders learn of delays when it is too late to act. Which Core Value is most directly missing?

options.text: Transparency
Alignment
Relentless improvement
Respect for people

questions.explanation: Transparency means that facts, including bad news, are visible in time to act on them. Alignment is the tempting alternative, but the teams may agree fully on the goal; what is absent is visibility of the real status. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Source: SAFe · Core Values.

questions.prompt: Six teams on a train each deliver what their own manager asks for, and the combined result serves no clear customer goal. Which Core Value is most directly missing?

options.text: Transparency
Alignment
Relentless improvement
Respect for people

questions.explanation: Alignment keeps everyone working toward the same vision and objectives. The teams may be perfectly transparent about their work and still pull in different directions. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Source: SAFe · Core Values.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs to Lean thinking as SAFe summarises it?

options.text: Maximise the utilisation of experts
Let the customer pull value
Batch releases to cut overhead
Push work to keep everyone busy

questions.explanation: Lean thinking specifies value, identifies the value stream, makes value flow, lets the customer pull value and pursues perfection. Maximising utilisation is the classic opposite: it creates queues and slows flow. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Source: SAFe · Principle #6.

questions.prompt: A company has adopted stand-ups, boards and two-week iterations, yet decisions, funding and deadlines work as they did before. What does SAFe say is missing?

options.text: A change of mindset, since agility is more than practices
A stricter rollout of the practices across all the teams
A dedicated tool to track compliance with the ceremonies
A longer iteration length that gives teams more time

questions.explanation: SAFe stresses that agility is a mindset change, not only a set of practices. Rolling the practices out more strictly is the tempting answer, and it produces the same mechanical result on a larger scale. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Mindset.

questions.prompt: Which statement is one of the four values of the Agile Manifesto?

options.text: Processes and tools over individuals and interactions
Comprehensive documentation over working software
Responding to change over following a plan
Contract negotiation over customer collaboration

questions.explanation: The manifesto values responding to change over following a plan. The other three options reverse the manifesto's own pairs, placing the item it values less in front. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each SAFe Lean-Agile Principle number to its name.

options.text: Maximize the utilization of specialists
Take an economic view
Decentralize decision-making
Make value flow without interruptions
Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles

questions.explanation: The ten principles are numbered, and the exam uses the numbers. Principle #1 is the economic view, #4 is incremental building with learning cycles, #6 is flow and #9 is decentralised decisions; the extra option is not a SAFe principle at all. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: Match each of these SAFe Lean-Agile Principle numbers to its name.

options.text: Deliver working software at the end of each sprint
Apply systems thinking
Assume variability; preserve options
Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: Principle #2 is systems thinking, #3 is variability and options, #5 is objective milestones and #7 is cadence and synchronisation. Numbers 3 and 5 are swapped most often, so link #3 with options and #5 with milestones. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: Which is SAFe Lean-Agile Principle #10?

options.text: Organize around value
Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
Take an economic view
Apply systems thinking

questions.explanation: Principle #10 is Organize around value, the last of the ten. Unlocking intrinsic motivation is Principle #8 and is the usual wrong pick, because both sit near the end of the list. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: A product manager must choose between delaying a feature by one PI and paying for extra capacity now. Which principle asks for this decision to be framed in terms of Cost of Delay?

options.text: #9 Decentralize decision-making
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
#1 Take an economic view
#3 Assume variability; preserve options

questions.explanation: Principle #1 asks for decisions to be made in a proper economic context, which includes the Cost of Delay. Principle #9 covers who decides; Principle #1 covers the economic reasoning used to decide. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe ask leaders to give teams an economic framework such as guardrails and Cost of Delay?

options.text: So that every decision is escalated for approval
So that teams can be ranked by cost efficiency
So that budgets can be fixed for several years
So that local decisions rest on sound trade-offs

questions.explanation: An economic framework lets people decide locally and still decide well, connecting Principle #1 to Principle #9. Escalating every decision is the opposite of the intent: the framework exists so that approval queues are not needed. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: A test department maximises its own throughput by testing in large batches, and the end-to-end delivery time of the train gets worse. Which principle explains what went wrong?

options.text: #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#2 Apply systems thinking
#10 Organize around value

questions.explanation: Systems thinking says that optimising a component does not optimise the system. The test department improved its local measure and harmed the whole value stream, which is the pattern Principle #2 warns about. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Architects at Brightwater Utilities must choose a messaging technology, and the best choice depends on load data that will exist only after two more iterations. What does Principle #3 advise?

options.text: Pick the most familiar option now to avoid any delay
Ask the steering committee to choose on the team's behalf
Keep several design options open until the data arrives
Freeze the requirements so that the choice is simpler

questions.explanation: Principle #3 preserves options through set-based design, keeping alternatives alive until learning allows a sound choice. Choosing early is the point-based approach, which the principle says is often wrong. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #3.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe consider an early commitment to a single design risky?

options.text: Designs that are chosen early cost more to build than later ones
Architects lose motivation when the design is fixed before they start
Uncertainty is highest at the start, so the early choice is often wrong
Early commitment prevents the team from using cadence and synchronisation

questions.explanation: Early in development the cone of uncertainty is at its widest, so a single point-based choice made then is frequently wrong and expensive to reverse. Variability is not bad in itself; committing before learning is. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #3.

questions.prompt: A solution is designed for nine months before any part of it is assembled, so the teams get no feedback on their design assumptions until the end. Which principle does this most directly ignore?

options.text: #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
#4 Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: Principle #4 calls for building in increments so that integrated results give fast feedback. Nine months without integration postpones all learning to the end, when changing course costs the most. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: A steering committee approves each phase when its documents are signed off. What would Principle #5 use as a milestone?

options.text: A signed requirements specification for the phase
A demonstration of the integrated, working system
A percentage of the budget spent to date
A status report with a green traffic light

questions.explanation: Principle #5 bases milestones on objective evaluation of working systems, using integration points to show real progress. Signed documents are the phase-gate answer and show only that documents exist. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: Why are phase-gate milestones a weak indicator of progress in SAFe's view?

options.text: Documents can be complete while the solution still does not work
Gates measure the working system when they should measure plans
Phase gates take place too often to be of use to stakeholders
Stakeholders are unable to attend reviews at the end of a phase

questions.explanation: Phase gates assess plans and documents, so they can all pass while integration risk stays hidden. Only an evaluation of working, integrated increments gives objective evidence. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train has thirty features in progress and finishes two per PI. Which principle addresses this most directly?

options.text: #8 Unlock the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers
#6 Make value flow without interruptions
#3 Assume variability; preserve options
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems

questions.explanation: Too much work in process blocks flow, and Principle #6 is about making value move smoothly and quickly through the value stream. The situation is a flow problem, not a motivation or milestone problem. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which action improves flow?

options.text: Releasing less frequently
Starting more work in parallel
Reducing the size of work batches
Keeping each specialist fully utilised

questions.explanation: Smaller batches move through the system faster and give earlier feedback. Starting more work in parallel feels productive, but it raises work in process and lengthens every queue. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Teams on a train use different iteration lengths and start dates, so the train has no common rhythm and its events never line up. Which principle addresses this?

options.text: #9 Decentralize decision-making
#4 Build incrementally with fast, integrated learning cycles
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning
#2 Apply systems thinking

questions.explanation: Principle #7 uses a shared cadence and synchronisation so that teams plan and integrate together. Systems thinking is the tempting alternative, but the specific gap here is the missing common rhythm. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: What do cadence and synchronisation each contribute?

options.text: Cadence removes variability from the work; synchronisation removes dependencies between teams
Cadence integrates the work of the teams; synchronisation sets the release dates in advance
Cadence fixes the scope of each increment; synchronisation fixes the size of each team
Cadence makes events predictable; synchronisation lets perspectives be integrated together

questions.explanation: Cadence gives a predictable rhythm, and synchronisation causes several perspectives to be understood, resolved and integrated at one time. Neither removes variability; together they help manage it. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A manager proposes an individual bonus for the developer who closes the most stories. What is SAFe's view under Principle #8?

options.text: Knowledge workers are moved more by autonomy, mastery and purpose
Story counts are a sound basis for comparing people fairly
Bonuses should be paid to the Product Owner, not to developers
Individual bonuses are the strongest motivator for complex work

questions.explanation: Principle #8 says that knowledge work is driven by intrinsic motivation and that extrinsic rewards can degrade performance on problem-solving tasks. Individual targets also set team members against each other. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #8.

questions.prompt: Which idea, credited to Peter Drucker, supports Principle #8?

options.text: Knowledge workers need closer supervision than manual workers do
Knowledge workers produce more when their tasks are standardised
Knowledge workers know more about their work than their managers do
Knowledge workers respond best to pay that depends on output

questions.explanation: Drucker's point is that knowledge workers understand their own work better than anyone above them. The leader's job therefore shifts from directing tasks to creating an environment in which people can do their best work. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #8.

questions.prompt: Which decision is the best candidate to keep centralised under Principle #9?

options.text: Deciding when a team holds its retrospective
Choosing a common technology platform for the whole portfolio
Deciding how a team should split one of its larger user stories
Choosing the order of work within a team's iteration

questions.explanation: Strategic decisions that are global, long-lasting and bring economies of scale are worth centralising. The other decisions are frequent, local and time-critical, and belong with the people who have the context. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #9; SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: Which decision should be decentralised under Principle #9?

options.text: How much budget each value stream receives
How a team sequences the stories in its own backlog
Which enterprise-wide cloud provider to standardise on
Which strategic themes the portfolio will pursue

questions.explanation: Frequent, time-critical decisions that need local information belong with the team. Strategic themes and budgets are infrequent, long-lasting and global, so they are decided centrally. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #9.

questions.prompt: Every design change waits a week in the queue of one architecture manager, and delivery has slowed. What is the SAFe answer?

options.text: Ask the manager to work through the queue more quickly
Define a decision framework and let teams decide within it
Move all design decisions to the PI Planning event
Add a second manager so that approvals are shared

questions.explanation: Principle #9 removes the approval queue by decentralising decisions inside a clear framework. A faster manager is the trap: the manager is still deciding where the team should, and the queue comes back. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #9.

questions.prompt: Analysts, developers and testers sit in separate departments, and each feature crosses five handoffs. Which principle addresses the cause?

options.text: #5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#1 Take an economic view
#10 Organize around value
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: Principle #10 organises people around the flow of value, in value streams and trains, to remove handoffs between functional silos. Cadence would line up the departments' calendars and leave the handoffs in place. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Principle #10.

questions.prompt: A recommended SAFe practice does not fit a team's regulatory context. What should guide the adaptation?

options.text: The practice as written, without change
The process used before SAFe
The preference of the most senior manager
The underlying Lean-Agile principles

questions.explanation: SAFe describes its principles as immutable and underlying, so practices can be adapted as long as the principles are honoured. Following the practice unchanged puts the mechanics above their purpose. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe's public guidance, where can AI be applied?

options.text: At all levels of SAFe, in solutions, value streams and customer insight
At the portfolio level, as a tool for automating funding decisions
At the team level, as a tool for writing and testing code more quickly
In a separate data science department that serves the trains

questions.explanation: The guidance says AI can be applied at all SAFe levels: to build intelligent customer solutions, automate value stream activities and improve customer insight. Treating AI as a coding tool for teams is the narrow view the guidance moves beyond. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Source: SAFe · Artificial Intelligence in SAFe.

questions.prompt: An Agilist asks an AI assistant to summarise the risks raised in PI Planning for a leadership update. What should happen before the summary is sent?

options.text: The summary is shortened so that any errors matter less
The summary is sent quickly, since speed is the benefit of AI
The assistant is asked to confirm that the summary is right
A person evaluates the output against what was actually said

questions.explanation: The course stresses human-in-the-loop evaluation of AI output, so a person checks the summary before it informs decisions. Asking the assistant to confirm its own work adds no independent check. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: Which prompt is most likely to give an Agilist a useful draft for a stakeholder update?

options.text: Make the perfect update that every stakeholder will love and that leaves no question open
Summarise all the important points
Summarise these PI objectives for business owners in five bullets, with risks first
Write something good about our PI

questions.explanation: A useful prompt gives the source material, the audience, the format and the emphasis. The long prompt that asks for perfection is the trap, since it adds words without adding any direction. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: According to SAFe's guidance, which kind of problem suits AI better than conventional rule-based software?

options.text: Situations that predefined rules cannot cover
Processes with a small number of fixed steps
Reports that follow a standard template
Calculations that must give exact results

questions.explanation: The guidance contrasts rule-based software with AI for scenarios that predefined rules cannot cover. Fixed steps and exact calculations are where conventional software remains the better tool. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Source: SAFe · Artificial Intelligence in SAFe.

questions.prompt: Which SAFe core value rests on the idea that staff, rather than processes, do all the work?

options.text: Transparency
Alignment
Respect for people
Relentless improvement

questions.explanation: Respect for people recognises that people, not processes, do the work, and extends to customers, suppliers and partners. Alignment and transparency are about direction and visibility rather than how people are treated. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train holds a retrospective every iteration, runs a problem-solving workshop each PI and keeps a constant sense of danger about complacency. Which core value is this?

options.text: Alignment
Relentless improvement
Transparency
Respect for people

questions.explanation: Relentless improvement means a constant sense of danger, regular reflection and structured problem solving. The events named are its mechanisms; transparency is about visibility of the truth, not about improving. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Leaders communicate the mission and vision again and again so that every team understands how its work contributes. Which core value does this build?

options.text: Transparency
Alignment
Relentless improvement
Respect for people

questions.explanation: Alignment means everyone understands and pursues the same goals, which needs leaders to communicate the mission, vision and strategy repeatedly. Teams that are aligned can then make good local decisions. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe link transparency to trust?

options.text: People share bad news only when it is safe to do so
Trust means nobody needs to check the work again
Transparent teams no longer need any metrics
Trust lets leaders skip all status reports and reviews

questions.explanation: Transparency requires people to surface problems early, and they do that only where it is safe to bring bad news. Trust does not replace evidence; it makes honest evidence possible. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company treats a key supplier as a cost to squeeze, with penalties for every change. Which core value does this neglect?

options.text: Transparency
Respect for people
Alignment
Relentless improvement

questions.explanation: SAFe's respect for people extends beyond employees to customers, suppliers and partners, with long-term, trust-based relationships. Treating a supplier as an adversary damages the flow of value that depends on it. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the five Lean thinking principles that SAFe summarises?

options.text: Plan the full scope up front
Measure individual productivity
Identify the value stream
Maximise resource utilisation

questions.explanation: The five principles are: precisely specify value, identify the value stream, make value flow without interruptions, let the customer pull value, and pursue perfection. Maximising utilisation is a classic cause of long queues. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Arrange the five Lean thinking principles in order.

options.text: Make value flow without interruptions
Precisely specify value by product
Let the customer pull value from the producer
Identify the value stream for each product
Pursue perfection

questions.explanation: Lean thinking starts from value as the customer defines it, maps the stream that delivers it, makes it flow, lets demand pull it, and keeps improving. Pursuing perfection comes last because it repeats the cycle. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team builds stock of features ahead of any request, hoping they will be wanted later. Which Lean thinking principle does this ignore?

options.text: Identify the value stream
Precisely specify value
Let the customer pull value
Make value flow without interruptions

questions.explanation: Pull means producing in response to demand, so work is not built ahead and left to wait. Features built speculatively are inventory: they tie up effort and may never be used. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In Lean thinking, what is waste?

options.text: Any activity that a manager did not approve in advance of it
Any time a person spends at work without a task assigned to them
Any feature that took longer than its estimate
Activity that uses resources but adds no value for the customer

questions.explanation: Waste is anything that consumes time, money or effort without adding value the customer would pay for, such as waiting, handoffs and rework. Idle time is not waste in itself; people kept busy on the wrong work produce it. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team demonstrates a running product to its customer every two weeks instead of sending detailed specifications. Which Agile Manifesto value does it follow?

options.text: Working software over comprehensive documentation
Responding to change over following a plan
Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
Customer collaboration over contract negotiation

questions.explanation: Showing working software in place of documents is the second Manifesto value. Customer collaboration is also at work in a demo, but the contrast in the scenario is between software and documentation. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: According to the Agile Manifesto, what is the primary measure of progress?

options.text: Hours worked
Completed documents
Working software
Tasks assigned

questions.explanation: One of the twelve Manifesto principles states that working software is the primary measure of progress. SAFe applies the same idea at scale through objective evaluation of working systems. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A stakeholder asks for a change a few weeks before release. Which Agile Manifesto principle guides the team's response?

options.text: Record the change and plan it for the next major project
Welcome changing requirements, even late in development
Accept the change only if it needs no extra work
Deliver on the original plan to keep the contract intact

questions.explanation: The Manifesto welcomes changing requirements, even late, because Agile processes harness change for the customer's competitive advantage. The trade-off is then managed through priorities, not refused by default. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the Agile Manifesto say about the pace of work?

options.text: A pace set by the slowest member of the team
Overtime before each release to meet the deadline
Maximum velocity in each iteration, whatever the cost
A sustainable pace that can be kept up indefinitely

questions.explanation: The Manifesto calls for sustainable development, with sponsors, developers and users able to keep a constant pace indefinitely. Overtime before releases borrows from future quality and capacity. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: The Agile Manifesto says that while there is value in the items on the right, the items on the left are valued more. What does this mean?

options.text: Both sides matter equally, and teams choose between them
The items on the right should be removed from Agile projects
The items on the left apply to teams, and those on the right to managers
Plans and documents still matter, but less than their counterparts

questions.explanation: The Manifesto is about emphasis, not rejection: processes, documentation, contracts and plans keep a place, but people, working software, collaboration and responding to change come first. Removing them altogether is a common misreading. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A leader believes people's abilities are fixed and avoids giving anyone stretch assignments. Which idea in SAFe's guidance on leadership and learning does this contradict?

options.text: Set-based design
A growth mindset
Systems thinking
Cost of Delay

questions.explanation: SAFe contrasts a fixed mindset, which assumes ability cannot change, with a growth mindset, which treats ability as something developed through effort and learning. Lean-Agile leaders need the growth mindset to grow others. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe treat the Lean-Agile mindset as a foundation rather than an optional extra?

options.text: Certification requires a mindset test for each employee
Practices without it become rituals that change little
The mindset can be measured precisely, unlike the practices
The mindset removes the need for practices of any kind

questions.explanation: Events and artifacts deliver results only when the beliefs behind them, about value, flow, people and learning, drive decisions. Without the mindset, teams go through the motions while the old system stays in charge. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour shows the core value of transparency on an ART?

options.text: Keeping risks inside the team until they are solved
Showing only the best results at the System Demo
Sharing progress and problems openly, bad news early
Reporting each feature as on track until it is finished

questions.explanation: Transparency means making the real state of work visible, including problems, as early as possible so others can help. Hiding risks or showing only good news removes the chance to act. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice best supports the core value of alignment across an ART?

options.text: Managers assigning tasks to individuals daily
Each team setting its own goals at the start of each iteration
Separate roadmaps for each component team
PI Planning with a shared vision and PI objectives

questions.explanation: PI Planning brings the whole train together around one vision and one set of priorities, then turns them into team objectives everyone has seen. Separate goals and roadmaps pull teams in different directions. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A manager asks why SAFe keeps talking about 'value' instead of 'scope' or 'requirements'. Which Lean idea explains this?

options.text: Value is the number of hours of work completed
Value means the features listed in the original contract
Value is whatever the team can deliver fastest
Value is defined by the customer, and the rest serves it

questions.explanation: Lean thinking starts by specifying value from the customer's point of view; scope and requirements are means to it and may change as the team learns. Measuring hours or contract lines confuses effort with value. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does the Agile Manifesto describe simplicity?

options.text: The art of maximising the amount of work not done
Keeping each iteration to exactly one week
Writing code that beginners can understand at once
Using the smallest possible team for each project

questions.explanation: The Manifesto calls simplicity, the art of maximising the amount of work not done, essential. It is about building only what delivers value, not about team size, code style or iteration length. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.
