questions.prompt: Team members on a train talk face to face at the planning board instead of exchanging tickets. Which Agile Manifesto principle does this apply?

options.text: Business people and developers must work together daily
The best designs emerge from self-organising teams
Build projects around motivated individuals
Face-to-face talk is the best way to convey information

questions.explanation: The Manifesto says the most efficient and effective way of conveying information to and within a team is face-to-face conversation. PI Planning applies it at scale by putting the whole train in one room, real or virtual. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does relentless improvement need time set aside, such as the Inspect and Adapt event?

options.text: Improvement work is not allowed during normal iterations
Otherwise delivery pressure crowds improvement out
Teams cannot find problems without an outside facilitator
Improvement only counts if leaders approve it in an event

questions.explanation: Urgent delivery work always seems more pressing than improving the system, so SAFe builds in events and the IP iteration to protect improvement. Improvement can happen any time; the events make sure it does happen. Topic 2.1, lesson “2.1 · The Lean-Agile mindset and the SAFe Core Values”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Under Principle #1, which of these is one of the economic trade-off parameters SAFe asks teams to understand?

options.text: Meeting length
Team size
Lead time
Office location

questions.explanation: Taking an economic view means understanding trade-offs between development expense, lead time, product cost, value and risk. Changing one moves the others, so decisions are made with all of them in view. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Under Principle #1, why does SAFe favour delivering early and in increments?

options.text: Small deliveries need no testing or integration
Value delivered sooner earns returns and feedback sooner
Incremental work is cheaper because it needs fewer people
Early delivery lets teams skip the planning events

questions.explanation: Delivering early and often starts the flow of value sooner and brings feedback that reduces the risk of building the wrong thing. Small deliveries still need testing and integration, ideally continuous. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: According to Principle #2, what should be viewed as a system?

options.text: The software components that interact with each other at runtime
Both the solution and the enterprise that builds it
The customer's environment where the solution runs
The IT department and its suppliers

questions.explanation: Principle #2 says the solution itself is a system, the enterprise building it is a system too, and the full value stream should be optimised. Looking at software components alone misses the organisation that shapes them. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does systems thinking warn against local optimisation?

options.text: Improving one part can worsen the performance of the whole
Local improvements cost more than system-wide ones
Optimisation is a task for the managers rather than the teams
Local teams lack the skills to improve their own work

questions.explanation: A system's results come from the interactions between its parts, so speeding up one step can build queues or rework elsewhere. The goal is the end-to-end flow of value. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is set-based design?

options.text: Basing all designs on a standard set of company templates
Designing each component in a separate fixed set of teams
Choosing one design early and refining it until it finally works
Keeping several options open and narrowing them as you learn

questions.explanation: Under Principle #3, set-based design keeps multiple design options open and eliminates the weaker ones as knowledge grows. Choosing one design early, point-based design, risks committing before the facts are known. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Under Principle #4, what is the purpose of an integration point?

options.text: To lock the requirements before the next phase begins
To review each person's productivity with their line manager
To get objective evidence about the system and reduce risk
To hand work from development to a separate test team

questions.explanation: Integration points pull the parts together often so that the system can be evaluated and learning can happen. They are not handoffs or phase gates. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which learning cycle does SAFe use for fast, integrated learning under Principle #4?

options.text: Define, Measure, Analyse, Control
Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing
Initiate, Plan, Execute, Close
Plan, Do, Check, Adjust

questions.explanation: SAFe builds solutions in short Plan, Do, Check, Adjust cycles, each ending in an integration point. The distractors come from Six Sigma, traditional project management and team development models. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe prefer frequent integration to a single integration at the end?

options.text: It means teams no longer need to plan
Problems surface while they are still cheap to fix
It lets teams work on separate branches for longer
It removes the need for automated testing

questions.explanation: Late integration hides problems until they are expensive and the schedule has no room; frequent integration brings them out early. It needs more automation and planning, not less. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which milestone best fits Principle #5?

options.text: A PI System Demo of the integrated solution
Completion of the requirements phase
Sign-off of the detailed design document by the board
Approval of the full test plan

questions.explanation: Principle #5 bases milestones on objective evaluation of working systems, so progress is judged by what the integrated solution actually does. Document sign-offs and phase completions can look finished while the solution is not. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each flow accelerator to an example of it.

options.text: Releasing a feature in small slices
Adding capacity where work piles up
A Kanban board with a WIP limit per column
Adding more meetings to each iteration
Keeping the backlog short enough to act on

questions.explanation: These are four of SAFe's eight flow accelerators. Each removes a cause of delay: too much work in progress, large batches, long queues and constrained steps. Extra meetings add to the load. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How many flow accelerators does SAFe describe?

options.text: Five
Eight
Ten
Twelve

questions.explanation: SAFe lists eight: visualize and limit WIP, address bottlenecks, minimize handoffs and dependencies, get faster feedback, work in smaller batches, reduce queue length, optimize time in the zone, and remediate legacy policies and practices. Ten is the number of principles. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train's work waits for weeks in front of one shared database team. Which flow accelerator applies first?

options.text: Address bottlenecks
Get faster feedback
Remediate legacy policies and practices
Optimize time 'in the zone'

questions.explanation: A single constrained step that work queues in front of is a bottleneck, and the flow of the whole train is limited by it. Options include adding capacity, cross-training or reducing the demand on it. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: According to Little's Law, what happens to wait time when a queue grows while the processing rate stays the same?

options.text: It falls, since larger queues are processed in bulk
It becomes impossible to predict in any way
It stays the same, since the rate has not changed
It rises in proportion to how much is waiting

questions.explanation: Little's Law says average wait time equals queue length divided by processing rate, so a longer queue at the same rate means proportionally longer waits. This is why SAFe asks trains to reduce queue length. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Developers are interrupted by meetings and requests all day and rarely get long stretches of focused work. Which flow accelerator addresses this?

options.text: Reduce queue length
Minimize handoffs and dependencies
Work in smaller batches
Optimize time 'in the zone'

questions.explanation: Knowledge work goes fastest when people can focus without constant switching, so SAFe asks trains to protect time in the zone. Smaller batches and shorter queues address other causes of delay. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do smaller batches improve flow?

options.text: Less waiting, less variability and faster feedback
They make each task cheaper to plan in detail
They let each person stay fully busy all of the time
They remove the need to integrate the work

questions.explanation: Small batches move through the system faster, reduce the variability that builds queues and return feedback sooner, which lowers the cost of mistakes. Keeping everyone busy is utilisation, which tends to lengthen queues. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Every change at a company needs approval from a monthly change board, even small, low-risk fixes. What does the relevant SAFe flow accelerator ask leaders to do?

options.text: Fix outdated policies that delay flow
Get feedback from customers sooner
Split work into smaller batches
Limit the work in progress on each team

questions.explanation: The accelerator is 'remediate legacy policies and practices': old rules designed for a different way of working often cause the biggest delays. A risk-based approval route for small changes would remove a month of waiting. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which SAFe event is the main example of the cross-domain synchronisation called for by Principle #7?

options.text: System Demo
Iteration Retrospective
PI Planning
Team Sync

questions.explanation: PI Planning brings business, product, architecture and teams together on a regular cadence to plan as one. Team Sync and the retrospective are team-level events, and the System Demo reviews work done. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does synchronisation help a train with many teams?

options.text: It removes the need for a shared ART backlog
Teams integrate and resolve issues at the same time
Each team can pick its own iteration start and end dates
Fewer teams need to attend the shared events

questions.explanation: Synchronisation lets multiple perspectives be understood, resolved and integrated at the same time, because everyone plans, integrates and demonstrates on shared dates. Different iteration dates break it. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Under Principle #8, which management approach best unlocks the motivation of knowledge workers?

options.text: Publish a weekly ranking of individual output
Specify the method for each task in detail
Give autonomy, a clear purpose and room to build mastery
Pay a bonus for each story that a person completes on time

questions.explanation: Knowledge workers are motivated mainly by autonomy, mastery and purpose, and they often know more about their work than their managers. Individual incentives and close control tend to undermine collaboration. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which three factors of intrinsic motivation, described by Daniel Pink, does SAFe cite?

options.text: Rules, rewards and regular reviews
Speed, scale and savings
Pay, status and job security
Autonomy, mastery and purpose

questions.explanation: SAFe draws on Pink's work to explain Principle #8: people do their best knowledge work when they control how they work, can get better at it and see why it matters. Pay must be fair, but beyond that it does not motivate creative work. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which three properties make a decision a candidate for centralisation under Principle #9?

options.text: Urgent, low-cost and easy to undo later
Frequent, time-critical and needing local information
Rare, long-lasting and with economies of scale
Small, reversible and affecting a single team

questions.explanation: Principle #9 centralises decisions that are infrequent, long-lasting and have significant economies of scale, and decentralises the rest, which are frequent, time-critical and need local information. A common technology platform is the classic example of a centralised decision. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team must decide today how to fix a defect affecting customers, and the manager who normally approves is travelling. What does Principle #9 suggest?

options.text: Escalate to the portfolio level for a ruling
Ask each team on the train to vote on it
Leave it to the team, since it is time-critical and local
Wait for the manager to return, since approvals keep quality high

questions.explanation: Time-critical decisions that need local knowledge should be made by the people closest to the work, within a decision framework. Waiting adds delay that costs customers. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Under Principle #10, what should a company do when a new value stream emerges?

options.text: Reorganise teams and trains around it
Assign it to the department with the most free capacity
Ask each existing team to take a share of the work
Create a project team and disband it after launch

questions.explanation: Organising around value means building long-lived teams and trains around how value flows, and reorganising when that flow changes. Spreading new work across departments recreates the handoffs SAFe tries to remove. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe say that functional silos slow the flow of value?

options.text: Specialists in silos are less skilled than the generalists
Silos cost more to staff than cross-functional teams
Departments cannot share Agile tools across silos
Work crosses many handoffs and queues between departments

questions.explanation: When each skill sits in its own department, every piece of work passes through several handoffs and waits in each queue. Cross-functional teams and trains remove those delays. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe its ten Lean-Agile principles?

options.text: Specific to software teams rather than business
Immutable and underlying, guiding the practices
Optional, to be chosen per team as needed
Temporary, to be replaced as teams mature

questions.explanation: SAFe calls its principles immutable and underlying: practices may be adapted to context, but the principles they rest on stay. That is why adaptation decisions are tested against the principles. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles.

questions.prompt: A team spends a month gathering data to make a small, reversible decision that costs little either way. Which principle would advise deciding sooner?

options.text: #1 Take an economic view
#5 Base milestones on objective evaluation of working systems
#3 Assume variability; preserve options
#7 Apply cadence, synchronize with cross-domain planning

questions.explanation: An economic view weighs the cost of delay against the value of more information; for a cheap, reversible decision, a month of delay costs more than a wrong first choice. Preserving options is for expensive, uncertain design choices. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How do Principles #3 and #4 work together?

options.text: #3 fixes the design early, so that #4 can then build it much faster
Both apply to portfolio funding but not to design
Options stay open while fast learning cycles show which to keep
#4 replaces the need for options once integration starts

questions.explanation: Set-based design keeps alternatives alive, and short build-integrate-learn cycles produce the evidence that narrows them. Together they let teams commit late and well. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train estimates what a delay would cost before choosing what to build next. Which principle is it applying?

options.text: #1 Take an economic view
#6 Make value flow without interruptions
#2 Apply systems thinking
#9 Decentralize decision-making

questions.explanation: Using the cost of delay to sequence work is an economic decision, and it is the basis of WSJF. Systems thinking and flow inform it, but the act of weighing economic impact is Principle #1. Topic 2.2, lesson “2.2a · The ten SAFe Lean-Agile Principles: the full set and #1 to #5”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A Product Owner uses AI to draft acceptance criteria for a story. What is the Product Owner's responsibility?

options.text: Accept them as written, since the AI covers more of the cases
Review and refine them with the team before accepting them
Send them straight to the testers without any review
Ask the AI to accept the story once the work is done

questions.explanation: AI can speed up drafting, but the Product Owner remains accountable for the content and the team needs a shared understanding of it, so the criteria are reviewed and refined together. AI drafts are inputs, not decisions. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which use of AI best supports a Scrum Master/Team Coach in a retrospective?

options.text: Rating each member's contribution to the iteration
Deciding which improvement the team must adopt next
Writing the retrospective outcome before the meeting
Clustering the team's anonymous comments into themes

questions.explanation: AI can take on preparation, such as grouping input into themes, so the team spends its time discussing and deciding. The decisions stay with the team, and rating individuals would damage the safety a retrospective needs. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: AI is used to automate some value stream activities. Which measure would show whether this has helped?

options.text: More prompts written by each team member
More tokens used per team in each iteration
Shorter flow time from request to delivery
More AI tools licensed across the train

questions.explanation: The goal is faster flow of value, so the right evidence is flow measures such as flow time and flow velocity. Tool counts, tokens and prompts measure activity, not improvement. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team adds an AI feature to a customer solution. Which SAFe practice still decides whether it delivered value?

options.text: Asking the AI model whether customers like the new feature
Checking that the feature uses the latest model
Validating its benefit hypothesis with real measures
Counting how many AI models the feature uses

questions.explanation: An AI feature is still a feature: it has a benefit hypothesis that is tested with real outcomes after release. The technology inside it says nothing about whether customers gained value. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe treat AI in relation to its Lean-Agile principles?

options.text: AI use is outside the scope of SAFe guidance
The principles still apply, and they guide how AI is used
The principles apply to people, but not to AI-enabled work
AI replaces the principles with data-driven rules

questions.explanation: AI changes the tools and the speed, not the principles: economic view, systems thinking and flow still decide where AI helps. SAFe's AI guidance sits inside the framework rather than beside it. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An ART wants to use AI to speed up its Continuous Delivery Pipeline. Which use fits best?

options.text: AI-generated automated tests that people review
Removing code review now that AI writes the code
Letting AI deploy to production without any checks
Skipping integration since AI-written code is consistent

questions.explanation: AI can help build and maintain the test automation that the pipeline depends on, with people reviewing what it produces. Removing checks, reviews or integration because AI is involved lowers built-in quality. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: AI helps a team write code twice as fast, but stories now wait longer in testing. What does systems thinking suggest?

options.text: Ask testers to work overtime until the queue clears
The bottleneck moved; improve the whole flow, not one step
Accept the wait, since development is now efficient
Generate code even faster to clear the whole backlog sooner

questions.explanation: Speeding up one step moves the constraint downstream, so the end-to-end flow barely changes. Systems thinking looks for the new bottleneck, for example by using AI to help with testing too. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A Product Manager uses AI to analyse thousands of customer reviews. How should the results be used?

options.text: As a replacement for interviews with customers
As proof that the current roadmap is correct
As input to hypotheses that are then tested with customers
As the final list of features to build in the next two PIs

questions.explanation: AI can find patterns in large volumes of feedback, which makes it a good source of hypotheses. Customer centricity still requires validating them with real customers before investing. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Before pasting a customer contract into an AI tool to summarise it, what should an Agilist check?

options.text: That the summary will be written in bullet points
That the tool is approved for confidential company data
That the contract runs to no more than ten pages in total
That the tool runs the newest model available

questions.explanation: Confidential documents may only go into tools approved for that data, because public tools may store or reuse what they receive. Length, format and model version do not address the risk. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does human-in-the-loop mean when an ART uses AI?

options.text: A person is named as the owner of each AI tool
A person checks AI output before it drives decisions
A person types each prompt the AI receives from the team
A person reviews AI output once a quarter in a report

questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop places a person's evaluation between the AI's output and the decision or action it informs. A quarterly report checks after the fact, and owning a tool is not the same as checking its output. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest reason to start AI adoption on an ART with small experiments?

options.text: They show cheaply where AI helps the flow of value
They prove that AI can replace whole roles on a train
They avoid having to involve the business in any way
They are required before any AI licence can be bought

questions.explanation: Small, measured experiments follow SAFe's build-measure-learn thinking: they find where AI really improves flow before money and time are committed. They involve the business, and replacing roles is not the aim. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant drafts PI objectives for each team before PI Planning. What is the risk if teams simply adopt them?

options.text: The AI itself will be held responsible for any missed objectives
People commit to objectives they neither wrote nor believe in
The objectives will be written in too much detail
Business Owners will be unable to read them

questions.explanation: PI objectives work because teams create them and commit to them. Adopting drafts wholesale skips the thinking and the ownership that make the commitment real; AI can at most offer a starting point. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which AI use helps make value flow without interruptions?

options.text: Doubling the work in progress with AI help
Generating extra reports for each iteration
Answering routine questions so experts stay focused
Adding an AI approval step to each handoff in the flow

questions.explanation: Routine questions pull experts out of focused work and add waits; an assistant that answers them protects time in the zone. Extra approval steps, reports and WIP add delay. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: SAFe's guidance says AI can improve customer insight. Which example fits?

options.text: Replacing personas with a list of AI features
Finding patterns in support tickets and usage data
Writing down customers' needs without speaking to them
Setting prices for customers without any review

questions.explanation: Analysing large volumes of tickets and usage data for patterns is a strength of AI and feeds customer insight. It complements talking to customers rather than replacing it. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Source: SAFe · Artificial Intelligence in SAFe.

questions.prompt: A team's AI-generated code passes its tests, but nobody on the team understands it. Which built-in quality concern does this raise?

options.text: Cost: AI-generated code needs a separate licence
Maintainability: unclear code is hard to change safely
Style: AI code always uses the wrong naming rules
Speed: the code was produced too quickly to be safe

questions.explanation: Built-in quality includes code the team can understand, change and own; passing tests is necessary but not enough. The team should review, simplify and document such code before it becomes a liability. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures 'empowering agility with AI'?

options.text: AI is a separate initiative run outside the ARTs
AI makes the SAFe events unnecessary for most of the trains
AI amplifies learning and delivery, under human judgement
AI replaces the Agile teams with fully automated pipelines

questions.explanation: The study guide topic is about using AI to strengthen how teams and trains learn and deliver, with people accountable for the results. AI used outside the ARTs, or in place of their events, misses the point. Topic 2.3, lesson “2.3 · Empowering agility with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe an Agile Team?

options.text: A group of specialists in one discipline who hand finished work to the next department
A temporary group formed for one project and disbanded when the project closes
A cross-functional group of ten or fewer who can define, build, test and deliver value
A group of any size that reports to a single project manager

questions.explanation: An Agile Team is cross-functional, typically ten or fewer people, with all the skills to define, build, test and deliver. A single-discipline team is the functional silo that cross-functional teams replace. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Source: SAFe · Agile Teams; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which two roles does every SAFe Agile Team include?

options.text: Product Owner and Scrum Master/Team Coach
Project Manager and Business Analyst
Product Manager and Business Owner
Release Train Engineer and System Architect

questions.explanation: Each Agile Team has a Product Owner and a Scrum Master/Team Coach. The Release Train Engineer and System Architect are real SAFe roles, which makes them tempting, but they serve the whole train. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Source: SAFe · Agile Teams; SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline.

questions.prompt: A new team expects its Scrum Master/Team Coach to hand out tasks and chase individuals for status. What is the role in SAFe?

options.text: A technical lead who makes the design decisions for the team
A servant leader who coaches the team and facilitates its events
A project manager who owns the schedule and reports on scope
A line manager who allocates the work and appraises each member

questions.explanation: The Scrum Master/Team Coach is a servant leader and coach and is usually not a people manager. Assigning tasks is the traditional management answer; in SAFe the team organises its own work. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Source: SAFe · Scrum Master/Team Coach.

questions.prompt: On a SAFe Agile Team, who decides the order of the work in the team backlog?

options.text: The Product Owner
The Scrum Master/Team Coach
The Release Train Engineer
The development manager

questions.explanation: The Product Owner maximises the value the team delivers by keeping the team backlog aligned with customer and stakeholder needs. A manager deciding the order is the trap: priority belongs to the Product Owner, not to the reporting line. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Source: SAFe · Product Owner.

questions.prompt: How many people does an Agile Release Train typically include?

options.text: 5 to 11

questions.explanation: An ART is typically 50 to 125 people. Five to eleven is the size of a single team, not of a team of teams. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Source: SAFe · Agile Release Train; SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline.

questions.prompt: Match each Agile Release Train role to its main responsibility.

options.text: Responsible for governance, fitness for use and return on investment
Assigns daily tasks to individual team members
Defines the architecture and identifies nonfunctional requirements
Servant leader and coach for the train
Defines features and prioritises the ART backlog

questions.explanation: The RTE coaches the train, Product Management owns what gets built, the System Architect guides the technical design and Business Owners carry business responsibility. Nobody on the train assigns daily tasks to individuals; teams manage their own work. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Source: SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline.

questions.prompt: A company forms a group of teams to deliver one release and plans to disband it afterwards. How does this differ from an Agile Release Train?

options.text: An ART is long-lived and keeps delivering in a value stream
An ART delivers one release and is then re-formed
An ART has no teams, only individual specialists
An ART is disbanded sooner, at the end of each Planning Interval

questions.explanation: An ART is a long-lived team of Agile teams that incrementally develops, delivers and often operates solutions in a development value stream. Forming and disbanding around a release is project thinking. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Source: SAFe · Agile Release Train; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which three dimensions make up Team and Technical Agility?

options.text: People and skills, process and flow, technology and tools
Scrum teams, Kanban teams, Extreme Programming teams
Agile Teams, Teams of Agile Teams, Built-In Quality
Planning, execution and delivery, retrospection

questions.explanation: The competency has three dimensions: Agile Teams, Teams of Agile Teams and Built-In Quality. Scrum and Kanban are methods teams use inside the first dimension; they are not the dimensions. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Source: SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline.

questions.prompt: One team provides self-service build and hosting services so that other teams on the train can deliver without waiting. Which team topology is this?

options.text: Enabling team
Complicated subsystem team
Platform team
Stream-aligned team

questions.explanation: A platform team provides services that reduce the load on stream-aligned teams. A stream-aligned team is the one that delivers value directly along a flow of work to a customer. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train builds for five iterations and plans a testing phase at the end of the PI. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: The testing phase should be moved into the following PI
A testing phase is acceptable when a separate team carries it out
Quality has to be built in throughout, not inspected in at the end
End-of-PI testing is preferred, since it is more efficient

questions.explanation: Built-In Quality means quality practices run throughout development and shift learning to the left. A late test phase finds problems when they are most expensive to fix. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Source: SAFe · Built-In Quality.

questions.prompt: A train drops automated tests to finish more stories this PI. What does SAFe predict?

options.text: Velocity and predictability fall as rework accumulates
Velocity rises for good, since testing was waste
Quality is unaffected, since demos reveal defects
Predictability improves, since the scope is smaller

questions.explanation: SAFe lists improved velocity and delivery predictability among the benefits of Built-In Quality, so removing it erodes both. The belief that tests are waste is the trap: the time saved returns later as rework. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Source: SAFe · Built-In Quality.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four aspects of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline in order.

options.text: Continuous Deployment
Continuous Integration
Continuous Exploration
Release on Demand

questions.explanation: The pipeline runs from Continuous Exploration through Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment to Release on Demand. Deployment comes before release: solutions reach production first and are released when the business chooses. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four activities of Continuous Integration in order.

options.text: Build
Develop
Test end-to-end
Stage

questions.explanation: Continuous Integration develops, builds, tests end-to-end and stages the solution. Staging comes last: the solution is validated in a staging environment before it moves on to deployment. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Integration.

questions.prompt: A feature is running in production behind a switch, invisible to customers, until marketing is ready. Which SAFe concept is this?

options.text: Separating deployment from release
Set-based design of the architecture
Continuous Exploration of customer needs
Synchronisation of the release train

questions.explanation: SAFe decouples deployment from release, so changes can reach production without changing what customers see. Release then becomes a business decision that needs no new deployment. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Source: SAFe · Continuous Deployment; SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: What does CALMR stand for in SAFe's approach to DevOps?

options.text: Cadence, Alignment, Learning, Metrics, Release
Collaboration, Agility, Leadership, Monitoring, Reliability
Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement, Recovery
Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement, Sharing

questions.explanation: CALMR is culture, automation, lean flow, measurement and recovery. The version ending in sharing is CALMS, the general DevOps acronym; SAFe replaces sharing with recovery and treats sharing as part of culture. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Source: SAFe · CALMR; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: In SAFe, who decides when deployed functionality is released to customers?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer, at the end of every PI
The business, through Product Management and Business Owners
The operations team, when production capacity allows
The developers, as soon as the code has passed all of its automated tests

questions.explanation: Release on Demand makes release a business decision based on market and customer needs, answered by Product Management and Business Owners. Releasing at each PI boundary confuses the planning cadence with release. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand.

questions.prompt: A company responds to slow releases by creating a DevOps team that sits between development and operations. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: DevOps is a mindset, a culture and practices shared by all, not another silo
A separate DevOps team is the recommended first step for any newly launched train
DevOps applies to operations staff and not to the Agile teams
DevOps is a set of tools, so a dedicated tooling team is sufficient

questions.explanation: SAFe defines DevOps as a mindset, a culture and a set of technical practices that break down the silos between those who build and those who operate. A team placed between the two adds a third silo. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Source: SAFe · DevOps.

questions.prompt: Which two ways of working does SAFe support for Agile Teams to manage their work?

options.text: SAFe Scrum and SAFe Team Kanban
Waterfall and PRINCE2 phases
Design Thinking and Lean Startup
Six Sigma and DMAIC projects

questions.explanation: SAFe teams use SAFe Scrum, with fixed-length iterations, or SAFe Team Kanban, with continuous flow and WIP limits, and both plan and integrate on the train's cadence. Design Thinking and Lean Startup are used in SAFe, but not as a team's way of managing its work. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team works mostly on unpredictable, interrupt-driven requests, such as system maintenance. Which way of working does SAFe suggest it consider?

options.text: A separate project for each request
SAFe Team Kanban
A waterfall phase for each request type
SAFe Scrum with four-week iterations

questions.explanation: Kanban suits work that arrives unpredictably, because it pulls items continuously within WIP limits instead of fixing a plan for each iteration. The team still plans with the train at PI Planning. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does a Scrum Master/Team Coach facilitate in SAFe?

options.text: Team events, flow and the removal of impediments
Assigning tasks and approving each person's work
Prioritising the team backlog and accepting stories
Setting the team's architecture and design standards

questions.explanation: The Scrum Master/Team Coach is a servant leader who coaches the team, facilitates its events, helps it improve flow and removes impediments. Backlog priority and story acceptance belong to the Product Owner. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility belongs to the Product Owner?

options.text: Accepting stories as done once they meet their criteria
Facilitating the team's retrospective and its team sync
Approving the train's budget for the coming PI
Running the System Demo for the whole train on their own

questions.explanation: The Product Owner owns the team backlog: defining, prioritising and accepting stories. Facilitation is the Scrum Master/Team Coach's job, and budgets and the System Demo sit at the train level. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe prefer cross-functional teams to teams organised by skill?

options.text: They let managers move people between projects each week
They can define, build and test value with few handoffs
They make it easier to measure each specialist's output
They need less training, because each person does one task

questions.explanation: A cross-functional team holds the skills to deliver a working increment itself, so work does not wait in queues between departments. Skill-based teams pass each item through several handoffs. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a team's iteration goal?

options.text: A brief summary of what the team aims to achieve
The velocity target that the manager sets for the team
The full scope of the PI, written out as stories
A list of each task assigned to each team member

questions.explanation: Iteration goals summarise the business and technical outcomes the team agrees to achieve in the iteration, which aligns the team and communicates its focus to others. They are not task lists or velocity targets. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team's Product Owner is away for weeks and nobody can answer questions about stories. What is the most likely effect?

options.text: Nothing changes, since the backlog is already written
Quality improves because developers decide alone
Work stalls or drifts for lack of decisions
Velocity rises because there are fewer interruptions

questions.explanation: Stories are placeholders for conversation, and the Product Owner answers the questions that arise while they are built. Without that, teams wait or guess, and guesses often have to be redone. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which team event does a SAFe team use to plan and commit to the work of the next iteration?

options.text: Team Sync
Iteration Review
Backlog Refinement
Iteration Planning

questions.explanation: In Iteration Planning the team agrees its iteration goals and the stories it will work on. Backlog Refinement prepares stories ahead of time, Team Sync coordinates daily, and the Iteration Review shows what was done. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe recommend that team members be dedicated to one team?

options.text: Shared people cannot be trained in SAFe methods
Teams with shared members cannot hold a Team Sync
Dedicated people can be paid less than shared ones
Splitting people adds switching and delays

questions.explanation: People split across several teams lose time switching contexts and make each team wait for them, which slows flow and weakens commitment. Dedicated, stable teams also build trust and shared knowledge. Topic 3.1, lesson “3.1 · Cross-functional Agile Teams”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which role serves as the chief Scrum Master for an ART?

options.text: Business Owner
Product Management
Solution Train Engineer
Release Train Engineer

questions.explanation: The Release Train Engineer is a servant leader and coach for the ART, facilitating its events and helping it deliver. The System Architect owns the architecture, Product Management the backlog and vision. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which group holds primary responsibility for governance, compliance and return on investment for an ART?

options.text: Product Owners
Scrum Masters/Team Coaches
Business Owners
System Architects

questions.explanation: Business Owners are the key stakeholders with business and technical responsibility for governance, compliance and return on investment for the solution the ART builds. They take part in PI Planning and assign business value to PI objectives. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train is organised as a front-end team, a back-end team and a database team, and every feature needs all three. What does SAFe suggest?

options.text: Favour stream-aligned teams that can work end to end
Add a coordination team to manage the handoffs between them
Merge the three into one large team of about thirty people
Keep the structure and plan the handoffs earlier in the PI

questions.explanation: Teams organised by technical layer make every feature a three-way dependency. Stream-aligned teams that can build a feature across layers remove most of those handoffs; a thirty-person team is too large to work as one. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each team topology to its purpose.

options.text: Approves the release of each feature
Delivers a continuous flow of value in one area
Owns a part that needs deep specialist knowledge
Provides services that other teams use
Helps other teams build new skills

questions.explanation: SAFe uses four team topologies. Most teams are stream-aligned; the others exist to reduce their load, through specialist subsystems, self-service platforms or help with new capabilities. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which situation best fits a complicated subsystem team?

options.text: A customer-facing checkout that changes each week
A codec that needs rare signal-processing skills
Coaching teams that are new to test automation
Shared build tools used by each team on the train

questions.explanation: A complicated subsystem team owns a part that needs specialist knowledge most teams do not have. Shared build tools suit a platform team, and coaching suits an enabling team. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Two teams on a train wait every iteration for a shared environment team to set up test environments. Which kind of team could reduce this dependency?

options.text: A complicated subsystem team for the whole network
Self-service environments from a platform team
An enabling team that writes more documentation
A second environment team doing the same work

questions.explanation: Platform teams turn shared needs into self-service, so stream-aligned teams can get what they need without waiting in a queue. Adding a second environment team keeps the handoff. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: About how many teams does a typical ART include?

options.text: Two or three
Twenty to thirty or more
About five to twelve
Exactly ten, always

questions.explanation: An ART typically has 50 to 125 people in around five to twelve teams. Fewer than that is usually a single team's work; many more exceeds the size at which a team of teams can plan and work together. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe keep an ART to roughly 125 people at most?

options.text: Typical PI Planning venues cannot hold more than about 125 people
Licence costs for SAFe tools rise above that number
Labour law limits the size of any single department
Larger groups struggle to keep the trust and contact it needs

questions.explanation: SAFe cites Dunbar's number: beyond about 150 people, personal relationships and trust are hard to maintain, and a train depends on them. Venue size is a practical concern, not the reason for the limit. Topic 3.2, lesson “3.2 · Organizing around value with Agile Release Trains”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of SAFe's basic built-in quality practices that apply to all teams?

options.text: Pairing and peer review
A separate quality department
Annual quality audit
End-of-PI test phase

questions.explanation: SAFe's basic practices for all teams include shifting learning left, pairing and peer review, collective ownership and T-shaped skills, artifact standards and a definition of done, and workflow automation. A test phase at the end treats quality as a stage. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team finds most of its defects in the last week before release. Which built-in quality idea is it missing?

options.text: A longer final test phase before each release
Shift learning left to find problems sooner
Collective ownership of the testing department
More detailed defect reports after each release

questions.explanation: Shifting learning left moves testing, review and feedback earlier, where problems are cheaper to fix. A longer test phase finds the same defects just as late. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does a definition of done do for built-in quality?

options.text: Fixes the deadline for each feature in the PI
Lists each person's tasks for the next iteration
Sets a shared standard for when work is finished
Records who approved each story for the release

questions.explanation: A definition of done states what must be true before work counts as complete, such as tested, reviewed and documented, so 'done' means the same to everyone and quality is not left for later. Task lists and deadlines say nothing about whether work is finished to standard. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: One developer is the only person who understands a critical module, so every change to it waits for them. Which built-in quality practice addresses this?

options.text: Collective ownership with T-shaped skills
A stricter definition of done
Workflow automation of the deployment
A longer review of each change

questions.explanation: Collective ownership and T-shaped skills spread knowledge so that several people can change any part, removing a single-person bottleneck and its risk. Pairing is a common way to get there. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe say built-in quality speeds delivery up rather than slowing it down?

options.text: Customers accept lower quality in early releases
Less rework and fewer defects let work flow faster
Testers work faster than developers on average
Quality work can be skipped when deadlines are near

questions.explanation: Defects found late cause rework, delays and unpredictability; building quality in avoids most of that cost. Skipping quality under pressure borrows time that is repaid with interest. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A marketing team adopts SAFe. How does built-in quality apply to it?

options.text: It does not, since built-in quality is for software teams
Only through automated unit tests of each campaign
Through standards, review and checks that suit its work
Through a quality phase at the end of each PI

questions.explanation: SAFe applies built-in quality to all kinds of work, including business functions, with practices suited to the domain, such as standards, peer review and definition of done. Unit tests are a software practice. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which built-in quality practice removes manual steps from the path to production?

options.text: Collective ownership
Pair programming
Definition of done
Workflow automation

questions.explanation: Workflow automation removes manual steps from the path to production, which makes delivery faster and more reliable. The other practices improve quality in other ways but do not automate the flow. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice best builds quality into software as it is written?

options.text: Test-first development, such as TDD and BDD
A code freeze two weeks before each release
Counting the lines of code each person writes
Manual regression testing at the end of the PI

questions.explanation: Writing tests before or alongside the code makes quality part of development itself and gives fast feedback. End-of-PI testing and code freezes are inspection after the fact. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team has many open defects, and its manager proposes a 'hardening' iteration before each release to fix them. What is SAFe's concern?

options.text: Managers may not schedule iterations in SAFe
It treats quality as a phase, not as part of the work
Defects should wait until customers report them
Hardening iterations are too short to fix any defects

questions.explanation: A regular hardening phase signals that quality is not built in, and it delays feedback on defects. The fix is to find and stop defects as work is done, so each increment is releasable. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of peer review in SAFe's built-in quality?

options.text: Catching problems early and spreading knowledge
Ranking developers by the quality of their work
Approving work on behalf of the Product Owner
Replacing automated tests with manual checks

questions.explanation: Peer review finds problems while they are cheap to fix and spreads understanding of the work across the team. It complements automated tests and is not a way to rank people. Topic 3.3, lesson “3.3 · Built-in Quality practices”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which aspect of the Continuous Delivery Pipeline turns ideas into a prioritised ART backlog?

options.text: Continuous Integration
Continuous Exploration
Continuous Deployment
Release on Demand

questions.explanation: Continuous Exploration researches the market and customers, forms hypotheses and defines features, producing a prioritised backlog. Integration, deployment and release follow it. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Code is merged, built and tested in a staging environment several times a day. Which aspect of the pipeline is this?

options.text: Continuous Exploration
Continuous Deployment
Release on Demand
Continuous Integration

questions.explanation: Continuous Integration develops, builds, tests end to end and validates the solution in a staging environment. Moving it to production is Continuous Deployment. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does Continuous Deployment do in SAFe's pipeline?

options.text: Merges developers' code into one shared branch
Releases every change to all customers at once
Decides which features to build next
Puts changes in production, ready to release

questions.explanation: Continuous Deployment takes validated changes into production, where they can be verified and monitored, often hidden behind feature toggles. Releasing them to customers is a separate business decision. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In CALMR, what does the 'L' stand for?

options.text: Licensing
Lean flow
Leadership
Learning

questions.explanation: CALMR stands for Culture, Automation, Lean flow, Measurement and Recovery. Lean flow means small batches, limited WIP and visible work across the pipeline. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team can restore service within minutes after a failed deployment by rolling back. Which CALMR element is this?

options.text: Culture
Measurement
Recovery
Automation

questions.explanation: Recovery is about designing for low-risk releases and quick restoration, such as rollback and fix-forward. Automation helps it happen, but the capability being described is recovery. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which DevOps practice reduces the risk that a release breaks for all customers at once?

options.text: Releasing to a small group first, as a canary
Waiting for all features before releasing any
Turning off monitoring during the release window
Releasing larger batches less often to save effort

questions.explanation: Canary and other progressive releases expose a change to a small group, watch the results and widen or roll back. Larger, rarer releases raise the risk of each one. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main point of a shared DevOps culture in SAFe?

options.text: Operations reviews and approves each developer's code
Builders and operators share responsibility for value
A separate DevOps team owns the pipeline for everyone
Development hands each release to operations to run

questions.explanation: DevOps culture breaks down the wall between building and running solutions, so both sides own the flow of value into production. A separate DevOps team in the middle recreates the handoff. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure best shows whether a train's Continuous Delivery Pipeline is improving?

options.text: More documents produced for each release
More features started at the same time as each other
Shorter lead time from idea to value in production
More approvals collected before each deployment

questions.explanation: The pipeline exists to move value from idea to customers quickly and safely, so lead time, with quality and recovery measures, shows whether it is improving. Documents, approvals and started work are not value. Topic 3.4, lesson “3.4 · The Continuous Delivery Pipeline and DevOps”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe define Customer Centricity?

options.text: A rule that customers approve each requirement before work begins
A mindset focused on positive customer experiences across products and services
A department that collects customer complaints and reports the trends to management
A metric that tracks the number of features delivered per customer

questions.explanation: Customer Centricity is a mindset focused on creating positive customer experiences through the full set of products and services. It is not a department or a sign-off step, which is how traditional organisations often treat the customer. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Source: SAFe · Customer Centricity; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A platform train builds services that are used only by other trains inside the company. Who are its customers in SAFe's terms?

options.text: The external buyers of the company's end products alone
Internal customers, the groups that use its services
The executives who approved the platform's budget
It has no customers, since nobody pays for the services

questions.explanation: SAFe distinguishes internal customers, who use what a train builds inside the company, from external ones. A platform still has customers, and treating it as having none is how platforms drift from real needs. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Source: SAFe · Customer Centricity.

questions.prompt: A sponsor wants a full requirements specification signed off before any customer has been consulted. How does design thinking differ?

options.text: It replaces customer research with rapid coding
It fixes the solution first and then looks for users who might want it
It postpones all design until after the release
It starts by understanding the problem and the context of use

questions.explanation: Design thinking focuses on understanding the problem, the context of use and how the solution evolves, where a waterfall approach focuses on requirements. It does not skip research; it starts with it. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Source: SAFe · Design Thinking.

questions.prompt: Which four qualities should a solution defined by Product Management have?

options.text: Desirable, viable, feasible, sustainable
Scalable, secure, stable, simple
Planned, funded, staffed, approved
Fast, cheap, good, complete

questions.explanation: Product Management defines solutions that are desirable, viable, feasible and sustainable. The other sets describe technical qualities or project status, not the balance of customer, business and technical fit. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Source: SAFe · Product Management.

questions.prompt: A team writes a short profile of 'Dana, a night-shift nurse who orders supplies on a phone' to guide its design. Which tool is this?

options.text: A benefit hypothesis
A persona
A story map
A portfolio canvas

questions.explanation: A persona is a representative characterisation of a user. A story map arranges user activities and stories; it shows what users do, not who they are. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Design thinking alternates between divergent and convergent thinking. What does that mean in practice?

options.text: Build one solution, then defend it against criticism
Collect requirements first, then freeze them for delivery
Split the team in two and merge the results at the end
Explore many possibilities, then narrow to the best choice

questions.explanation: Divergence widens the range of problems or solutions considered, and convergence narrows it to a choice. Collecting and freezing requirements is the waterfall pattern that design thinking is contrasted with. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Source: SAFe · Design Thinking.

questions.prompt: What does the ART backlog hold?

options.text: Epics awaiting portfolio approval
Features and enablers for the train
Defects reported by customers alone
Stories and tasks for one team

questions.explanation: The ART backlog holds the features and enablers that enhance the solution and extend its architectural runway. Epics sit in the portfolio backlog and stories in team backlogs, one level up and one level down. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Who is responsible for prioritising the features in the ART backlog?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer
The Product Owners by majority vote
The Business Owners' line managers
Product Management

questions.explanation: Product Management manages and prioritises the ART backlog. The Release Train Engineer is the common wrong answer: the RTE facilitates the train and its events and does not own the content. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · Product Management; SAFe · Features and Capabilities.

questions.prompt: Who defines the enablers that prepare a train's technical foundation for future features?

options.text: The System Architect
Product Management alone
The Epic Owner
The Scrum Master/Team Coach

questions.explanation: Product Management defines features, and the System Architect defines enablers. The Epic Owner works at the portfolio level, shepherding epics, and does not define a train's enablers. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · Features and Capabilities.

questions.prompt: How large is a feature in SAFe?

options.text: Small enough for one ART to deliver within a PI
Large enough to span several trains in a Solution Train
Large enough to need several PIs and a business case
Small enough for one team to finish in an iteration

questions.explanation: A feature is sized to be delivered by a single ART within one PI. Work that fits in an iteration is a story, and work that spans several PIs with a business case is an epic. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · Features and Capabilities; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Besides a name, what does a well-formed feature include?

options.text: A task breakdown and hour estimates
A project charter and a risk register
A Lean business case and an MVP definition
A benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: A feature carries a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria. A Lean business case and an MVP belong to epics, which is the confusion this question tests. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe calculate Weighted Shortest Job First?

options.text: Business value multiplied by the size of the job
Cost of Delay added to the risk exposure
Job size divided by the velocity of the team
Cost of Delay divided by job duration or size

questions.explanation: WSJF is the relative Cost of Delay divided by the relative job duration, for which job size is used as a proxy. Multiplying value by size would favour the largest jobs, the opposite of the intent. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · WSJF; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a component of Cost of Delay in WSJF?

options.text: Sunk cost to date
Stakeholder seniority
Team velocity
Time criticality

questions.explanation: Cost of Delay combines user-business value, time criticality and risk reduction or opportunity enablement. Sunk cost is explicitly ignored, and seniority of the requester has no place in the calculation. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: Four features have these relative scores. Ash: Cost of Delay 16, size 8. Elm: Cost of Delay 9, size 3. Oak: Cost of Delay 20, size 20. Yew: Cost of Delay 12, size 8. Which should be done first according to WSJF?

options.text: Elm
Oak
Ash
Yew

questions.explanation: WSJF is Cost of Delay divided by size: Elm scores 3, Ash 2, Yew 1.5 and Oak 1, so Elm goes first. Oak has the highest Cost of Delay, which makes it tempting, but its size gives it the lowest score. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: A feature has already consumed two PIs of effort, and a stakeholder argues that it must be finished first for that reason. How does WSJF treat this?

options.text: Money already spent is added to the Cost of Delay of the feature in question
Features that have been started are automatically ranked first
The feature is removed from the backlog and written off
Money already spent is ignored; only remaining work and Cost of Delay count

questions.explanation: WSJF ignores sunk costs and looks at the remaining job size against the Cost of Delay. Finishing what has been started feels right, but past spending does not change which job gives the best return now. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: Stakeholders ask for the Cost of Delay of each feature in dollars before any prioritisation can happen. What does SAFe recommend?

options.text: Estimate the items relative to one another
Ask each stakeholder to rank by importance
Wait until finance has calculated exact values
Use the cost of the development team per PI

questions.explanation: SAFe estimates WSJF with relative values, comparing jobs with each other instead of calculating absolute money figures. Waiting for exact numbers delays the decision the technique is meant to speed up. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe · WSJF.

questions.prompt: A train keeps postponing enablers and technical debt because features always score higher. Which SAFe mechanism addresses this?

options.text: A separate hardening PI each year
Capacity allocation by type of work
A dedicated technical debt team
A higher WSJF score for all enablers

questions.explanation: Capacity allocation reserves a share of capacity for each work type for the coming planning period, so enablers do not compete head to head with features. A hardening PI is the trap: it lets problems pile up instead of building quality in continuously. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Where do nonfunctional requirements such as security and performance apply in SAFe?

options.text: As tasks for the final iteration of the PI
As constraints on the design across the backlogs
As acceptance criteria of a single story
As features placed at the bottom of the backlog

questions.explanation: Nonfunctional requirements are system qualities that guide design and act as constraints on the backlogs. Treating them as low-priority backlog items means they are tested late or not at all. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Source: SAFe glossary; SAFe · Features and Capabilities.

questions.prompt: What is the standard format of PI Planning?

options.text: A one-week workshop for managers, held once a year
A half-day meeting of the team leads at the start of each month
A two-hour session for each team at the start of every iteration
A two-day event for the whole ART, every 8 to 12 weeks

questions.explanation: PI Planning is typically a two-day, cadence-based event for the entire ART, held every 8 to 12 weeks. A per-team session each iteration is iteration planning, a different event. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Source: SAFe · PI Planning.

questions.prompt: Who facilitates PI Planning?

options.text: The Release Train Engineer
The senior Business Owner
The Product Manager
The System Architect

questions.explanation: The Release Train Engineer leads and facilitates PI Planning. Product Management presents the vision and the backlog there, which is why it is the tempting wrong answer. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Source: SAFe · PI Planning; SAFe · Release Train Engineer.

questions.prompt: Which are the two primary outputs of PI Planning?

options.text: A detailed Gantt chart and a resource plan
Committed PI objectives and the ART planning board
A release planning calendar and a signed scope statement
An approved business case and a budget

questions.explanation: PI Planning produces committed PI objectives from the teams and an ART planning board. A Gantt chart and a resource plan are the project-management equivalents that SAFe does not produce. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Source: SAFe · PI Planning.

questions.prompt: What does the ART planning board show?

options.text: Individual task assignments and the hours remaining
Defect counts and test coverage for each team
Feature delivery dates and dependencies between teams
Budget spent and forecast spend per value stream

questions.explanation: The ART planning board shows when features are expected and the dependencies among teams. It is not a task board; task detail stays with each team. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Source: SAFe · PI Planning.

questions.prompt: Who assigns business value to the teams' PI objectives during PI Planning?

options.text: Product Owners
Business Owners
The Release Train Engineer
Business analysts on each team

questions.explanation: Business Owners assign business value, on a scale from 1 to 10, to each team's PI objectives in a conversation with the team. Product Owners help write the objectives, but they do not score them. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team's objective depends on a vendor delivery that may not arrive in time. How should the team treat it in its PI plan?

options.text: As an uncommitted objective
As a stretch goal for the IP iteration
As a committed objective with extra overtime
As a risk to leave out of the plan

questions.explanation: PI objectives are either committed or uncommitted, and uncommitted objectives cover work with significant uncertainty. The work is still planned; it is simply excluded from the commitment so that predictability stays honest. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In the confidence vote at the end of PI Planning, the average vote across the train is two fingers out of five. What should happen?

options.text: The low votes are recorded and the event closes on time
The teams that voted low are asked to vote again in private
The plans are reworked until the teams can commit
The managers adjust the plans after the event has ended

questions.explanation: A low confidence vote means the plan is not yet a commitment, so the concerns are addressed and the plan is reworked. Managers fixing the plan afterwards is the trap: the people who do the work must own the plan. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What do the letters ROAM stand for when risks are addressed in PI Planning?

options.text: Reported, Owned, Avoided, Measured
Reviewed, Ordered, Assigned, Monitored
Resolved, Owned, Accepted, Mitigated
Raised, Open, Active, Managed

questions.explanation: ART risks are categorised as Resolved, Owned, Accepted or Mitigated. Owned and Accepted are the two most often mixed up: an owned risk has a person responsible, an accepted risk is understood and left as it is. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During PI Planning a risk cannot be resolved in the room, and a director agrees to take responsibility for it afterwards. Which ROAM category applies?

options.text: Accepted
Mitigated
Owned
Resolved

questions.explanation: A risk that someone takes responsibility for after the event is Owned. Mitigated would require a plan that has already been identified to reduce the risk's impact. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: At the end of the first day of PI Planning, the draft plans show the train is overloaded. What happens next in the standard agenda?

options.text: The teams are told to raise their capacity estimates to fit the features
The overloaded features are moved into the IP iteration without discussion
A management review and problem-solving session adjusts scope or resources
The Release Train Engineer extends the Planning Interval by one iteration

questions.explanation: Day one ends with a management review and problem-solving meeting, where leaders make the adjustments the draft plans call for, and teams replan on day two. Inflating capacity estimates hides the problem and destroys the commitment. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who typically presents the product vision and the top features at PI Planning?

options.text: The Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
The Product Owners as a group
Product Management
The Scrum Masters/Team Coaches

questions.explanation: Product Management leads the vision and roadmap and presents the vision and the highest-priority features. Business Owners or senior leaders present the business context, a separate briefing. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which three areas of readiness does an ART prepare before PI Planning?

options.text: Design sign-off, build setup and test readiness
Legal review, security review and audit readiness
Organizational, content and logistics readiness
Budget approval, staffing levels and tooling readiness

questions.explanation: Preparation covers organisational readiness, content readiness and logistics readiness. Content readiness is the one most often neglected: a vision and a prioritised backlog must exist before the event. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Source: SAFe · PI Planning.

questions.prompt: To save cost, a director proposes that only the team leads attend PI Planning and brief their teams afterwards. What is SAFe's view?

options.text: The Business Owners should attend in place of the teams
The proposal is fine for trains with more than eight teams
The whole ART plans together, since those who do the work own the plan
The proposal is fine, provided the leads take detailed notes and share them
