questions.explanation: PI Planning is for the entire ART, because alignment, dependency discovery and commitment come from everyone planning together. A plan relayed by team leads is a plan that the teams never committed to. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Source: SAFe · PI Planning.

questions.prompt: What is the most common structure of a Planning Interval?

options.text: Two development iterations followed by two test iterations
One planning iteration followed by ten development iterations
Four or five development iterations followed by one IP iteration
Three hardening iterations followed by a release weekend

questions.explanation: A PI typically runs 8 to 12 weeks, most often as four or five development iterations and one Innovation and Planning iteration. SAFe has no hardening or test-only iterations. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · Planning Interval.

questions.prompt: A Product Manager wants to schedule two features into the Innovation and Planning iteration to raise throughput. What is SAFe's guidance?

options.text: The IP iteration is reserved for defect fixing
No feature work is planned into the IP iteration
Features may be planned there if the teams agree
The IP iteration should carry the largest features

questions.explanation: During PI Planning no work is planned into the IP iteration, which provides an estimating buffer and time for innovation, learning, PI Planning and Inspect and Adapt. It is also not a defect-fixing iteration. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · Innovation and Planning Iteration.

questions.prompt: What is the likely effect of regularly filling the IP iteration with planned feature work?

options.text: Teams become better at estimating their capacity
Predictability improves because more of the capacity is planned
PI objectives are missed more often and innovation time disappears
The next PI Planning becomes shorter and easier to run

questions.explanation: The IP iteration acts as an estimating buffer for meeting PI objectives and as time for innovation and learning. Removing the buffer makes every estimation error visible as a missed objective. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · Innovation and Planning Iteration.

questions.prompt: What does the System Demo show?

options.text: The stories of one team, reviewed by that team's own stakeholders and users
A slide presentation of status and planned work for the next PI
The finished solution, once at the end of each release
The integrated work of all teams on the train from the latest iteration

questions.explanation: The System Demo gives an integrated view of the new features from all teams on the ART for the most recent iteration. One team showing its own stories is the Iteration Review. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · System Demo; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Each team on a train shows its own stories to its own stakeholders every iteration, and nothing is shown integrated until the end of the PI. What is missing?

options.text: The Coach Sync during each iteration
The System Demo after each iteration
The Strategic Portfolio Review each quarter
The Iteration Retrospective of each team

questions.explanation: The Iteration Review covers one team, while the System Demo shows the integrated increment of the whole train at the end of each iteration, in a production-like environment. Without it, integration problems stay hidden for the whole PI. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · System Demo.

questions.prompt: Arrange the three parts of the Inspect and Adapt event in order.

options.text: Retrospective and problem-solving workshop
Quantitative and qualitative measurement
PI System Demo

questions.explanation: Inspect and Adapt starts with the PI System Demo, continues with the measurement review and ends with the retrospective and problem-solving workshop. The demo comes first, because the measurements and the workshop build on what was actually delivered. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · Inspect and Adapt.

questions.prompt: What happens to the improvement items identified in the problem-solving workshop?

options.text: They are sent to the PMO for approval and funding
They are stored in the retrospective notes for reference
They are assigned to the Release Train Engineer to complete
They enter the ART backlog for the next PI Planning

questions.explanation: Improvement items go into the ART backlog and are planned into upcoming PIs, with the ART owning the actions. Giving them all to the RTE is the trap: the train, not one role, owns its improvement. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · Inspect and Adapt; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Match each ART event to its purpose.

options.text: Evaluating the solution and identifying improvements at the end of the PI
Reviewing progress toward PI objectives and adjusting scope where needed
Coordinating dependencies and raising impediments
Approving the budget for each value stream
An integrated view of new features from all teams

questions.explanation: The PO Sync tracks progress toward PI objectives, the Coach Sync coordinates dependencies and impediments, the System Demo shows integrated work and Inspect and Adapt closes the PI. The ART Sync combines the PO Sync and the Coach Sync. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe glossary; SAFe · System Demo; SAFe · Inspect and Adapt.

questions.prompt: How is ART predictability assessed?

options.text: By measuring the hours worked against the hours that were originally estimated
By tracking how many features were started during the PI
By comparing the business value achieved with the business value planned
By counting the story points completed by each team per iteration

questions.explanation: The ART Predictability Measure compares the actual business value achieved for PI objectives with the planned value. Story points measure a team's output and cannot be compared or summed across teams as a measure of predictability. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train plans in 10-week PIs, and a stakeholder concludes that customers can receive new functionality only every 10 weeks. What is wrong with this conclusion?

options.text: Releases happen every iteration, never at PI boundaries
The PI length must be shortened to release more often
Customers receive functionality once a year in SAFe
Planning cadence and release timing are separate in SAFe

questions.explanation: SAFe plans on cadence and releases on demand, so a release can happen whenever the business needs it. Shortening the PI treats the planning rhythm as the release schedule, which is the same mistake. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Source: SAFe · Release on Demand; SAFe · Continuous Deployment.

questions.prompt: Which two phases does SAFe's design thinking process move through?

options.text: Choose a vendor, then negotiate the contract
Build the full solution, then test it at the very end
Understand the problem, then find the right solution
Write the requirements, then get them signed off

questions.explanation: SAFe's design thinking first explores and defines the problem, then explores and narrows solutions, each phase diverging and then converging. Writing and signing off requirements skips the learning. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team draws each step a policyholder goes through when renewing a policy, noting feelings and pain points at each step. Which tool is this?

options.text: A story map
A value stream map for the renewal
An empathy map
A customer journey map

questions.explanation: A journey map follows the customer's experience step by step, with emotions and pain points, to show where to improve. An empathy map captures a user's thoughts and feelings without the sequence of steps. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team captures what a typical user says, thinks, does and feels about a problem. Which tool is this?

options.text: An empathy map
A journey map
A portfolio canvas
A Kanban board

questions.explanation: Empathy maps record what a user says, thinks, does and feels, which helps the team see the problem from the user's side. A journey map adds the sequence of steps the user goes through. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does a story map help a team do?

options.text: Order stories along the user journey to slice releases
Estimate each story's cost in money before work begins
Assign stories to developers by skill and availability
Record which stories were accepted in each iteration

questions.explanation: A story map lays out user activities in order, with stories beneath each, so the team can see the whole journey and slice it into releases that each deliver usable value. It does not assign work to people or record acceptance. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe ask that a solution be desirable, viable, feasible and sustainable?

options.text: The four words name the four PI Planning breakout sessions
Each word is a phase gate that the solution must pass in order
They describe the four roles who must approve each feature
It must work for customers, the business, technology and time

questions.explanation: Desirable means customers want it, viable that it works for the business, feasible that it can be built, and sustainable that it can be maintained over its life. Missing any one leads to a failed product. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team builds a clickable mock-up of a new screen and watches five customers try it before writing any code. What is this?

options.text: User acceptance testing at the end of the PI
A System Demo for the Business Owners
A gemba walk through the support centre
Prototyping to test a design idea cheaply

questions.explanation: Prototypes let a team learn about a design with real users before investing in building it. Acceptance testing at the end of the PI comes far too late to change the design cheaply. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which activity best expresses customer centricity for a team building a hospital supply app?

options.text: Copying the features of the market-leading competitor
Watching nurses order supplies during a real shift
Asking the hospital's IT director which features to build
Reading the original contract to see what was promised

questions.explanation: Customer centricity means understanding users' real needs and context, best seen where the work happens. Contracts, competitors and IT directors are second-hand views of what nurses need. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe's customer-centric mindset emphasise customer lifetime value?

options.text: Each sale should be maximised whatever the effect later
Long-term relationships beat any single sale
Customers who buy once are not worth further effort
A customer's value is fixed when they first sign up

questions.explanation: Thinking in terms of lifetime value focuses on keeping customers well served over time, not on extracting the most from one transaction. It shapes decisions about quality, support and trust. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A product team segments its market and finds two very different groups of users. What should it do next?

options.text: Learn each segment's needs, perhaps with personas
Average the two segments' needs into one requirement
Build for the larger segment and ignore the smaller one
Ask sales to choose which segment the team should serve

questions.explanation: Different segments have different needs, so the team studies each and may create personas to keep both in mind when designing. Averaging produces a solution that suits neither group. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which common mistake does design thinking try to prevent?

options.text: Spending too long on testing once the solution is built
Using too many colours in the user interface
Hiring too many designers for the size of the product
Building a solution before understanding the problem

questions.explanation: Design thinking puts understanding the problem first, because a well-built solution to the wrong problem has no value. Testing and visual choices come later. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question best tests a feature's desirability?

options.text: Can we support it for years to come?
Will it make money for the business?
Do customers want it, and will they use it?
Can our technology build it within the PI?

questions.explanation: Desirability is about customers wanting and using the solution. The other questions test feasibility, viability and sustainability. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question tests a feature's viability?

options.text: Can our technology build it within the PI?
Can we support it for years to come?
Will it create enough value for the business?
Do customers want it, and will they use it?

questions.explanation: Viability asks whether the solution works for the business, for example by creating enough revenue or savings. The other options test desirability, feasibility and sustainability. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team builds exactly what the specification says, and customers do not use it. Which part of SAFe's approach was missing?

options.text: Validating the problem and solution with users early
A larger team to deliver the specification faster
More testing of the code before the release
A more detailed specification signed off by the sponsor

questions.explanation: Building to a specification without testing assumptions with customers risks delivering the wrong thing perfectly. Customer centricity and design thinking validate early, before most of the money is spent. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team wants to learn whether customers value a feature before building all of it. Which approach fits?

options.text: Release a minimum marketable feature and measure its use
Run an internal vote on whether the feature is valuable
Write a longer business case predicting the feature's use
Build the complete feature and ask for feedback afterwards

questions.explanation: SAFe's Lean UX approach builds a minimum marketable feature, measures real use against the benefit hypothesis and then decides what to do next. Internal votes and longer predictions are not customer evidence. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In SAFe's Lean UX approach, what comes first?

options.text: A launch plan for marketing
A detailed design document for the team
A benefit hypothesis for the feature
A full user acceptance test

questions.explanation: Lean UX starts with a benefit hypothesis, then collaborative design, building a minimum marketable feature and evaluating it against the hypothesis. Detailed design documents are what it replaces. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A usability test shows that users cannot find the 'renew' button. What should happen next?

options.text: Train users to find the button after release
Ask the users to try harder in the next test
Change the design and test it again with users
Note the issue in the release notes and ship it

questions.explanation: Usability findings feed straight back into the design, which is then retested; that loop is the point of testing early. Training users to work around a poor design shifts the cost onto them. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should a team talk to customers even when its Product Manager 'already knows' what they want?

options.text: Talking to customers is required for SAFe certification
Product Managers are not allowed to make decisions
Customers will pay more if they are asked first
Assumptions about customers are often wrong

questions.explanation: Even experienced Product Managers hold assumptions that change when tested with real users. Talking to customers turns opinions into evidence before the train invests. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: For a customer-service product, which source of insight is closest to the gemba?

options.text: Sitting with agents as they handle real calls
Reviewing the product's marketing brochure
Reading the annual customer satisfaction report
Asking managers what agents probably struggle with

questions.explanation: The gemba is where the work happens, so watching agents handle calls shows the real problems. Reports, managers' guesses and brochures are second-hand. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A design team keeps adding features that only its own members want. Which practice would counter this?

options.text: Writing longer feature descriptions
Voting on features within the team
Adding more designers to the team
Testing ideas with real users first

questions.explanation: Testing ideas with real users replaces the team's preferences with evidence about customers. More designers, longer descriptions or internal votes keep the decision inside the team. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does customer centricity relate to the ART backlog?

options.text: Customers write the features directly into the ART backlog
The backlog is set by contract, so customers do not affect it
Customer insight shapes which features enter and how they rank
Customer insight matters for marketing rather than the backlog

questions.explanation: Product Management uses customer research, feedback and measured outcomes to decide which features to add and how to prioritise them. Customers inform the backlog; they do not edit it. Topic 4.1, lesson “4.1 · Customer centricity and design thinking”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a type of enabler in SAFe?

options.text: Promotional
Contractual
Architectural
Organisational

questions.explanation: SAFe names four types of enabler: exploration, architectural, infrastructure and compliance. They support future business functionality rather than deliver it directly. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team must research two possible payment providers before the train can commit to a design. Which enabler type is this?

options.text: Architectural enabler
Infrastructure enabler
Exploration enabler
Compliance enabler

questions.explanation: Exploration enablers cover research, prototypes and spikes that build the knowledge needed for a decision. Architectural enablers then build the chosen technical foundation. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is a capability in SAFe?

options.text: A skill that one team member brings to the train
A large solution behaviour needing several ARTs
A small story that one team can finish in a day
A tool that the platform team offers to others

questions.explanation: Capabilities are like features but larger, spanning several ARTs in a Large Solution; they are split into features for each train. A skill or a tool is not a backlog item. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement is a well-formed benefit hypothesis?

options.text: The team believes one-click reorder is easy to build
We will build one-click reorder in the next PI
We believe one-click reorder lifts repeat orders 10%
One-click reorder must be done by the end of June

questions.explanation: A benefit hypothesis states the measurable outcome expected if the feature works, so it can be tested after release. A delivery date or an ease-of-build opinion says nothing about benefit. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In WSJF, what does 'risk reduction and/or opportunity enablement' measure?

options.text: How likely the team is to finish the work on time
How risky it is for the team to estimate the work
How many risks the work has already caused
How much it lowers future risk or opens options

questions.explanation: This Cost of Delay component values work that reduces the risk of future delivery or enables new business opportunities, as enablers often do. It is not about estimation risk. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A regulatory change takes effect in three months, and missing it means fines. Which Cost of Delay component is highest?

options.text: Job size
Risk reduction
User-business value
Time criticality

questions.explanation: Time criticality captures how value decays with delay, as with a fixed regulatory deadline. Job size is the denominator of WSJF, not a part of Cost of Delay. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Two features have equal Cost of Delay, but one is half the size of the other. What does WSJF suggest?

options.text: Wait for a third feature
Do the smaller one first
Do both at the same time
Do the larger one first

questions.explanation: WSJF divides Cost of Delay by job size, so with equal Cost of Delay the smaller job scores higher and delivers value sooner. Doing both at once raises WIP and delays both. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe use job size as a proxy for duration in WSJF?

options.text: Duration is hard to know, and size tracks it well
Duration is irrelevant to economic decisions
Size is easier to argue about in planning meetings
Large jobs are always worth more than small ones

questions.explanation: Duration depends on who works on a job and when, which is not known when ranking, but larger jobs generally take longer, so relative size stands in for it. Duration is highly relevant; it is just hard to estimate. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In WSJF scoring, how are the components usually estimated?

options.text: In days, as precisely as the team can manage
In hours, from each team member's own view
In money, from each sponsor's own business case
Relatively, using a modified Fibonacci scale

questions.explanation: Each component is estimated relative to the other items, with the smallest set to 1, using a modified Fibonacci scale. Relative estimates are fast and good enough for ranking. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who estimates the Cost of Delay for features?

options.text: The RTE on their own, working from the ART's velocity
Developers on their own, since they build the features
The finance team on its own, working from the budget
Product Management with Business Owners

questions.explanation: Cost of Delay is a business judgement, so Product Management estimates it with Business Owners and other stakeholders; teams and architects help with job size. No single group estimates it alone. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why should features be sized to fit within one PI?

options.text: So that features never need to be split later
So one train can deliver and learn in a cycle
So the budget for each feature stays the same
So each team gets exactly one feature per iteration

questions.explanation: A feature that fits in a PI can be planned, delivered, demonstrated and measured within one planning cycle, which keeps feedback fast. Larger items are split or treated as epics or capabilities. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A feature is too large for one PI. What should Product Management do?

options.text: Give it to the team with the most spare capacity
Turn it into an epic without any further review
Keep it whole and plan it across three PIs
Split it into smaller slices that each add value

questions.explanation: Splitting a large feature into smaller valuable ones lets the train deliver and learn sooner. Spreading one feature over several PIs delays feedback and hides progress. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which acceptance criterion is best for the feature 'Customers can track deliveries in the app'?

options.text: The tracking feature is delivered on time by the team
Location updates appear within two minutes
The tracking code has been written and merged
Tracking looks good and works well for users

questions.explanation: Acceptance criteria describe observable, testable conditions for the feature to be accepted. 'Looks good' cannot be tested, and delivery dates or merged code describe the work, not the behaviour. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe keep near-term items in the ART backlog refined and leave later ones light?

options.text: Refining all items would leave the teams idle
The RTE alone may refine items beyond the next PI
Detail decays, so effort goes into near-term work
Later items are less important to the customers

questions.explanation: Detailed analysis of items far in the future is often wasted because needs change before they are built. Refining just in time keeps the backlog ready without that waste. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During backlog refinement, Product Management finds a feature with no clear benefit hypothesis. What should happen?

options.text: Rank it last but keep it in the plan for the PI
Remove it from the backlog with no further discussion
Clarify what value it should bring before ranking it
Give it to a team to discover the benefit while building

questions.explanation: Without a benefit hypothesis there is no basis for estimating its value or testing it later, so it is clarified before it competes for capacity. Removing it without discussion may lose a real need. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train reserves 20% of each PI for enablers and 10% for maintenance. What is this practice called?

options.text: Participatory budgeting
Investment horizons
Flow distribution
Capacity allocation

questions.explanation: Capacity allocation sets the share of capacity for each type of work, so that features do not crowd out enablers and maintenance. Flow distribution measures the actual split after the fact. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs in the ART backlog rather than in a team backlog?

options.text: A defect found in one team's code yesterday
A story that one developer can finish in a day
A feature several teams will deliver in the PI
A task to update a single unit test

questions.explanation: The ART backlog holds features and enablers for the train; teams split them into stories in their own backlogs. Stories, tasks and local defects live at team level. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why is WSJF reapplied in each PI instead of ranking the backlog once?

options.text: SAFe requires a new tool for each PI's ranking
Job size always doubles between PIs
Cost of Delay and size change over time
Ranking once would let teams skip PI Planning

questions.explanation: WSJF is relative and time-sensitive: deadlines approach, opportunities appear and work is learned about, so the ranking is refreshed before each PI Planning. A ranking made once goes stale within months. Topic 4.2, lesson “4.2 · Prioritizing the ART backlog”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the first item on the agenda of PI Planning day 1?

options.text: Team breakouts
Confidence vote
Business context
Draft plan review

questions.explanation: Day 1 opens with the business context, then the product or solution vision, the architecture vision and development practices, and the planning context, before the first team breakouts. The confidence vote and plan reviews come later. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who usually presents the business context at the start of PI Planning?

options.text: A Scrum Master/Team Coach
The Release Train Engineer
The System Architect
A senior executive

questions.explanation: The business context is given by a senior executive or Business Owner, who describes the current state of the business and how the solutions address it. The RTE facilitates the event. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: On day 1 of the big-room event, which session follows the architecture vision and development practices briefing?

options.text: Planning context and lunch
Draft plan review
Confidence vote
Management review and problem-solving

questions.explanation: After the architecture briefing, the RTE presents the planning process and expected outputs, then teams break out to plan. Draft plan review and management review come later on day 1. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During PI Planning team breakouts, what does each team produce?

options.text: A final budget for the PI and a request for extra staff
Draft objectives, iteration plans, risks, dependencies
A detailed design document for each of the features
A list of each person's tasks for every day

questions.explanation: In breakouts, teams estimate capacity, plan features into iterations, draft PI objectives and identify risks and dependencies. Budgets are not set in breakouts, and daily task lists are far too detailed. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What happens at the start of PI Planning day 2?

options.text: The RTE presents the business context again
Teams vote on their confidence in the final plan
Managers share adjustments from the evening review
Business Owners assign business value to objectives

questions.explanation: Day 2 opens with planning adjustments agreed in the management review the evening before, such as changes to scope or priorities. The confidence vote comes near the end of day 2. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team has one objective that delivers a feature to a key customer and another that improves an internal report. During PI Planning, who decides which objective matters more?

options.text: The RTE, based on the train's velocity last PI
The Product Owner, based on the story points
The team, based on which objective is harder to do
The Business Owners, by scoring each objective

questions.explanation: Business Owners assign business value to each team's PI objectives, which captures their priorities and is later used to measure predictability. Difficulty and story points measure effort, not value. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: On what scale do Business Owners assign business value to PI objectives?

options.text: 1 to 10
1 to 5
Low, medium, high

questions.explanation: Business value is scored from 1 to 10 for each objective during PI Planning. At the end of the PI the actual value achieved is scored on the same scale. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why are uncommitted objectives included in the plan rather than left out?

options.text: They are planned within capacity but not promised
They are extras that teams do only if they finish early
They are next PI's objectives written in advance
They are objectives the Business Owners have rejected

questions.explanation: Uncommitted objectives are planned and count toward capacity and business value, but they are not part of the commitment, so uncertainty does not damage predictability. They are not optional extras. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A risk is real, but the train decides it can live with it because nothing more can be done. How is it ROAMed?

options.text: Accepted
Resolved
Owned
Mitigated

questions.explanation: Accepted risks are understood and cannot be resolved or reduced further, so the train acknowledges them. Resolved risks are no longer a concern, owned ones have someone taking responsibility, mitigated ones have a plan to reduce their impact. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team agrees to build a fallback option that would reduce a risk's impact if it happens. How is the risk ROAMed?

options.text: Mitigated
Accepted
Owned
Resolved

questions.explanation: A plan to reduce the likelihood or impact of a risk makes it mitigated. It is not resolved, because the risk still exists. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How is the confidence vote at the end of PI Planning usually taken?

options.text: With an online survey sent a week later
With a show of hands for yes or no
With a fist of five, from one to five fingers
With a secret ballot on paper, counted by the RTE

questions.explanation: Teams and the whole train vote with a fist of five; three or more fingers means confidence. Low votes are discussed and the plan is reworked if needed. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During the confidence vote, one person holds up two fingers while everyone else shows four or five. What should happen?

options.text: The person is asked to vote again with more fingers
The RTE records the vote and ends the event
They explain the concern so the plan can be adjusted
Their vote is ignored, since the majority is confident

questions.explanation: Every low vote is heard, because it may reveal a risk others have missed, and the plan is adjusted if the concern is valid. Overriding a lone voice wastes the purpose of the vote. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does PI Planning end with a planning retrospective?

options.text: To decide which teams performed best in planning
To approve the budget for the next PI
To improve the next PI Planning while fresh
To reassign people between teams for the PI

questions.explanation: The retrospective collects what worked and what did not in the event itself, so the next PI Planning runs better. It is not a performance review of teams. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the System Architect's role at PI Planning?

options.text: Assigning business value to each team's objectives
Facilitating the event and keeping it to time
Approving each team's architecture on the business's behalf
Presenting the architecture vision and advising teams

questions.explanation: The System Architect presents the architecture vision and helps teams with technical choices and enablers. Business value is assigned by Business Owners, and the RTE facilitates. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which item belongs to content readiness for PI Planning?

options.text: A booked room with enough tables and power for all
A list of who will attend from each team
A finished design for each feature in the backlog
The top features, with acceptance criteria

questions.explanation: Content readiness means the vision, top features and business context are prepared. Rooms and attendance are logistics and organisational readiness, and full designs are neither needed nor wanted. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A distributed ART cannot meet in person. What does SAFe recommend for PI Planning?

options.text: Skip PI Planning until the train can meet in person
Let each team plan alone and send its plan by email
Plan together online, with the same agenda
Let the RTE plan the PI for the whole train

questions.explanation: The value of PI Planning comes from everyone planning together, so remote trains hold it online with the same structure. Planning alone or skipping it removes the alignment. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does PI Planning plan by iteration but commit at the level of PI objectives?

options.text: Iterations are too short to plan in any detail
The commitment is to value, not to detail
Commitments by iteration are not allowed in SAFe
Business Owners cannot read iteration plans

questions.explanation: The iteration plan helps teams check what is feasible, but the commitment is to outcomes in the PI objectives, so teams can change the detail as they learn without breaking the commitment. Iteration plans are a tool for checking feasibility, not a promise. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During breakouts, two teams find that both depend on a third team in iteration 2. Where is this made visible?

options.text: In the RTE's personal notebook
In the minutes sent after the event
On the ART planning board
In each team's private task list

questions.explanation: The ART planning board shows feature delivery, milestones and dependencies between teams, often with string, so everyone can see and discuss them. Hidden notes do not help coordination. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which role facilitates a team's own breakout during PI Planning?

options.text: The Epic Owner
The Scrum Master/Team Coach
The Business Owner for the ART
The Enterprise Architect

questions.explanation: Within the breakouts, each team's Scrum Master/Team Coach facilitates its planning, while the RTE facilitates the event as a whole. Business Owners circulate and answer questions. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train's draft plans show it can commit to only half the features Product Management hoped for. What is the right response?

options.text: Add the features as committed objectives regardless
Remove the IP iteration to make room for features
Adjust scope to capacity rather than force more in
Tell teams to raise their velocity to fit the features

questions.explanation: PI Planning matches demand to capacity; the management review adjusts scope and priorities. Forcing in more work or removing the IP iteration produces plans nobody believes. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What happens to a team's committed objectives after PI Planning?

options.text: The team works to deliver them and reports progress
They are replaced by the Business Owners' own goals
They are archived until the next PI Planning
They are locked and cannot change during the PI

questions.explanation: Teams deliver against their objectives, review progress at events such as the System Demo, and adapt the detail as they learn. Objectives can change if the business needs it, through agreed scope changes. Topic 4.3, lesson “4.3 · Participating in PI Planning”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which two meetings make up the ART sync?

options.text: Coach sync and PO sync
Iteration review and retrospective
Management review and planning
Team sync and System Demo

questions.explanation: The ART sync combines the coach sync, about impediments and dependencies, and the PO sync, about scope and priorities. They are often held together. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which meeting brings Scrum Masters/Team Coaches together to address impediments and dependencies across the train?

options.text: PO sync
System Demo
Iteration Planning
Coach sync

questions.explanation: The coach sync, led by the RTE, reviews progress, impediments and dependencies across teams. The PO sync deals with scope and priorities. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Product Owners and Product Management meet weekly to adjust scope and priorities across the train. Which event is this?

options.text: Coach sync
Team sync
Inspect and Adapt
PO sync

questions.explanation: The PO sync gives Product Management and Product Owners a regular place to adjust scope, priorities and acceptance across the train. Inspect and Adapt happens once per PI. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In the problem-solving workshop, which tool groups possible causes into categories?

options.text: A burn-up chart
A portfolio canvas
A cumulative flow diagram
A fishbone diagram

questions.explanation: The fishbone diagram arranges possible causes under categories such as people, process, tools and environment. The five whys then dig into each to find root causes. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In the problem-solving workshop, which technique asks 'why' repeatedly to reach a root cause?

options.text: The five whys
The confidence vote
The Pareto chart
The fist of five

questions.explanation: Asking 'why' about five times moves from a symptom to its root cause. The fist of five is the confidence vote, and Pareto analysis ranks causes by impact. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: After brainstorming causes, a team votes and finds that a few causes explain most of the problem. Which analysis is this?

options.text: WSJF ranking
Pareto analysis
SWOT analysis
Value stream mapping

questions.explanation: Pareto analysis, the 80/20 rule, identifies the vital few causes so the workshop focuses on the biggest one. SWOT is used for strategy, and WSJF for prioritising backlog items. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Arrange the steps of the Inspect and Adapt problem-solving workshop in order.

options.text: Brainstorm solutions
Restate the new problem
Identify improvement backlog items
Agree on the problem to solve
Identify the biggest root cause
Apply root cause analysis

questions.explanation: The workshop agrees the problem, finds causes with fishbone and five whys, picks the biggest with Pareto analysis, restates the problem for that cause, brainstorms solutions, and turns the best into backlog items. Solutions come only after the root cause is clear. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When actual business value is compared with planned value, which range does SAFe treat as a predictable ART?

options.text: 100 to 120 percent
30 to 50 percent
80 to 100 percent
50 to 70 percent

questions.explanation: An ART achieving 80 to 100 percent of planned business value is considered predictable enough for the business to plan around. Consistently above 100 suggests too little is being committed. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does the PI System Demo take place as part of Inspect and Adapt?

options.text: It lets teams avoid showing work during the PI
It replaces the System Demos held in each iteration
It is the first time teams integrate their work
It shows stakeholders the PI's integrated results

questions.explanation: The PI System Demo shows everything the train delivered in the PI, so stakeholders can review it before the metrics and the problem-solving workshop. Integration happens throughout the PI, not first here. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which activities belong in the IP iteration?

options.text: Finishing the features that slipped during the PI
Innovation, planning, Inspect and Adapt, learning
Holidays for the whole train between two PIs
Hardening and testing everything built so far

questions.explanation: The Innovation and Planning iteration provides time for innovation, Inspect and Adapt, PI Planning, learning and infrastructure work. Using it for slipped features or hardening hides problems in the plan. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe describe the IP iteration as an estimating buffer?

options.text: Its slack absorbs overruns without breaking commitments
It removes the need for any capacity planning
It doubles the time teams have for each feature
It is where teams plan extra features as a stretch goal

questions.explanation: Because no features are planned into it, the IP iteration gives slack that protects the PI objectives if estimates were too low. Planning features into it removes that protection. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who typically runs the System Demo each iteration?

options.text: An external auditor hired for each PI
Each Business Owner, one team at a time
Product Management, with the teams demoing
The finance team, to check what has been spent

questions.explanation: Product Management usually runs the System Demo, with teams demonstrating the integrated increment to stakeholders, who give feedback. It is a review of the solution, not an audit. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which team often helps build the integrated environment used to demonstrate the whole solution?

options.text: The LACE
The Epic Owners
The VMO
The System Team

questions.explanation: The System Team supports integration, the pipeline and the demo environment. The LACE drives the transformation, and the VMO supports portfolio management. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the ART Kanban visualise?

options.text: Each person's tasks in the current iteration
The flow of features across the train
The train's holiday and leave calendar
The portfolio's epics and their budgets

questions.explanation: The ART Kanban shows features moving through states such as funnel, analysing, backlog, implementing and done, with WIP limits. Team tasks and epics have their own boards. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train meets its PI objectives, but customers see no new value until a year-end release. What should it improve?

options.text: Its documentation, so releases are better described
Its ability to release on demand
Its PI Planning, so that plans are more detailed
Its velocity, so that even more features are built

questions.explanation: Developing on cadence while releasing on demand lets value reach customers when they need it. Building more or planning in more detail does not shorten the wait for value. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Mid-PI, a team finds a dependency that will delay another team. Where should this be raised first?

options.text: In a private message to the Business Owners
At the next PI Planning, in about two months
In the team's retrospective, for the team alone
In the coach sync, so the train can address it

questions.explanation: The coach sync exists to surface and resolve cross-team impediments and dependencies during the PI. Waiting for PI Planning lets the delay land. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In the quantitative part of Inspect and Adapt, what does the train review?

options.text: Each person's hours and attendance
The cost of each team's tools
The number of meetings held
Metrics such as predictability and flow

questions.explanation: The quantitative and qualitative measurement part of I&A reviews agreed metrics, such as the predictability measure and flow metrics, to inform the problem-solving workshop. Individual hours and attendance are not reviewed, because I&A looks at the system. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does SAFe call the metric that compares the business value teams achieved with what they planned?

options.text: The confidence vote result
The ART predictability measure
The flow efficiency score
The team velocity ratio

questions.explanation: The ART predictability measure compares actual with planned business value for the PI objectives, at team and train level. Flow efficiency compares active time with total time. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team finishes all its committed objectives early in the PI. What should it do?

options.text: Start planning the next PI's features on its own
Pull uncommitted work or other backlog items
Help nobody, since its commitments are complete
Take the IP iteration early as rest

questions.explanation: Uncommitted objectives were planned for exactly this case, and teams can also help others or take further backlog items. Planning the next PI alone breaks the train's shared planning. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps a train execute the PI with fewer surprises at the end?

options.text: Integrating and demoing the whole system often
Waiting to integrate until the final iteration
Skipping the System Demo when the work is not ready
Reporting progress by percent complete each week

questions.explanation: Frequent integration and System Demos give objective evidence of progress throughout the PI. Late integration and percent-complete reports hide problems until it is too late. Topic 4.4, lesson “4.4 · Executing the PI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does Lean Portfolio Management do?

options.text: Assigns people to projects according to their utilisation
Aligns strategy and execution using Lean and systems thinking
Tracks project budgets and reports variances each month
Approves the detailed requirements of every feature

questions.explanation: LPM aligns strategy and execution by applying Lean and systems thinking to strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations and governance. Tracking project variances is traditional portfolio management, which LPM replaces. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Which three areas does Lean Portfolio Management cover?

options.text: Strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations, Lean governance
Continuous Exploration, Continuous Integration, Continuous Deployment
Scope management, schedule management, cost management and quality management
Team backlogs, ART backlogs, portfolio backlogs and Solution Train backlogs

questions.explanation: LPM covers strategy and investment funding, Agile portfolio operations and Lean governance. Scope, schedule and cost are the project-management triple constraint, the frame LPM moves away from. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe define a portfolio?

options.text: A set of value streams that deliver solutions within common funding and governance
A group of applications that is maintained by one IT department
A collection of teams that report to the same vice president
A list of approved projects with their budgets, owners and delivery deadlines

questions.explanation: A SAFe portfolio is a set of value streams delivering solutions under common funding and governance. A list of projects is the traditional definition and the one the exam expects you to reject. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: At Tessel Bank, staff take a mortgage from application to payout, and three trains build the software those staff use. How does SAFe classify the two?

options.text: The mortgage process is a development value stream; the trains form an operational value stream
Both are operational value streams, since both serve the bank's customers
Both are development value streams, since both depend on software
The mortgage process is an operational value stream; the trains form a development value stream

questions.explanation: An operational value stream delivers the product or service to the customer, and a development value stream builds the solutions that make it possible. Reversing the two is the usual error. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe · Development Value Streams; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: How are development and operational value streams related?

options.text: Operational value streams fund and staff the development ones
The two are independent of each other and are managed in separate portfolios
Development value streams build the solutions that operational ones use
Development value streams replace operational ones over time

questions.explanation: Development value streams build and maintain the solutions that operational value streams use to serve customers. They are connected, which is why operational streams are identified first when trains are designed. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline; SAFe · Development Value Streams.

questions.prompt: What does a development value stream consist of?

options.text: One project and its steering committee
One or more Agile Release Trains
A set of functional departments
A single cross-functional Agile Team

questions.explanation: Each development value stream consists of one or more ARTs. A single team is too small to be a value stream, and functional departments are the structure value streams cut across. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe · Development Value Streams.

questions.prompt: What are Strategic Themes?

options.text: Marketing messages that describe the strategic roadmap
Epics that the portfolio has approved for the current year
Topics for the next Inspect and Adapt problem-solving workshop agenda
Portfolio-level business objectives tied to enterprise strategy

questions.explanation: Strategic Themes are portfolio-level business objectives that give competitive differentiation and connect the portfolio to the enterprise strategy. They are not epics; they are the context in which epics are judged. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Strategic Themes; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: In which format does SAFe recommend stating Strategic Themes?

options.text: User stories with acceptance criteria
Objectives and Key Results
A Lean business case
A SWOT quadrant

questions.explanation: Strategic Themes are best stated as OKRs, in plain business language, so progress can be measured. A Lean business case belongs to an epic. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Strategic Themes.

questions.prompt: Epic Owners at Quarry Insurance propose epics that have no connection to any Strategic Theme. What role should the themes play?

options.text: They are informational and do not affect epic decisions
They are rewritten each PI to match the epics chosen
They apply to teams but not to the portfolio backlog
They provide the business context for portfolio decisions

questions.explanation: Strategic Themes give the business context for portfolio strategy and decisions, and trains refer to them when defining epics and features. Rewriting themes to fit the epics turns the strategy upside down. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Strategic Themes.

questions.prompt: Which question should an enterprise strategy answer, according to SAFe?

options.text: Which defects are fixed first?
Which developer joins which team?
Which customers and markets do we serve?
Which stories fit into the next iteration?

questions.explanation: The enterprise strategy answers which customers and markets are served, which products and solutions are provided, what unique value and resources are brought, and how these will be extended. The other questions are team-level decisions. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Enterprise.

questions.prompt: What does the Portfolio Vision describe?

options.text: The current organisation chart of the portfolio's departments
The approved budget of the portfolio for the financial year
The detailed release plan of every train in the portfolio
The future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions

questions.explanation: The Portfolio Vision describes the future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions and is a key input for identifying epics. It is aspirational yet achievable, not a budget or a release plan. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Portfolio Vision; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Leaders want one page that captures the portfolio's value streams, solutions, customers and revenue streams. Which SAFe tool is this?

options.text: The ART planning board
The portfolio Kanban board
The portfolio canvas
The epic hypothesis statement

questions.explanation: The portfolio canvas defines a portfolio's development value streams, solutions, revenue streams, customers and other key elements. The Lean business case describes one epic, not the whole portfolio. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Portfolio Vision; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: A portfolio has completed a SWOT analysis and now wants to derive strategic options for its future state from it. Which technique does SAFe use?

options.text: Value stream mapping
Pareto analysis
WSJF scoring
TOWS analysis

questions.explanation: TOWS takes the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats from a SWOT analysis and combines them into strategic options. Pareto analysis is used in the problem-solving workshop to select the biggest root cause. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the portfolio backlog hold?

options.text: Business and enabler epics
Stories and defects for one team
Features and enablers for one train
Strategic themes and OKRs

questions.explanation: The portfolio backlog is a Kanban system for business and enabler epics. Features and enablers for a train sit one level down, in the ART backlog. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Portfolio Backlog; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Arrange the states of the portfolio Kanban in order.

options.text: Analyzing
Implementing
Funnel
Ready
Reviewing
Done

questions.explanation: Epics enter the funnel, are reviewed, analysed, made ready, implemented and finished. Reviewing comes before Analyzing: an idea is first shaped into an epic hypothesis and only then given the deeper analysis. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In which state of the portfolio Kanban is the Lean business case developed and the MVP defined?

options.text: Analyzing
Funnel
Done
Implementing

questions.explanation: The Analyzing state is where the Lean business case and the MVP are worked out, leading to a go or no-go decision. The funnel only captures ideas, with no analysis effort yet. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A portfolio proposes moving its services to a new cloud platform to support future business needs, with no direct customer feature. What kind of epic is this?

options.text: A business epic
An enabler epic
A capability
A strategic theme

questions.explanation: Enabler epics extend the architectural runway for future business or technical needs, while business epics deliver value directly to customers. A capability is large-solution functionality, a different level. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Epic.

questions.prompt: A sponsor says an approved epic is 'just a project with a new name'. Which statement reflects SAFe?

options.text: An epic is closed when its planned scope is delivered, whatever the outcome
An epic needs an MVP and a Lean business case and is managed through the portfolio Kanban
An epic has a fixed scope, a fixed budget and a named project manager who is accountable
An epic is a financial allocation that teams draw down as they complete tasks

questions.explanation: SAFe states that an epic is not a project: it needs an MVP and a Lean business case and flows through the portfolio Kanban. Fixed scope and a project manager describe the model that epics replace. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Epic.

questions.prompt: What does an Epic Owner do?

options.text: Prioritises the backlog of one Agile Team
Approves the budget of the whole portfolio each year
Facilitates the PI Planning event for a train
Coordinates an epic through the portfolio Kanban

questions.explanation: The Epic Owner coordinates the progress of an epic through the portfolio Kanban. The Epic Owner does not approve the epic or the budget; that is Portfolio Leadership's role. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Portfolio Backlog; SAFe · Epic; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the MVP for an epic?

options.text: To demonstrate the team's velocity to the sponsor
To satisfy the audit requirement for a prototype
To prove or disprove the epic's hypothesis early
To deliver the first release of the full planned scope

questions.explanation: An MVP is an early, minimal version of a solution used to prove or disprove the epic hypothesis. It is not the first slice of a fixed scope; its job is learning. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Epic; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: An epic's MVP shows that customers do not value the idea, but the sponsor argues the full scope must be built because the epic was approved. What does SAFe expect?

options.text: Completion of the scope, since approval is a commitment
A pivot or stop decision based on the evidence
A change of Epic Owner to restore confidence
A larger MVP, built before any decision is taken

questions.explanation: The Lean Startup cycle ends in a pivot-or-persevere decision driven by the MVP's evidence. Approval to implement is approval to test a hypothesis, not a commitment to deliver the whole scope. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Epic; SAFe · Business Agility.

questions.prompt: Who approves epics for implementation?

options.text: The Product Owners
Portfolio Leadership
The Epic Owner
The Release Train Engineer

questions.explanation: Because of their scope, epics must be approved by Portfolio Leadership, the term the current framework pages use; older material names Lean Portfolio Management. The Epic Owner is the tempting answer, but that role shepherds the epic and prepares the case; it does not approve its own epic. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Portfolio Backlog; SAFe · Epic.

questions.prompt: Which role establishes the technology vision, strategy and roadmap for a portfolio?

options.text: Product Manager
Release Train Engineer
System Architect
Enterprise Architect

questions.explanation: The Enterprise Architect sets the portfolio's technology vision, strategy and roadmap. The System Architect does similar work for a single train, which is why the two are confused. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Source: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: What do Lean Budgets fund?

options.text: Functional departments
Individual projects
Named features
Value streams

questions.explanation: Lean Budgets fund value streams instead of projects. Funding projects is the practice SAFe identifies as a blocker to agility. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Budgets; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: At Larkspur Logistics every new initiative needs its own cost approval, and people are reassigned between projects several times a year. What does SAFe recommend?

options.text: Approve projects faster through a weekly funding committee meeting
Fund long-lived value streams and bring the work to them
Merge small projects into fewer, larger programmes
Give each project a dedicated cost controller

questions.explanation: Lean Budgets fund value streams with stable teams, which removes the overhead of project cost accounting and repeated approvals. A faster committee keeps the project model and only shortens one of its queues. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Budgets.

questions.prompt: A value stream has an approved budget, and a feature takes longer than expected. What happens under Lean Budgets?

options.text: A change request is raised for additional project funding
The feature is cancelled because it exceeded its estimate
The budget is recalculated and approved again by finance
The budget stays the same and priorities are adjusted locally

questions.explanation: With value stream funding, content decisions and trade-offs are made locally within the budget, so an overrun on one feature needs no re-approval. A change request is the project-accounting reflex this model removes. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each Lean budget guardrail to what it balances or ensures.

options.text: Ongoing business involvement in priorities
Sign-off of each story before work starts
The mix of new features, enablers and maintenance
Spending across near-term and longer-term solutions
Portfolio review of large epics

questions.explanation: The four guardrails are investment horizons, capacity allocation, approval of significant initiatives and continuous Business Owner engagement. The first two are quantitative, and the last two are about how the budget is governed. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Budget Guardrails.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the four Lean budget guardrails?

options.text: Continuous Business Owner engagement
Monthly project status reporting
Annual zero-based budgeting
Fixed scope per Planning Interval

questions.explanation: Continuous Business Owner engagement is one of the four guardrails. Status reporting and fixed scope are project controls, which the guardrails replace with lighter governance. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Budget Guardrails.

questions.prompt: In SAFe's investment horizons, which horizon covers solutions that are being retired?

options.text: Horizon 1
Horizon 3
Horizon 2
Horizon 0

questions.explanation: Horizon 0 covers solutions being decommissioned, while Horizon 1 covers solutions that deliver value today. Horizon 3 is at the other end: early evaluation of future opportunities. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A value stream has its own budget and wants to start a very large initiative that exceeds the portfolio's epic threshold. What applies?

options.text: The portfolio is informed after the work has started
The initiative is split into stories to avoid review
The Release Train Engineer decides at PI Planning
The initiative needs portfolio approval as an epic

questions.explanation: The guardrail on approving significant initiatives requires large initiatives to go through portfolio review, even when a value stream is funded. Value stream budgets give local freedom over content, not over portfolio-sized bets. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Budget Guardrails; SAFe · Epic.

questions.prompt: How often is the Strategic Portfolio Review typically held?

options.text: Each iteration, before iteration planning
Quarterly, at least a month before the next PI Planning
Weekly, on the day after each System Demo has been held
Annually, as part of the budgeting cycle

questions.explanation: The Strategic Portfolio Review is typically quarterly and is held at least one month before the next PI Planning, so its decisions can shape the backlog. An annual review is the traditional cycle that is too slow to steer by. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline.

questions.prompt: How often is the Portfolio Sync generally held?

options.text: Each iteration
Twice a year
Daily
Monthly

questions.explanation: The Portfolio Sync is generally a monthly event with an operational focus. In a month when the Strategic Portfolio Review takes place, that review may replace it. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Source: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline.

questions.prompt: Portfolio stakeholders meet to decide together how the portfolio's funds are divided among value streams. Which LPM event is this?

options.text: Inspect and Adapt
PI Planning
The Portfolio Sync
Participatory budgeting

questions.explanation: Participatory budgeting is the collaborative event in which stakeholders allocate the portfolio budget to value streams; the current glossary also calls it Strategic Investment Planning. The Portfolio Sync reviews operations and does not set the budgets. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company adopting SAFe asks what becomes of its Project Management Office. What does SAFe suggest?

options.text: It continues unchanged and approves each train's plans
It becomes the management office for all Release Train Engineers
It can evolve into a Value Management Office that supports LPM
It is closed, and its staff are assigned to Agile Teams

questions.explanation: The Value Management Office supports Lean Portfolio Management with governance and operations, and a PMO's skills are often redirected there. Closing the PMO outright throws away knowledge the portfolio still needs. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe identify operational value streams before development value streams?

options.text: To set the budget for each project in the coming year
To decide which managers will run each of the existing departments
To see how customers are served before designing systems
To list each IT system the company owns and runs today

questions.explanation: Operational value streams show the steps customers experience, and development value streams are then formed around the systems and people that support those steps. Starting from departments or projects recreates silos. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A bank's operational value stream runs from a customer applying for a loan to the money being paid out. Which development value streams does this help identify?

options.text: Those that build the systems used along that journey
Those that have the largest annual IT budget today
Those that report to the bank's chief financial officer
Those that the auditors reviewed most recently

questions.explanation: Development value streams build and support the solutions the operational value stream uses, so mapping the loan journey shows which systems, and therefore which trains, matter. Reporting lines and budgets do not. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which type of operational value stream sells customers an application they install or subscribe to?

options.text: Supporting value stream
Fulfillment value stream
Software product value stream
Manufacturing value stream

questions.explanation: SAFe describes four types: fulfillment, manufacturing, software product and supporting. In a software product value stream the solution itself is what customers buy. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An internal process for hiring and onboarding staff is an example of which type of operational value stream?

options.text: Manufacturing
Software product
Fulfillment
Supporting

questions.explanation: Supporting value streams serve internal customers, such as hiring, procurement or internal finance processes. Fulfillment value streams serve external customers' requests. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An insurer's process from a customer reporting a claim to the claim being paid is which type of operational value stream?

options.text: Software product
Manufacturing
Fulfillment
Supporting

questions.explanation: A fulfillment value stream takes a customer request, such as a claim or an order, through to its completion. It serves an external customer, unlike a supporting value stream. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Who typically makes up the Lean Portfolio Management function?

options.text: Release Train Engineers, Product Owners and Scrum Masters
Executives, Enterprise Architects and the Agile PMO
Team members elected by each ART for one PI at a time
External auditors, the board and the finance department

questions.explanation: LPM is carried out by the people with the authority for strategy, investment and governance: business owners and executives, enterprise architects and the Agile PMO or Value Management Office. Train roles execute rather than govern the portfolio. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe define a portfolio as a set of development value streams rather than a set of projects?

options.text: Value streams need no budget once they are formed
Projects cannot be tracked in the tools that SAFe uses
A portfolio of projects is too small to need managing
Stable value streams avoid project start-stop costs

questions.explanation: Projects bring work to temporary teams that form, ramp up and disband, losing knowledge each time. Funding long-lived value streams keeps teams stable and lets work flow to them. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A large enterprise has three distinct business units, each with its own strategy, budget and customers. How might it structure its SAFe portfolios?

options.text: One portfolio for each project in the plan
One portfolio for each head of department
One portfolio for each ART in the company
One portfolio per division of the company

questions.explanation: A portfolio usually aligns with a business unit or line of business that has its own strategy and budget, so three distinct units suggest three portfolios. A portfolio normally contains several ARTs. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In SAFe, what is the enterprise?

options.text: The executive team's plan for the coming financial year
The largest ART in the company, which leads the others
The IT department that runs the systems for the business
The business entity that owns one or more portfolios

questions.explanation: SAFe's enterprise is the business entity that owns its portfolios and sets their strategy and budgets. A small enterprise may have one portfolio; a large one has several. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Source: SAFe · Enterprise.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe form development value streams around the people and systems that support an operational value stream?

options.text: So trains match the way customers are actually served
So that teams can be grouped by the skills they already have
So that each manager keeps the same reports after the change
So that each system gets its own dedicated train

questions.explanation: Building trains around the systems an operational value stream needs means each train can deliver end-to-end value with few dependencies. Grouping by skill or reporting line recreates the handoffs. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which statement about development value streams and ARTs is correct?

options.text: A big value stream may need several ARTs
Value streams are formed inside a single team
Each ART must serve exactly two value streams
An ART cannot exist without a solution train

questions.explanation: A development value stream with more people than one train can hold is split into several ARTs, often coordinated in a solution train. A small value stream may be a single ART. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the Value Management Office (VMO) typically do in SAFe?

options.text: Supports LPM with metrics, budgeting and governance
Runs the projects left over from the old way of working
Assigns developers to ARTs at the start of each PI
Approves each team's stories before they are accepted
