questions.explanation: The VMO, often an evolved PMO, supports Lean Portfolio Management with value stream metrics, Lean budgeting, governance and portfolio events. It does not approve stories or assign people. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Several shared services are used by every train in a portfolio. How does SAFe usually organise them?

options.text: By assigning each service to the Business Owners
By moving each service outside the portfolio entirely
By splitting each service equally among all the teams
As platform teams or services serving the trains

questions.explanation: SAFe treats specialist services that many trains use as shared services or platform teams, scheduled with the trains on the same cadence. Splitting them across all teams spreads scarce skills thin. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which question should a portfolio ask first when defining its scope?

options.text: Which managers will report to the portfolio's leader?
Which projects will close at the end of this year?
Which value streams does it fund and govern?
Which tools will the portfolio buy for its teams?

questions.explanation: A SAFe portfolio is defined by the value streams and solutions it funds and governs. Reporting lines, tools and project closures follow from that scope rather than define it. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which well-known one-page planning tool did SAFe adapt to describe a portfolio?

options.text: The Gantt chart
The Value Proposition Canvas
The Balanced Scorecard
The Business Model Canvas

questions.explanation: The portfolio canvas adapts the Business Model Canvas to describe a portfolio's value streams, solutions, customers, channels, budget and key metrics on one page. The Kano model classifies features by customer satisfaction. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which section of the portfolio canvas describes whom the portfolio's solutions serve?

options.text: Key partners
Cost structure
Value propositions
Customer segments

questions.explanation: Customer segments name the groups of customers each value stream serves. Key partners are suppliers and partners, and the cost structure shows where money goes. Topic 5.1, lesson “5.1 · Defining a SAFe portfolio”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is an OKR made of?

options.text: A team's velocity and its count of defects
A fixed budget and a list of the approved projects
A product vision and a fixed release date
A qualitative objective and measurable key results

questions.explanation: An Objective and Key Results pairs an inspiring, qualitative objective with a few measurable key results that show whether it is being achieved. SAFe recommends this format for strategic themes. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which key result is best written for the objective 'Delight our mobile customers'?

options.text: Make the app much better for all our customers
Build ten new features in the mobile app this year
Raise the app store rating from 3.6 to 4.4 by Q3
Hold three workshops about mobile design

questions.explanation: A key result is measurable and time-bound and shows progress toward the objective. 'Much better' is not measurable, and counting features or workshops measures output rather than the customer outcome. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do strategic themes matter to ARTs as well as to the portfolio?

options.text: They replace the ART backlog once they are approved
They are used only to work out the executives' annual bonuses
They shape the vision, backlogs and PI objectives of trains
They set each team's velocity target for the coming PI

questions.explanation: Strategic themes influence the portfolio vision, budget and backlog, and through them the ART vision, backlog and PI objectives, so trains' work connects to strategy. They do not set velocity or replace backlogs. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A new strategic theme commits the company to expanding into small-business banking. Where should the portfolio see its effect first?

options.text: In the dates of the next Inspect and Adapt event
In each team's choice of programming language
In the job titles used across the whole portfolio
In new epics and in how the budget is split

questions.explanation: Strategic themes steer investment: they shape which epics enter the portfolio backlog and how budgets are allocated across value streams. Technical choices and event dates are not where strategy shows first. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In SAFe, which two things does the enterprise pass to each portfolio to guide it?

options.text: Story points and velocity targets
Strategic themes and a budget
Project charters and Gantt charts
Team assignments and iteration goals

questions.explanation: The enterprise's strategy reaches each portfolio as strategic themes and a portfolio budget, within which the portfolio decides how to invest. Team-level plans are made by the teams. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Enterprise.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an input to enterprise strategy that SAFe describes?

options.text: Iteration goals of teams
Defect counts
Each team's velocity
Distinctive competence

questions.explanation: Enterprise strategy draws on the mission and vision, business drivers, distinctive competence, financial goals, the competitive environment and the portfolio context. Team metrics are far too detailed for it. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Enterprise.

questions.prompt: What does a portfolio send back to the enterprise to inform its strategy?

options.text: Each team's iteration plan for the next two PIs
A list of each person's completed tasks
Context such as performance and solution status
Detailed requirements for each new feature

questions.explanation: Strategy is a two-way process: the portfolio reports its context, such as key performance indicators and the state of its solutions, so the enterprise can adjust its strategy. Detailed plans stay with the trains. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Source: SAFe · Enterprise.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe treat strategy formulation as continuous and collaborative rather than as a yearly event?

options.text: Markets change faster than annual cycles can respond to
SAFe forbids planning anything longer than one PI
Yearly strategies are too expensive to write and publish
Continuous strategy lets executives avoid making choices

questions.explanation: In the digital age, opportunities and threats appear faster than an annual cycle can absorb, so strategy is revisited regularly with the people who carry it out. SAFe still plans over longer horizons, such as roadmaps. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An Epic Owner wants to show that their epic matters. Which link makes the strongest case in LPM?

options.text: How it advances a strategic theme's key results
How many teams it would keep busy working on it
How long the sponsor has wanted it to be built
How much the vendor's discount on it would save

questions.explanation: Strategic themes provide the business context for portfolio decisions, so an epic's contribution to their key results is the strongest argument. Keeping teams busy and seniority are not. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A portfolio's strategic themes are 'increase customer retention' and 'reduce cost to serve'. Which epic fits best?

options.text: A new logo and colour scheme for the brand
A research project on unrelated hardware
A self-service portal for common issues
A rewrite of the intranet's internal news pages

questions.explanation: Self-service can raise customer satisfaction and retention while reducing support costs, so it serves both themes. The other epics may have merit but serve neither theme. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A team's PI objectives do not relate to any strategic theme. What should the train consider?

options.text: Removing the objectives from the PI Planning board
Rewriting the strategic themes to cover the objectives
Nothing, since themes apply at the portfolio level alone
Whether the work is still the right priority for now

questions.explanation: Work that connects to no theme may still be needed, such as enablers or compliance, but it deserves a check against strategy and priorities. Rewriting themes to fit the work reverses the direction of alignment. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: At a Strategic Portfolio Review, leaders find that one value stream no longer serves any strategic theme. What might they decide?

options.text: Ask its teams to rewrite their iteration goals
Keep its budget, since budgets never change between years
Merge it with the largest ART to save on travel costs
Move its funding to areas with higher priority

questions.explanation: Lean budgets can be adjusted at portfolio reviews so that spending follows strategy. A value stream that no longer serves any theme is a candidate for less investment or retirement. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In a SWOT analysis, which two factors are internal to the organisation?

options.text: Opportunities and threats
Weaknesses and opportunities
Strengths and threats
Strengths and weaknesses

questions.explanation: Strengths and weaknesses describe the organisation itself; opportunities and threats come from its environment. SAFe uses SWOT, and then TOWS, to help shape portfolio strategy. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In a TOWS matrix, which kind of strategy uses internal strengths to exploit external opportunities?

options.text: Weakness-opportunity (WO) strategies
Strength-threat (ST) strategies
Weakness-threat (WT) strategies
Strength-opportunity (SO) strategies

questions.explanation: TOWS pairs internal and external factors: SO strategies use strengths to seize opportunities, ST use strengths to counter threats, WO overcome weaknesses to take opportunities, and WT minimise weaknesses and avoid threats. SO strategies usually look most attractive, because they build on what the organisation already does well. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why do OKRs suit strategic themes better than lists of projects?

options.text: They are easier to put in a Gantt chart and track
They state outcomes and leave the 'how' open
They fix the scope so that no change is possible
They give each manager a separate project to run

questions.explanation: OKRs describe the outcomes the portfolio wants, so trains and teams can find the best way to reach them and adapt as they learn. A project list fixes solutions before the work has begun. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which key result describes an outcome rather than an output?

options.text: Cut average claim time from 12 days to 5
Hire four more claims handlers by the summer
Launch the new claims portal in March
Write a claims process manual

questions.explanation: An outcome is a change in results for customers or the business, here faster claims. Launching a portal, hiring and writing a manual are outputs that may or may not produce it. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Leaders draft strategic themes on their own and announce them. What does SAFe suggest would improve them?

options.text: Keeping the themes confidential from the ARTs
Involving portfolio stakeholders in shaping them
Making the themes longer and much more detailed
Changing the themes at the end of each iteration

questions.explanation: Strategy formulated collaboratively benefits from the knowledge of those closest to customers and solutions, and it is better understood when they help shape it. Secret or constantly changing themes cannot guide anyone. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How do strategic themes help decentralised decision-making?

options.text: They replace the need for a decision framework
They require each decision to go to the executives
They list each decision that teams are allowed to make
They give everyone the context to choose well locally

questions.explanation: When everyone understands the strategic themes, local decisions can follow the strategy without escalation. Themes give direction; they do not list or centralise decisions. Topic 5.2, lesson “5.2 · Connecting the portfolio to enterprise strategy”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does the Funnel state of the portfolio Kanban hold?

options.text: New epic ideas, captured for later review
Epics whose MVP has been delivered
Epics approved and being built by trains
Epics rejected by the portfolio's leaders for now

questions.explanation: The Funnel captures significant new ideas without commitment; they move to Reviewing when there is capacity to look at them. Approved epics in progress are in Implementing. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An epic idea has a short hypothesis statement and a first estimate, and its Epic Owner is preparing it for WSJF ranking. Which Kanban state is it in?

options.text: Reviewing
Implementing
Done
Funnel

questions.explanation: In Reviewing the epic is described with a hypothesis statement, sized roughly and prioritised with WSJF to decide whether it is worth analysing. Detailed analysis and the Lean business case come in Analyzing. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What does an epic hypothesis statement contain?

options.text: Value statement, business outcomes, leading indicators
The code design, the tests and the tools for each team
The budget, the vendor and the contract terms for the epic
The task list, the owners and the deadlines for the work

questions.explanation: The epic hypothesis statement describes the epic's value proposition, the business outcomes expected if the hypothesis is true, the leading indicators that will give early evidence, and any nonfunctional requirements. Task lists, contracts and code designs come later, if at all, and belong to the trains. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which measure is a leading indicator for an epic that aims to grow online sales?

options.text: Weekly sign-ups to the new checkout in the MVP
Number of developers working on the epic
Total annual revenue reported at the end of the year
Date the epic entered the portfolio Kanban

questions.explanation: Leading indicators move early and predict the business outcome, so they give evidence during the MVP. Annual revenue is a lagging outcome that arrives too late to steer the epic. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe limit WIP in the Analyzing and Implementing states of the portfolio Kanban?

options.text: To avoid writing a Lean business case for each epic
To make sure each ART receives an epic in each PI
To keep demand in line with capacity and speed up flow
To reduce the number of Epic Owners the portfolio needs

questions.explanation: Too many epics in progress overload the trains and slow everything down. WIP limits make the portfolio finish before it starts more, which shortens the time to value. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An epic's MVP is complete, and the evidence supports the hypothesis. What happens next in the portfolio Kanban?

options.text: It returns to the Funnel to be reviewed all over again
It moves to Done because the MVP itself is now finished
It stays in Implementing as trains build more features
It is closed and a separate project is started for the rest

questions.explanation: A confirmed hypothesis means persevere: the epic stays in Implementing while trains build more features through their own backlogs. It moves to Done when it no longer needs portfolio attention. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which artifact shows the planned timing of epics and major milestones across the coming PIs?

options.text: The iteration backlog
The portfolio roadmap
The ART planning board
The team's Kanban board

questions.explanation: The portfolio roadmap shows the expected sequence and timing of epics and milestones over a longer horizon. The ART planning board covers one PI for one train. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an epic's Lean business case?

options.text: To support a go or no-go decision on the epic's MVP
To give each team a detailed task list for the whole epic
To fix the epic's full scope and cost before any work begins
To remove the need for an Epic Owner on the epic

questions.explanation: The Lean business case captures the hypothesis, the MVP, a cost estimate and the expected outcomes so LPM can decide whether to go ahead. It is light by design, not a full specification. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does the portfolio canvas help create a portfolio vision?

options.text: Contrasting current and future states shows the gap
It lists each team's velocity for the year ahead
It records which epics were rejected and why
It replaces the need for strategic themes

questions.explanation: LPM describes the current state on a canvas, explores future states, and the difference between them points to the epics needed. The vision is then realised through those epics. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A portfolio must comply with a new data residency law. Which kind of epic fits?

options.text: A team story to update the text on one screen
A feature to redesign the company website
A business epic for a new customer loyalty app
A compliance enabler epic for data storage

questions.explanation: Enabler epics cover work that supports future business needs, including exploration, architecture, infrastructure and compliance. A law affecting all systems is portfolio-sized compliance work. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: An initiative needs work across four ARTs over many PIs and exceeds the portfolio's cost threshold. How should it be handled?

options.text: As a portfolio epic with a Lean business case
As a single feature in the largest ART's backlog
As an emergency handled outside the portfolio Kanban
As a set of stories in each team's own backlog

questions.explanation: Work of this size goes through the portfolio Kanban as an epic, with a Lean business case and LPM approval. Breaking it into stories or one feature hides it from portfolio governance. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which flow metric would show how long epics take to move from the Funnel to Done?

options.text: Flow velocity
Flow load
Flow distribution
Flow time

questions.explanation: Flow time measures elapsed time from start to finish, here through the portfolio Kanban. Flow load counts work in progress, and flow velocity counts items completed per period. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: The portfolio Kanban shows twenty epics in Implementing and few finishing. What should LPM do?

options.text: Add more epics so that each ART stays busy all the time
Move some epics back to the Funnel to hide them
Lower the WIP limit and complete epics before new ones
Ask Epic Owners to report progress more often

questions.explanation: A crowded Implementing state shows demand exceeding capacity; limiting WIP and finishing work improves flow. Adding epics or more reporting makes the overload worse. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: In which portfolio Kanban state is an epic once it no longer needs portfolio governance?

options.text: Reviewing
Done
Ready
Funnel

questions.explanation: An epic reaches Done when it no longer needs portfolio attention, either because its hypothesis was disproved or because the remaining work continues in the trains' backlogs. Ready and Reviewing come before implementation, and the Funnel holds new ideas. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps LPM decide which epic to pull next from Ready?

options.text: A vote by each team on each of the trains
The order in which the epics were first proposed
WSJF ranking, within the capacity available
The seniority of each epic's executive sponsor

questions.explanation: Epics are pulled from Ready by economic priority, using WSJF, when the trains have capacity. Seniority and first-come order ignore the cost of delay. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe ask for leading indicators in an epic hypothesis statement?

options.text: They tell finance how much the epic will cost
They are easier to adjust than lagging indicators
They give early evidence, before outcomes arrive
They replace the need to measure business outcomes

questions.explanation: Business outcomes often take months to appear, so leading indicators give early signals during the MVP to support the pivot-or-persevere decision. They complement outcome measures. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A portfolio vision says the business will move from in-store to digital sales within three years. Which tool turns this into work?

options.text: Team retrospectives held at the end of each iteration
A three-year fixed contract with a single vendor
Epics that close the gap to the future state
A new organisation chart with more layers of managers

questions.explanation: SAFe realises the portfolio vision through epics: the significant initiatives that close the gap between the current and future states. Retrospectives and org charts do not deliver the change. Topic 5.3, lesson “5.3 · Portfolio vision and portfolio flow”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which investment horizon covers new ideas explored through small, time-boxed experiments?

options.text: Horizon 0, Retiring
Horizon 3, Evaluating
Horizon 2, Emerging
Horizon 1, Investing and extracting

questions.explanation: SAFe's horizons are Horizon 3 Evaluating, Horizon 2 Emerging, Horizon 1 Investing and extracting, and Horizon 0 Retiring. Evaluating is where new ideas get small investments to test them. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A solution earns strong revenue today, and the portfolio keeps funding it to improve and profit from it. Which horizon is it in?

options.text: Horizon 2, Emerging solutions
Horizon 1, Investing and extracting
Horizon 0, Retiring solutions
Horizon 3, Evaluating new ideas

questions.explanation: Horizon 1 holds today's solutions that earn the returns, funded to extend and improve them. Horizon 2 holds promising solutions still being built up. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe use investment horizons as a Lean budget guardrail?

options.text: To fix each value stream's budget for five years
To rank employees for promotion each year
To decide which teams are disbanded in each PI
To balance spending now and in the future

questions.explanation: Guiding investments by horizon keeps the portfolio from spending everything on today's solutions or everything on speculative ones. It is one of the four guardrails. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A train spends nearly all its time on new features while technical debt grows. Which guardrail addresses this?

options.text: Approval of significant initiatives
Investment horizons for the portfolio
Capacity allocation for enablers and debt
More frequent Business Owner reviews

questions.explanation: The guardrail 'applying capacity allocation to optimize value and solution integrity' reserves capacity for enablers, debt and maintenance, so the solution stays healthy. The other guardrails govern different risks. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which guardrail keeps the people with fiduciary responsibility involved in how the budget is spent?

options.text: Capacity allocation by work type
Guiding investments by horizon
Continuous Business Owner engagement
Approving significant initiatives

questions.explanation: Continuous Business Owner engagement keeps them involved through PI Planning, System Demos and Inspect and Adapt, so spending stays aligned. The other three guardrails cover approvals, horizons and capacity. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A value stream's budget is set for the next six months. Within it, who decides which features to build?

options.text: The executives, at a monthly approval meeting
Its ARTs, through backlogs and PI Planning
The portfolio's finance team, feature by feature
Each developer, according to personal interest

questions.explanation: Lean budgets fund value streams and decentralise content decisions to them: Product Management prioritises the backlog and the train plans in PI Planning, within the guardrails. Finance and executives set the budget and the guardrails, not each feature. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: What is the main trade-off that Lean budgets make compared with project funding?

options.text: Higher total cost, in exchange for fewer meetings
Less control over spending, with no guardrails at all
Longer approval times, in exchange for certainty
Less up-front cost detail, for speed and flexibility

questions.explanation: Lean budgets give up detailed project cost estimates in favour of funding value streams, which removes approval delays and lets money follow priorities. Control comes from guardrails and frequent evidence. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: When must an epic go to LPM for approval under the guardrails?

options.text: When it is first written in the Funnel
When it has an Epic Owner assigned to it
When it needs more than one team for a single iteration
When its estimated cost exceeds a threshold

questions.explanation: The guardrail 'approving significant initiatives' sends epics above a cost threshold to LPM, while smaller initiatives are decided within the value stream's budget. Team counts, Epic Owners and the Funnel have nothing to do with the threshold. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How do LPM and Business Owners use the PI System Demo for budget governance?

options.text: To approve each story the teams completed
To set the velocity target for the next PI
To see real progress and adjust spending
To audit the hours each person logged

questions.explanation: Objective evidence from working systems replaces status reports as the basis for governance, so spending can be adjusted to what is actually being achieved. Approving stories and auditing hours would be micromanagement, not governance. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which investment horizon holds solutions that show promise and are being built up?

options.text: Horizon 0, Retiring
Horizon 3, Evaluating
Horizon 1, Investing and extracting
Horizon 2, Emerging

questions.explanation: Emerging solutions have passed early evaluation and are being developed toward profitability. Evaluating holds earlier ideas, and Investing and extracting holds established earners. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe say Lean budgets still need guardrails?

options.text: Guardrails replace the need for strategic themes
Guardrails let finance approve each story's cost
Lean budgets are always larger than project budgets
Decentralised spending needs clear, agreed boundaries

questions.explanation: Funding value streams moves spending decisions closer to the work; guardrails keep those decisions within agreed policies on horizons, capacity, approvals and Business Owner involvement. Without them, decentralised budgets could drift away from the strategy. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Priorities change, and a portfolio wants to move budget from one value stream to another mid-year. What does SAFe suggest?

options.text: Ask each team to fund the change from its own budget
Start a new project with a separate budget instead
Adjust it through LPM's regular budget reviews
Wait for the next annual budget cycle to change it

questions.explanation: Lean budgets are reviewed and adjusted periodically, for example through participatory budgeting at portfolio reviews, so money can follow changing priorities without waiting a year. Waiting for the annual cycle is the project-funding habit that Lean budgets replace. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which practice helps a portfolio forecast epics without detailed up-front planning?

options.text: Asking vendors to quote a fixed price for each epic
Planning each epic to the day for the next two years
Writing every story for every epic before starting
Relative sizing compared with known capacity

questions.explanation: Relative estimates of epic size, compared with the trains' known capacity, give a good enough forecast for portfolio decisions. Detailed up-front plans cost much and are soon out of date. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Match each investment horizon to its description.

options.text: Retiring solutions
Outsourcing solutions to suppliers
Investing in and extracting value from current solutions
Evaluating new ideas
Emerging solutions being built up

questions.explanation: The horizons run from evaluating ideas, to emerging solutions, to established solutions that are invested in and extracted from, to retiring ones. Outsourcing is not a horizon. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A portfolio funds value streams but still requires a detailed business case for each feature. What problem remains?

options.text: Business cases make the features cheaper to build
Content decisions stay slow and centralised as before
Value streams cannot be funded without business cases
Features cannot be estimated once value streams are funded

questions.explanation: Lean budgets pay off only when content decisions are decentralised within guardrails. Demanding a business case per feature reintroduces the delays of project funding. Topic 5.4, lesson “5.4 · Lean budgets and guardrails”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does SAFe describe Lean-Agile Leadership?

options.text: Leaders step back and let teams define the strategy
Leaders drive and sustain change by empowering individuals and teams
Leaders delegate the transformation to certified coaches
Leaders set detailed plans and check each week that all the teams follow them

questions.explanation: Lean-Agile Leadership describes how leaders drive and sustain organisational change and operational excellence by empowering individuals and teams to reach their potential. Delegating the change is the tempting answer and the one SAFe rejects. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership; SAFe glossary.

questions.prompt: Teams at Pinecrest Telecom work in an Agile way, but annual budgeting, performance reviews and approval boards are unchanged, and nobody below the executives can alter them. What does this illustrate?

options.text: That the Release Train Engineer should redesign the policies
That SAFe is unsuitable for a company of this size
That only leaders can change the system in which people work
That teams need more Agile training before SAFe can work

questions.explanation: SAFe holds that only managers, executives and other leaders can change the systems that govern how work is done. More team training cannot fix policies the teams have no authority over. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership.

questions.prompt: A director asks teams for full transparency about problems, yet never admits to mistakes of their own. Which leadership behaviour is missing?

options.text: Applying cadence
Leading by example
Decentralising decisions
Taking an economic view

questions.explanation: Leaders lead by example, modelling the mindset, values and behaviours they ask of others. People copy what leaders do far more than what leaders say. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Source: SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership.

questions.prompt: What is the first step of the SAFe Implementation Roadmap?

options.text: Create the Implementation Plan
Reaching the Tipping Point
Train Teams and Launch ART
Organize Around Value

questions.explanation: The roadmap begins with Reaching the Tipping Point, where the need for change overcomes resistance to it. Launching a train is the visible step, but it comes much later in the sequence. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap; SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point.

questions.prompt: Arrange these steps of the SAFe Implementation Roadmap in order.

options.text: Train Lean-Agile Change Agents
Organize Around Value
Train Teams and Launch ART
Coach ART Execution
Create the Implementation Plan
Reaching the Tipping Point

questions.explanation: The roadmap moves from the tipping point through training change agents and leaders, organising around value and planning, to launching and coaching the first train. Organising around value comes before the implementation plan, since the plan needs to know which value streams and trains exist. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: A profitable company faces no crisis, but its executives foresee disruption and set out a compelling vision for change. Which route to the tipping point is this?

options.text: A grassroots movement
A regulatory mandate
Proactive leadership
A burning platform

questions.explanation: SAFe names two routes to the tipping point: a burning platform, where failure to compete is obvious, and visionary leaders who act before a crisis. With no crisis in sight, this is the proactive route. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Source: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point.

questions.prompt: Which three benefits does a vision for change provide?

options.text: Authority, control and compliance
Scope, schedule and budget
Speed, savings and headcount
Purpose, motivation and alignment

questions.explanation: A vision for change gives purpose, motivation and alignment. Scope, schedule and budget belong to a project plan, not to a vision. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point.

questions.prompt: One enthusiastic Agile coach is trying to drive a SAFe transformation across three business units without executive involvement. What does SAFe say is needed?

options.text: A stricter rollout schedule
A new tool for tracking adoption
A sufficiently powerful guiding coalition
A larger budget for external coaching days

questions.explanation: A vision is not enough; a powerful guiding coalition of influential leaders is needed to carry the change. A single coach lacks the authority to change the system, however capable. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point; SAFe · Leadership and Culture discipline.

questions.prompt: Which group is a small Agile team dedicated to implementing the SAFe way of working?

options.text: The Lean-Agile Center of Excellence
The System Team
The Agile Program Management Office
The Value Management Office

questions.explanation: The Lean-Agile Center of Excellence is a small Agile team that implements the Lean-Agile way of working. The Value Management Office supports portfolio governance, a different job. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe glossary; SAFe · Leadership and Culture discipline.

questions.prompt: Whose work on change management does the SAFe Implementation Roadmap draw on?

options.text: Frederick Taylor
Henry Gantt
Michael Porter
John Kotter

questions.explanation: The roadmap's strategy is sourced partly from John Kotter's change management work, including the guiding coalition and short-term wins. Taylor and Gantt represent the scientific management tradition that Lean-Agile thinking moves away from. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: An AI assistant analyses a train's flow metrics and recommends disbanding one team. What is the leader's responsibility?

options.text: Evaluate the recommendation and remain accountable for the decision
Ask the assistant to announce the decision to the team
Ignore the output, since AI cannot understand teams
Carry out the recommendation, since it comes straight from the data

questions.explanation: The course emphasises human-in-the-loop evaluation, so the leader checks the analysis and owns the decision. Following the output because it is data-driven hands accountability to a tool. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: Which use of AI by a leader fits SAFe's guidance?

options.text: Letting an assistant decide which epics are approved
Pasting confidential salary data into a public chatbot for analysis
Replacing the System Demo with generated status text
Summarising Inspect and Adapt findings as input to a decision

questions.explanation: AI supports leaders by preparing and summarising information, while people evaluate the output and decide. Replacing the System Demo with generated text removes the objective evidence of a working system. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page; SAFe · Artificial Intelligence in SAFe.

questions.prompt: Which three dimensions make up the Lean-Agile Leadership competency?

options.text: Planning the work; budgeting the teams; controlling the results
Hiring the right people; training them; rewarding the high performers
Setting the vision; writing the strategy; driving the execution
Mindset, values and principles; leading by example; leading change

questions.explanation: SAFe describes Lean-Agile Leadership through three dimensions: a mindset, values and principles; leading by example; and leading change. The distractors describe traditional management cycles. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a behaviour SAFe associates with leading by example?

options.text: Assigning tasks
Growing others
Approving designs
Tracking utilisation

questions.explanation: Leading by example includes authenticity, emotional intelligence, lifelong learning, growing others and decentralised decision-making. Assigning tasks, tracking utilisation and approving designs are command-and-control habits that SAFe asks leaders to move away from. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A director openly admits a mistake in a planning decision and explains to the team what was learned from it. Which leading-by-example behaviour is this?

options.text: Emotional intelligence
Growing others
Decentralized decision-making
Authenticity

questions.explanation: Authenticity means being honest and consistent, including about one's own mistakes, which makes it safe for others to do the same. Emotional intelligence is about recognising and managing emotions, one's own and others'. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A manager sees that a team is tense after a failed release and opens the retrospective by acknowledging the pressure before discussing causes. Which behaviour does this show?

options.text: Decentralized decision-making
Authenticity
Emotional intelligence
Lifelong learning

questions.explanation: Recognising how people feel and responding in a way that helps the conversation is emotional intelligence. Authenticity would be the manager being open about their own part or feelings. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A leader regularly takes courses, reads widely and asks for feedback on their own leadership. Which behaviour is this?

options.text: Lifelong learning
Decentralized decision-making
Growing others
Authenticity

questions.explanation: Lifelong learning is a leader continuing to learn, including about their own leadership, and showing that learning is valued. Growing others is about developing the people around the leader. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe ask leaders to 'go and see' where the work happens?

options.text: To understand the real problems first-hand before deciding
To stand in for the Scrum Master when problems arise
To approve each team's work before it is released
To check that each person is busy for the whole working day

questions.explanation: Going to see the work, the Lean idea of the gemba, gives leaders a first-hand view of the problems and the system that causes them. It is not inspection of individuals or a way to take over the team's roles. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A senior manager wants to grow the people on a train. Which action fits SAFe's view of the leader's role?

options.text: Review each person's tasks each morning before work starts
Write detailed instructions so that nobody needs to think
Coach and mentor them, and give them room to try and learn
Rank team members against each other each quarter

questions.explanation: SAFe sees leaders as coaches and teachers who develop people's skills and judgement, which includes room to experiment and learn from mistakes. Close task control and forced ranking work against the intrinsic motivation of knowledge workers. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does SAFe expect leaders to model the Lean-Agile mindset rather than just sponsor it?

options.text: Sponsorship costs more than taking part in person
Modelling the mindset removes the need to train the teams
People copy what leaders do more than what they say
Leaders are the only ones allowed to attend SAFe training

questions.explanation: Behaviour sets culture: when leaders work in the new way, people believe the change is real, and when they do not, people conclude the old rules still apply. Modelling complements training; it does not replace it. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: During PI Planning, a Business Owner overrides a team's estimates to fit a date already promised to a customer. Which leadership behaviour has been ignored?

options.text: Authenticity, since the Business Owner hid the promise
Decentralized decision-making, since teams own their estimates
Emotional intelligence, since nobody's feelings were discussed
Lifelong learning, since the Business Owner misread the estimates

questions.explanation: The people closest to the work estimate and commit; a leader who overrides estimates undermines the commitment and the predictability that PI Planning is meant to create. Business Owners influence priorities and business value, not the teams' estimates. Topic 6.1, lesson “6.1 · Leading by example”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How many steps does the SAFe Implementation Roadmap have?

options.text: Thirteen
Ten
Twelve
Eight

questions.explanation: The current roadmap has thirteen steps, from Reaching the Tipping Point to Accelerate. Older versions had twelve, and Kotter's change model, which the roadmap draws on, has eight, so both are common wrong answers. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: A company has reached the tipping point and trained its change agents. Which roadmap step comes next?

options.text: Launch More ARTs and Value Streams
Create the Implementation Plan
Train Executives, Managers, and Leaders
Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence

questions.explanation: The current roadmap runs: Reaching the Tipping Point, Train Lean-Agile Change Agents, Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence, Train Executives, Managers, and Leaders, Lead in the Digital Age, then Organize Around Value. Older versions trained executives before creating the LACE, so check the order in your workbook. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: Which roadmap step defines the operational and development value streams and the ARTs that will serve them?

options.text: Launch More ARTs and Value Streams
Organize Around Value
Prepare for ART Launch
Create the Implementation Plan

questions.explanation: Organize Around Value is step six of the current roadmap: it finds how value flows to customers and which trains should build the solutions; older versions called it Identify Value Streams and ARTs. The implementation plan then decides where to start. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: What is the final step of the SAFe Implementation Roadmap?

options.text: Coach ART Execution
Enhance the Portfolio
Accelerate
Launch More ARTs and Value Streams

questions.explanation: The last steps are Launch More ARTs and Value Streams, Enhance the Portfolio, and Accelerate, which is about sustaining and improving the new way of working. A transformation does not end like a project, which is why the last step is not a hand-over. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: In Kotter's change model, which SAFe draws on, which step follows creating a sense of urgency?

options.text: Build a guiding coalition
Generate short-term wins
Enable action by removing barriers
Enlist a volunteer army

questions.explanation: Kotter's steps run: create a sense of urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a strategic vision, enlist a volunteer army, enable action by removing barriers, generate short-term wins, sustain acceleration and institute change. The coalition comes second because urgency alone needs influential people to carry it. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Why does the roadmap train executives, managers and leaders before the first ART is launched?

options.text: Executives must be certified before any team may be trained
Training leaders removes the need to train the teams
Leaders must understand the new way of working to lead it
It gives leaders time to choose which teams to disband

questions.explanation: Leaders own the system the teams work in, so they need to understand and support Lean-Agile ways before the teams start, or old policies will undo the change. Teams are still trained, at launch. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A company plans to train its first ART's teams one at a time over several months. What does SAFe's approach to launching an ART recommend instead?

options.text: Train the teams together, close to the first PI Planning
Train the Scrum Masters and let them train their own teams
Skip team training and begin with the first System Demo
Train one team per PI until each team has been trained

questions.explanation: SAFe launches an ART by training its teams together, typically just before the first PI Planning, so everyone learns the same way of working at once and applies it straight away. Training one team at a time leaves the train half-changed for months. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: After the first ART has launched successfully, what does the roadmap suggest doing next?

options.text: Coach its execution, then launch more ARTs and value streams
Disband the LACE, since its work is now finished
Move straight to the portfolio before launching any more ARTs
Pause the change for a year to let the train settle

questions.explanation: After launch come Coach ART Execution and Launch More ARTs and Value Streams; Enhance the Portfolio comes later. The LACE keeps driving the change throughout. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap.

questions.prompt: In which situation is a company most likely to reach the tipping point through a 'burning platform'?

options.text: A new executive wants to try out a popular framework
Its leaders foresee disruption while results are still strong
Its teams ask for training in Agile methods
Its market share is collapsing and the old way is failing

questions.explanation: SAFe describes two ways to reach the tipping point: a burning platform, a crisis that makes change unavoidable, or proactive leadership, where leaders choose to change before a crisis. Foreseeing disruption while results are strong is the proactive route. Topic 6.2, lesson “6.2 · Leading the change”. Source: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point.

questions.prompt: A leader wants teams to experiment with AI in their work. Which action models the behaviour SAFe expects of leaders?

options.text: Let teams use any public AI tool with company data
Ban AI until a full policy has been written by the legal team
Use AI openly in their own work and share what they learn
Require each team to report its AI hours every week

questions.explanation: Leading by example applies to AI: leaders who use it visibly, share results and talk about its limits make experimentation safe. A blanket ban stalls learning, and unmanaged use of public tools with company data creates risk. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A leader uses AI to draft a vision for change. Why should the leader still own the final message?

options.text: Visions drafted with AI are not allowed in SAFe
AI tools cannot write more than a few hundred words at a time
The AI vendor owns the rights to the text it drafts
Accountability and authenticity cannot be handed to a tool

questions.explanation: AI can speed up drafting, but people follow a vision because they trust the leader behind it, so the leader must shape, check and stand behind the words. Nothing in SAFe forbids AI-assisted drafting. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: A Business Owner asks AI to summarise customer feedback before PI Planning. What makes this use responsible?

options.text: Pasting the customers' names into a public chatbot for accuracy
Using the AI summary instead of talking to customers
Presenting the summary as the customers' exact words
Checking the summary against what customers actually said

questions.explanation: AI summaries can omit or distort what people said, so a leader checks them against the source before using them in decisions, and protects personal data. A summary supplements customer contact; it does not replace it. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: Which leadership task is AI best placed to accelerate?

options.text: Setting the organisation's values and its ethics
Building trust with a team through personal contact
Taking the decision and carrying its accountability
Synthesising large volumes of data into options

questions.explanation: The Leading SAFe course page lists using AI to synthesise complex data and to streamline the creation of strategic artifacts. Decisions, trust and values remain human work that AI can inform but not carry. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: A leader notices that AI use is very uneven, with a few experts and many people who never try it. What should the leader do?

options.text: Let the experts do the AI work for all of the teams
Create time, training and safe ways for everyone to experiment
Wait for the tools to become easy enough on their own
Set a target number of prompts per person each week

questions.explanation: Leaders shape the environment: time to learn, training and safe experiments spread capability across the organisation. Concentrating AI in a few experts creates a bottleneck, and prompt quotas measure activity rather than value. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

questions.prompt: How does the Leading SAFe course page describe the role of AI for organisational value and flow?

options.text: A powerful accelerant
A temporary experiment
A substitute for PI Planning
A replacement for leadership

questions.explanation: The course page says learners will use AI as a powerful accelerant for organisational value and flow. An accelerant speeds up what is already there, good or bad, which is why it complements Lean-Agile leadership rather than replacing it. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: Which AI assistant does the Leading SAFe course page say learners can use to navigate framework guidance?

options.text: SAFe Studio Guide
Framework Navigator
SAFe CoPilot
Agile Assistant

questions.explanation: The course page names the SAFe CoPilot AI assistant for navigating framework guidance, synthesising complex data and drafting strategic artifacts. SAFe Studio is the learning platform, not the assistant. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Source: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page.

questions.prompt: An AI tool recommends removing the IP iteration to gain capacity. How should a Lean-Agile leader respond?

options.text: Reject it without review, since AI advice is unreliable
Apply it at once, since the AI analysed more data than anyone
Test the advice against SAFe principles and evidence first
Ask the AI to decide the next PI's scope as well

questions.explanation: AI advice is an input to a decision, judged against principles and evidence; here, removing the IP iteration would remove the buffer and the time for innovation and planning. Blind acceptance and blanket rejection both skip the leader's judgement. Topic 6.3, lesson “6.3 · Empowering leaders with AI”. Not checked against a public page.

notes.front: What is Business Agility?
notes.back: The ability to compete and thrive in the digital age by responding quickly with digitally enabled solutions.
notes.explanation: It is an enterprise capability, not a team practice.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility

notes.front: What are the two parts of the dual operating system?
notes.back: The hierarchy, for efficiency and stability, and a value stream network, for speed and adaptability.
notes.explanation: SAFe keeps the hierarchy and adds the network.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility
SAFe · Principle #10 (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Business Agility rests on {{c1::seven}} core competencies and is measured by {{c2::flow}}, {{c3::outcomes}} and {{c4::competency}}.
notes.explanation: Flow is efficiency of delivery, outcomes are business results, competency is how well the practices are done.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility

notes.front: In the Business Agility Value Stream, what follows Deliver MVP?
notes.back: Pivot or Persevere.
notes.explanation: Evidence from the MVP decides what happens to the investment.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility

notes.front: Which SAFe configuration is the simplest starting point?
notes.back: Essential SAFe.
notes.explanation: It holds the minimal elements an ART needs.

sources.title: SAFe glossary

notes.front: Who has to lead a SAFe transformation?
notes.back: The organisation's leaders; it cannot be delegated.
notes.explanation: Only leaders can change the system people work in.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Technological revolutions (Perez)
notes.back: Five ages, from the industrial revolution to today's age of software and digital; each is installed, then deployed across the economy.
notes.explanation: Why SAFe treats digital disruption as structural. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Who must use Lean and Agile practices for Business Agility?
notes.back: Everyone involved in delivering solutions: business and technology leaders, development, IT operations, legal, marketing, finance, support and more.
notes.explanation: Not just IT, and not just coaches.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility

notes.text: BAVS: {{c1::Sense Opportunity}}, {{c2::Fund MVP}}, {{c3::Organize Around Value}}, {{c4::Connect to Customer}}, Deliver MVP, {{c5::Pivot or Persevere}}, Deliver Value Continuously, Learn and Adapt.
notes.explanation: The Business Agility Value Stream.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility

notes.front: What is the first step of the Business Agility Value Stream?
notes.back: Sense Opportunity.
notes.explanation: Fund MVP comes second.

sources.title: SAFe · Business Agility

notes.front: What does 'every business is a software business' mean?
notes.back: Competitiveness depends on delivering digitally enabled solutions quickly.
notes.explanation: True of banks, freight firms and hospitals alike.

notes.text: The four SAFe configurations: {{c1::Essential}}, {{c2::Large Solution}}, {{c3::Portfolio}} and {{c4::Full}}.
notes.explanation: Team SAFe and Enterprise SAFe are not configurations.

notes.text: Six flow metrics: flow {{c1::distribution}}, {{c2::velocity}}, {{c3::time}}, {{c4::load}}, {{c5::efficiency}} and {{c6::predictability}}.
notes.explanation: Part of the flow measurement domain. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Which two core competencies did the current glossary rename?
notes.back: Agile Product Delivery became Product Development Flow; Enterprise Solution Delivery became Large Solution Integration and Delivery.
notes.explanation: Recognise both sets of names.

sources.title: SAFe glossary

notes.front: Which configuration fits several ARTs and suppliers building one very big system, without portfolio management?
notes.back: Large Solution SAFe.
notes.explanation: Full SAFe adds the portfolio as well.

notes.front: Which competency extends Lean and Agile into finance, HR and legal?
notes.back: Organizational Agility.
notes.explanation: Its dimensions include Lean business operations and strategy agility.

notes.front: Which measurement domain asks whether solutions achieve their intended benefits?
notes.back: Outcomes.
notes.explanation: Flow asks how efficiently value is delivered; competency how proficient the organisation is.

notes.front: What does the Lean-Agile mindset combine?
notes.back: Lean thinking and the Agile Manifesto.
notes.explanation: Agility is a mindset change, not only a set of practices.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean-Agile Mindset (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: The four SAFe Core Values are {{c1::alignment}}, {{c2::transparency}}, {{c3::respect for people}} and {{c4::relentless improvement}}.
notes.explanation: The earlier set included built-in quality and program execution; it is a common distractor.

sources.title: SAFe · Core Values (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Lean thinking: specify {{c1::value}}, identify the {{c2::value stream}}, make value {{c3::flow}}, let the customer {{c4::pull}}, pursue {{c5::perfection}}.
notes.explanation: Five ideas, in this order.

notes.front: Which decisions stay centralised under Principle #9?
notes.back: Those that are infrequent, long-lasting and have significant economies of scale.
notes.explanation: Everything frequent, time-critical and local is decentralised. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What drives knowledge workers, according to Principle #8?
notes.back: Autonomy, mastery and purpose.
notes.explanation: Individual incentives can harm problem-solving work. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What must happen to AI output before it informs a decision?
notes.back: A person evaluates it: human in the loop.
notes.explanation: The course lists human-in-the-loop evaluation among its AI points.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page

notes.front: What is a growth mindset?
notes.back: The belief that abilities can be developed through effort and learning.
notes.explanation: The opposite of a fixed mindset.

notes.front: Alignment (Core Value)
notes.back: Everyone understands and works toward the same mission, vision and objectives.
notes.explanation: Built by leaders communicating repeatedly, and by PI Planning.

notes.front: Transparency (Core Value)
notes.back: Facts are visible, including bad news, which needs trust.
notes.explanation: People share problems only where it is safe.

notes.front: Respect for people (Core Value)
notes.back: Everyone who does the work, and customers, suppliers and partners, are valued, developed and trusted.
notes.explanation: People, not processes, do the work.

notes.front: Relentless improvement (Core Value)
notes.back: A constant sense of danger, regular reflection and structured problem solving.
notes.explanation: Needs protected time, such as I&A.

notes.text: Agile Manifesto: {{c1::individuals and interactions}} over processes and tools, {{c2::working software}} over comprehensive documentation, {{c3::customer collaboration}} over contract negotiation, {{c4::responding to change}} over following a plan.
notes.explanation: The right-hand items still have value.

notes.front: What is the primary measure of progress in the Agile Manifesto?
notes.back: Working software.
notes.explanation: SAFe scales it as objective evaluation of working systems.

notes.front: How does the Agile Manifesto describe simplicity?
notes.back: The art of maximising the amount of work not done.
notes.explanation: Build only what delivers value.

notes.front: What is waste in Lean thinking?
notes.back: Activity that uses resources but adds no value for the customer.
notes.explanation: Waiting, handoffs and rework are typical.

notes.text: Flow accelerators: visualize and limit {{c1::WIP}}, address {{c2::bottlenecks}}, minimize {{c3::handoffs}} and dependencies, get faster {{c4::feedback}}, work in smaller {{c5::batches}}, reduce {{c6::queue}} length, optimize time in the zone, remediate {{c7::legacy policies}} and practices.
notes.explanation: Eight accelerators under Principle #6. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What does Little's Law say?
notes.back: Average wait time equals queue length divided by processing rate.
notes.explanation: Longer queues at the same rate mean longer waits.

notes.front: Set-based design
notes.back: Keeping several design options open and narrowing them as knowledge grows.
notes.explanation: Principle #3.

notes.front: Which learning cycle does SAFe use under Principle #4?
notes.back: Plan, Do, Check, Adjust.
notes.explanation: Each cycle ends in an integration point.

notes.front: Name the economic trade-off parameters of Principle #1.
notes.back: Development expense, lead time, product cost, value and risk.
notes.explanation: Changing one moves the others. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What does synchronisation add to cadence?
notes.back: Multiple perspectives are understood, resolved and integrated at the same time.
notes.explanation: Cadence makes events predictable.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean-Agile Principles

notes.front: Where can AI be applied in SAFe?
notes.back: At all levels: intelligent customer solutions, automating value stream activities and improving customer insight.
notes.explanation: From SAFe's public AI guidance.

sources.title: SAFe · Artificial Intelligence in SAFe (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Which problems suit AI better than rule-based software?
notes.back: Situations that predefined rules cannot cover.
notes.explanation: Fixed steps and exact calculations stay with conventional software.

sources.title: SAFe · Artificial Intelligence in SAFe (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: How do you tell whether AI has helped a value stream?
notes.back: With flow and outcome measures, such as shorter flow time, not tool or token counts.
notes.explanation: Activity is not value.

notes.front: What must you check before pasting confidential data into an AI tool?
notes.back: That the tool is approved for that data.
notes.explanation: Public tools may store or reuse inputs.

notes.front: AI-written code passes its tests but nobody understands it. What is the problem?
notes.back: Maintainability: built-in quality needs code the team can change safely.
notes.explanation: Review and simplify before it becomes a liability.

notes.front: What is an Agile Team in SAFe?
notes.back: A cross-functional group of ten or fewer who can define, build, test and deliver value.
notes.explanation: Its two roles are the Product Owner and the Scrum Master/Team Coach.

sources.title: SAFe · Agile Teams (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What is an Agile Release Train?
notes.back: A long-lived team of Agile teams, typically 50 to 125 people, in a development value stream.
notes.explanation: It is not formed for one release and disbanded.

sources.title: SAFe · Agile Release Train (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Release Train Engineer
notes.back: Servant leader and coach for the train who facilitates ART events.
notes.explanation: The RTE does not prioritise features.

sources.title: SAFe · Release Train Engineer (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Product Management
notes.back: Defines features and prioritises the ART backlog.
notes.explanation: Works with the System Architect, the RTE and Business Owners.
