notes.back: Defines the architecture and enablers and identifies nonfunctional requirements for a train.
notes.explanation: The Enterprise Architect does this for the portfolio.

sources.title: SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline

notes.front: Business Owners
notes.back: Key stakeholders responsible for governance, fitness for use and return on investment.
notes.explanation: They assign business value to PI objectives.

sources.title: SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline

notes.front: Product Owner
notes.back: Maximises the value a team delivers by ordering the team backlog.
notes.explanation: The voice of the customer on the team.

sources.title: SAFe · Product Owner (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: CALMR: {{c1::Culture}}, {{c2::Automation}}, {{c3::Lean flow}}, {{c4::Measurement}}, {{c5::Recovery}}.
notes.explanation: The industry acronym CALMS ends in sharing; SAFe uses recovery.

sources.title: SAFe · CALMR (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: The Continuous Delivery Pipeline: Continuous {{c1::Exploration}}, Continuous {{c2::Integration}}, Continuous {{c3::Deployment}}, {{c4::Release on Demand}}.
notes.explanation: Deployment is separated from release.

sources.title: SAFe · Continuous Delivery Pipeline (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What does Built-In Quality mean?
notes.back: Quality practices run throughout development; quality is not inspected in at the end.
notes.explanation: It improves velocity and predictability.

sources.title: SAFe · Built-In Quality (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Which two ways of working do SAFe teams use?
notes.back: SAFe Scrum and SAFe Team Kanban.
notes.explanation: Both plan with the train.

sources.title: SAFe · Team and Technical Agility discipline

notes.front: Scrum Master/Team Coach
notes.back: A servant leader and coach who facilitates team events, improves flow and removes impediments.
notes.explanation: Does not assign tasks or prioritise the backlog.

sources.title: SAFe · Scrum Master/Team Coach (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Team events: iteration {{c1::planning}}, team {{c2::sync}}, backlog {{c3::refinement}}, iteration {{c4::review}} and iteration {{c5::retrospective}}.
notes.explanation: Kanban teams hold the equivalents on the train's cadence.

notes.front: Iteration goals
notes.back: A brief summary of the business and technical outcomes a team aims to achieve in an iteration.
notes.explanation: Not a task list or a velocity target.

notes.front: When does SAFe Team Kanban suit a team better than Scrum?
notes.back: When work arrives unpredictably, such as maintenance or support.
notes.explanation: It pulls work continuously within WIP limits.

notes.front: Why should team members be dedicated to one team?
notes.back: Splitting people adds context switching and makes teams wait.
notes.explanation: Stable teams build trust and shared knowledge.

notes.text: Team topologies: {{c1::stream-aligned}}, {{c2::complicated subsystem}}, {{c3::platform}} and {{c4::enabling}}.
notes.explanation: Most teams are stream-aligned. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: How big is an ART, and why the cap?
notes.back: About 50 to 125 people in five to twelve teams; beyond Dunbar's number, trust is hard to keep.
notes.explanation: Larger value streams use several ARTs.

sources.title: SAFe · Agile Release Train (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: System Team
notes.back: Supports the train by building the development environment and helping with integration and demos.
notes.explanation: Not a test phase at the end.

notes.front: Teams keep waiting for a shared environment team. Which topology helps?
notes.back: A platform team offering environments as self-service.
notes.explanation: Self-service removes the queue.

notes.text: Basic built-in quality practices: shift learning {{c1::left}}, {{c2::pairing}} and peer review, {{c3::collective ownership}} and T-shaped skills, artifact standards and a {{c4::definition of done}}, {{c5::workflow automation}}.
notes.explanation: Practices for all teams. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Shift learning left
notes.back: Moving testing, review and feedback earlier, where problems are cheap to fix.
notes.explanation: Defects found in the last week are a sign it is missing.

notes.front: Definition of done
notes.back: A shared standard for when work is finished, such as tested, reviewed and documented.
notes.explanation: Quality is not left for later.

notes.front: Why is a regular hardening iteration a warning sign?
notes.back: It treats quality as a phase instead of building it in.
notes.explanation: Each increment should be releasable.

notes.front: Why does built-in quality make delivery faster?
notes.back: Less rework and fewer defects let work flow predictably.
notes.explanation: Cutting quality borrows time.

sources.title: SAFe · Built-In Quality (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Does built-in quality apply to non-software teams?
notes.back: Yes, through standards, peer review and checks suited to their work.
notes.explanation: SAFe applies it to business functions too.

notes.front: What is the difference between deployment and release?
notes.back: Deployment moves changes to production; release makes them available to customers when the business decides.
notes.explanation: Feature toggles keep deployed work hidden.

sources.title: SAFe · Release on Demand (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Continuous Integration: {{c1::develop}}, {{c2::build}}, {{c3::test end-to-end}}, {{c4::stage}}.
notes.explanation: Validated in a staging environment.

sources.title: SAFe · Continuous Integration (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Continuous Deployment: {{c1::deploy}}, {{c2::verify}}, {{c3::monitor}}, {{c4::respond}}.
notes.explanation: Moves changes to production, ready to release.

sources.title: SAFe · Continuous Deployment (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: DevOps (SAFe)
notes.back: A mindset, culture and set of technical practices for integration, automation and collaboration; not a team or a toolset.
notes.explanation: Its approach is CALMR.

sources.title: SAFe · DevOps (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Which release practice limits the damage of a bad change?
notes.back: Releasing to a small group first, such as a canary release, then widening.
notes.explanation: With quick recovery if needed.

notes.front: What is the WSJF formula?
notes.back: Cost of Delay divided by job duration (job size).
notes.explanation: Highest WSJF goes first. Sunk cost is ignored.

sources.title: SAFe · WSJF (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Cost of Delay = {{c1::user-business value}} + {{c2::time criticality}} + {{c3::risk reduction or opportunity enablement}}.
notes.explanation: All three are relative estimates.

sources.title: SAFe · WSJF (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What does the ART backlog hold, and who prioritises it?
notes.back: Features and enablers; Product Management.
notes.explanation: The System Architect defines enablers.

sources.title: SAFe glossary
SAFe · Product Management (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What is the format of PI Planning?
notes.back: Two days, the whole ART, every 8 to 12 weeks, facilitated by the RTE.
notes.explanation: Outputs: committed PI objectives and the ART planning board.

sources.title: SAFe · PI Planning (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: ROAM: {{c1::Resolved}}, {{c2::Owned}}, {{c3::Accepted}}, {{c4::Mitigated}}.
notes.explanation: The categories for ART risks at PI Planning. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Who assigns business value to PI objectives?
notes.back: Business Owners, on a scale of 1 to 10.
notes.explanation: Not the Product Owners. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What is an uncommitted PI objective?
notes.back: Planned work with significant uncertainty that is left out of the commitment.
notes.explanation: It keeps the commitment reliable.

sources.title: SAFe · PI Objectives (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What is the Innovation and Planning iteration for?
notes.back: An estimating buffer, plus innovation, learning, PI Planning and Inspect and Adapt.
notes.explanation: No feature work is planned into it.

sources.title: SAFe · Innovation and Planning Iteration (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What is the System Demo?
notes.back: An integrated view of new features from all teams, at the end of each iteration.
notes.explanation: The Iteration Review covers one team only.

sources.title: SAFe · System Demo (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Inspect and Adapt has three parts: {{c1::PI System Demo}}, {{c2::measurement review}}, {{c3::retrospective and problem-solving workshop}}.
notes.explanation: Improvement items go into the ART backlog.

sources.title: SAFe · Inspect and Adapt (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Customer centricity
notes.back: A mindset focused on creating positive customer experiences across the full set of products and services.
notes.explanation: Internal teams have customers too.

sources.title: SAFe · Customer Centricity (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Which two phases does design thinking move through?
notes.back: Understand the problem, then design the right solution, each diverging then converging.
notes.explanation: It starts from the problem, not from requirements.

sources.title: SAFe · Design Thinking (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: A good solution is {{c1::desirable}}, {{c2::viable}}, {{c3::feasible}} and {{c4::sustainable}}.
notes.explanation: Customers, business, technology and time.

sources.title: SAFe · Product Management (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Persona
notes.back: A fictional but realistic description of a user, used to keep real needs in view.
notes.explanation: A design thinking tool.

sources.title: SAFe · Design Thinking (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Empathy map
notes.back: A record of what a user says, thinks, does and feels about a problem.
notes.explanation: No sequence of steps.

notes.front: Customer journey map
notes.back: Each step of the customer's experience, with feelings and pain points.
notes.explanation: Shows where to improve.

notes.front: Story map
notes.back: User activities laid out in order, with stories beneath, sliced into releases.
notes.explanation: Helps plan releases that each deliver value.

sources.title: SAFe · Design Thinking (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What does SAFe's Lean UX start with?
notes.back: A benefit hypothesis, then collaborative design, an MMF and evaluation.
notes.explanation: Not a detailed design document. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Does a platform train have customers?
notes.back: Yes: the internal teams and trains that use what it builds.
notes.explanation: SAFe recognises internal and external customers.

sources.title: SAFe · Customer Centricity (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Enabler types: {{c1::exploration}}, {{c2::architectural}}, {{c3::infrastructure}} and {{c4::compliance}}.
notes.explanation: Enablers support future business functionality.

sources.title: SAFe · Features and Capabilities (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Feature (SAFe)
notes.back: Solution functionality that delivers value and fits one ART in one PI, with a benefit hypothesis and acceptance criteria.
notes.explanation: Larger items are capabilities or epics.

sources.title: SAFe · Features and Capabilities (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Capability (SAFe)
notes.back: Large solution behaviour that spans several ARTs and is split into features.
notes.explanation: Used in Large Solution SAFe.

sources.title: SAFe · Features and Capabilities (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Give an example of a benefit hypothesis.
notes.back: 'We believe one-click reorder will lift repeat orders by 10%.'
notes.explanation: Measurable, so it can be tested after release.

notes.front: How are WSJF components estimated?
notes.back: Relatively, on a modified Fibonacci scale, with the smallest item set to 1.
notes.explanation: Not in money.

notes.front: Does money already spent affect WSJF?
notes.back: No: WSJF ignores sunk cost; only the remaining work counts.
notes.explanation: Finish-what-we-paid-for is the trap.

sources.title: SAFe · WSJF (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Capacity allocation
notes.back: Reserving a share of capacity for each type of work, such as enablers and maintenance.
notes.explanation: Flow distribution measures the actual split.

notes.front: Which backlog holds what?
notes.back: Portfolio: epics. ART: features and enablers. Team: stories.
notes.explanation: Owned by LPM, Product Management and the Product Owner.

notes.text: PI Planning readiness: {{c1::organizational}}, {{c2::content}} and {{c3::logistics}}.
notes.explanation: Prepared before the event.

sources.title: SAFe · PI Planning (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: PI Planning's primary outputs: committed {{c1::PI objectives}} and the {{c2::ART planning board}}.
notes.explanation: The board shows feature dates and dependencies.

sources.title: SAFe · PI Planning (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What opens day 1 of PI Planning?
notes.back: The business context, usually from a senior executive or Business Owner.
notes.explanation: Then the vision, architecture and planning context. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Who facilitates PI Planning?
notes.back: The Release Train Engineer.
notes.explanation: Product Management presents the vision.

sources.title: SAFe · PI Planning (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: On what scale is business value assigned to PI objectives?
notes.back: 1 to 10, by Business Owners.
notes.explanation: Compared with achieved value at the end of the PI. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: How is the confidence vote taken?
notes.back: With a fist of five; low votes are discussed and the plan reworked.
notes.explanation: Three or more fingers signals confidence. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: What happens at the end of PI Planning day 1?
notes.back: A draft plan review, then a management review and problem-solving session that adjusts scope.
notes.explanation: Adjustments are presented on day 2. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: ROAM: what separates Owned from Accepted?
notes.back: Owned: someone takes responsibility after the event. Accepted: understood, and nothing more can be done.
notes.explanation: Mitigated has a plan to reduce impact.

notes.text: The ART sync combines the {{c1::coach sync}} and the {{c2::PO sync}}.
notes.explanation: Impediments and dependencies; scope and priorities.

sources.title: SAFe · Planning Interval (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: A PI is usually {{c1::four or five}} development iterations followed by one {{c2::Innovation and Planning}} iteration, 8 to 12 weeks in all.
notes.explanation: A planning cadence, not a release schedule.

sources.title: SAFe · Planning Interval (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Problem-solving workshop: agree on the {{c1::problem}}, apply {{c2::root cause}} analysis, find the {{c3::biggest root cause}}, restate the problem, brainstorm {{c4::solutions}}, create {{c5::improvement backlog items}}.
notes.explanation: The items go into the ART backlog. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagram
notes.back: Groups possible causes of a problem into categories for root cause analysis.
notes.explanation: Used in the problem-solving workshop.

notes.front: Five whys
notes.back: Asking 'why' repeatedly to move from a symptom to its root cause.
notes.explanation: Used with the fishbone diagram.

notes.front: Pareto analysis
notes.back: Finding the vital few causes that explain most of a problem.
notes.explanation: The 80/20 rule.

notes.front: Which range counts as a predictable ART?
notes.back: 80 to 100 percent of planned business value achieved.
notes.explanation: The ART predictability measure. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Where is a cross-team dependency raised mid-PI?
notes.back: In the coach sync.
notes.explanation: Not at the next PI Planning.

notes.front: Is the PI a release schedule?
notes.back: No: trains plan on cadence and release on demand.
notes.explanation: Value reaches customers when they need it.

sources.title: SAFe · Planning Interval (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: LPM covers {{c1::strategy and investment funding}}, {{c2::Agile portfolio operations}} and {{c3::Lean governance}}.
notes.explanation: It aligns strategy and execution.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline

notes.front: What is a SAFe portfolio?
notes.back: A set of value streams that deliver solutions within common funding and governance.
notes.explanation: Not a list of projects.

sources.title: SAFe glossary

notes.front: Operational or development value stream: which one builds the solutions?
notes.back: The development value stream. The operational one delivers the service to the customer.
notes.explanation: Distractors often reverse them.

sources.title: SAFe · Development Value Streams (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What are Strategic Themes, and how are they written?
notes.back: Portfolio-level business objectives linking the portfolio to enterprise strategy, written as OKRs.
notes.explanation: They give the context for epic decisions.

sources.title: SAFe · Strategic Themes (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What does every epic need before implementation?
notes.back: A Lean business case, an MVP and approval by Portfolio Leadership.
notes.explanation: The Epic Owner coordinates; Portfolio Leadership approves.

sources.title: SAFe · Epic (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What do Lean Budgets fund?
notes.back: Value streams, not projects.
notes.explanation: Priorities are adjusted locally within the budget.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Budgets (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Guardrails: guiding investments by {{c1::horizon}}, applying {{c2::capacity allocation}}, approving {{c3::significant initiatives}}, continuous {{c4::Business Owner engagement}}.
notes.explanation: The first two are quantitative; the last two are about process.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Budget Guardrails (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Portfolio Kanban: {{c1::Funnel}}, {{c2::Reviewing}}, {{c3::Analyzing}}, {{c4::Ready}}, {{c5::Implementing}}, {{c6::Done}}.
notes.explanation: The Lean business case is developed in Analyzing. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: How often is the Strategic Portfolio Review held?
notes.back: Quarterly, at least a month before the next PI Planning.
notes.explanation: The Portfolio Sync is generally monthly.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline

notes.front: What is the enterprise in SAFe?
notes.back: The business entity that owns one or more portfolios.
notes.explanation: It sets their strategy and budgets.

sources.title: SAFe · Enterprise

notes.text: Operational value stream types: {{c1::fulfillment}}, {{c2::manufacturing}}, {{c3::software product}} and {{c4::supporting}}.
notes.explanation: Supporting value streams serve internal customers. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Who carries out Lean Portfolio Management?
notes.back: Business executives, Enterprise Architects and the Agile PMO or VMO.
notes.explanation: Train roles execute rather than govern.

notes.front: Value Management Office (VMO)
notes.back: Supports LPM with metrics, budgeting, governance and portfolio events; often an evolved PMO.
notes.explanation: It does not approve stories.

notes.front: What is the portfolio canvas adapted from?
notes.back: The Business Model Canvas.
notes.explanation: It describes a portfolio on one page.

notes.front: How many portfolios for three distinct business units?
notes.back: Usually one per unit, each with its own strategy and budget.
notes.explanation: A portfolio normally holds several ARTs.

notes.front: OKR
notes.back: A qualitative objective with a few measurable key results; SAFe's format for strategic themes.
notes.explanation: Key results measure outcomes.

sources.title: SAFe · Strategic Themes (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What do strategic themes influence?
notes.back: The portfolio vision, budget and backlog, and through them ART visions, backlogs and PI objectives.
notes.explanation: They give business context for decisions.

sources.title: SAFe · Strategic Themes (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What does the enterprise pass to each portfolio?
notes.back: Strategic themes and a portfolio budget.
notes.explanation: The portfolio decides how to invest within them.

sources.title: SAFe · Enterprise

notes.front: What does a portfolio send back to the enterprise?
notes.back: Its context, such as performance and solution status.
notes.explanation: Strategy is two-way.

sources.title: SAFe · Enterprise

notes.front: Which SWOT factors are internal?
notes.back: Strengths and weaknesses.
notes.explanation: Opportunities and threats are external.

notes.front: SO strategy (TOWS)
notes.back: Using internal strengths to seize external opportunities.
notes.explanation: ST, WO and WT are the other three.

notes.front: Outcome or output: 'launch the claims portal in March'?
notes.back: Output. An outcome would be 'cut claim time from 12 days to 5'.
notes.explanation: Key results should be outcomes.

notes.front: Portfolio vision
notes.back: The future state of the portfolio's value streams and solutions; aspirational yet realistic.
notes.explanation: Realised through epics.

sources.title: SAFe · Portfolio Vision (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: An epic hypothesis statement gives the {{c1::value statement}}, the {{c2::business outcomes}}, the {{c3::leading indicators}} and any NFRs.
notes.explanation: Leading indicators give early evidence. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: In which Kanban state are the Lean business case and MVP defined?
notes.back: Analyzing.
notes.explanation: Then a go or no-go decision.

notes.front: In which Kanban state is an epic described with a hypothesis statement and ranked with WSJF?
notes.back: Reviewing.
notes.explanation: Before Analyzing.

notes.front: An epic's MVP confirms its hypothesis. What next?
notes.back: Persevere: it stays in Implementing while trains build more features.
notes.explanation: Done comes when it no longer needs portfolio attention.

notes.text: Epics are {{c1::business}} epics or {{c2::enabler}} epics.
notes.explanation: Both go through the portfolio Kanban.

sources.title: SAFe · Epic (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Why limit WIP in the portfolio Kanban?
notes.back: To keep demand in line with capacity and finish epics faster.
notes.explanation: Finish before starting more.

notes.text: Investment horizons: Horizon 3 {{c1::Evaluating}}, Horizon 2 {{c2::Emerging}}, Horizon 1 {{c3::Investing and extracting}}, Horizon 0 {{c4::Retiring}}.
notes.explanation: A guardrail balances spending across them. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Participatory budgeting
notes.back: Stakeholders deciding together how the portfolio budget is split across value streams; also called Strategic Investment Planning.
notes.explanation: Held periodically, often twice a year.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Budgets (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: How often is the Portfolio Sync held?
notes.back: Monthly.
notes.explanation: The Strategic Portfolio Review is quarterly.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Portfolio Management discipline

notes.front: When must an epic go to LPM for approval?
notes.back: When its estimated cost exceeds the portfolio's threshold.
notes.explanation: The guardrail 'approving significant initiatives'.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Budget Guardrails (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Within a value stream budget, who decides which features to build?
notes.back: The value stream's ARTs, through Product Management's backlog and PI Planning.
notes.explanation: Not finance, feature by feature.

notes.front: A feature takes longer than planned. Is a change request needed?
notes.back: No: the budget stays and priorities are adjusted locally.
notes.explanation: The value stream is funded, not the project.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean Budgets (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: Why can a transformation not be delegated?
notes.back: Only leaders can change the systems that govern how work is done.
notes.explanation: Budgeting, incentives and approvals are outside a team's control.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.front: What are the two routes to the tipping point?
notes.back: A burning platform, or proactive leadership.
notes.explanation: It is the first step of the Implementation Roadmap.

sources.title: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point

notes.text: A vision for change provides {{c1::purpose}}, {{c2::motivation}} and {{c3::alignment}}.
notes.explanation: A vision also needs a powerful guiding coalition.

sources.title: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point

notes.front: Lean-Agile Center of Excellence (LACE)
notes.back: A small Agile team dedicated to implementing the Lean-Agile way of working.
notes.explanation: Not the same as the Value Management Office.

sources.title: SAFe glossary

notes.front: Which roadmap step follows Reaching the Tipping Point?
notes.back: Train Lean-Agile Change Agents.

notes.front: How should a leader treat an AI recommendation?
notes.back: Evaluate it and stay accountable for the decision.
notes.explanation: AI prepares; people decide.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page

notes.text: Lean-Agile Leadership: {{c1::mindset, values and principles}}, {{c2::leading by example}} and {{c3::leading change}}.
notes.explanation: Its three dimensions.

sources.title: SAFe · Lean-Agile Leadership (public introduction; the rest of the article needs a login)

notes.text: Leading by example: {{c1::authenticity}}, {{c2::emotional intelligence}}, {{c3::lifelong learning}}, {{c4::growing others}}, {{c5::decentralized decision-making}}.
notes.explanation: Behaviours leaders model. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: Authenticity (leadership)
notes.back: Being honest and consistent, including about one's own mistakes.
notes.explanation: Makes it safe for others to do the same.

notes.front: Go and see (gemba)
notes.back: Visiting where the work happens to understand problems first-hand.
notes.explanation: Not inspection of individuals.

notes.front: Why must leaders model the mindset, not just sponsor it?
notes.back: People copy what leaders do more than what they say.
notes.explanation: Behaviour sets culture.

notes.front: Who owns a team's estimates in PI Planning?
notes.back: The team; leaders influence priorities, not estimates.
notes.explanation: Overriding them undermines the commitment.

notes.front: How many steps does the current SAFe Implementation Roadmap have?
notes.back: Thirteen; older versions had twelve.
notes.explanation: Kotter's model has eight.

sources.title: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap

notes.front: Which roadmap step follows Train Lean-Agile Change Agents?
notes.back: Create a Lean-Agile Center of Excellence.
notes.explanation: Then Train Executives, Managers, and Leaders.

sources.title: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap

notes.front: What are the last three roadmap steps?
notes.back: Launch More ARTs and Value Streams, Enhance the Portfolio, Accelerate.
notes.explanation: Steps 11 to 13.

sources.title: SAFe · Implementation Roadmap

notes.text: Kotter: create {{c1::urgency}}, build a {{c2::guiding coalition}}, form a strategic vision, enlist a {{c3::volunteer army}}, remove barriers, generate {{c4::short-term wins}}, sustain acceleration, institute change.
notes.explanation: The model the roadmap draws on. Written from author knowledge; not checked against a public page on 13 Nov 2026.

notes.front: How does SAFe launch the first ART's teams?
notes.back: It trains them together, close to the first PI Planning.
notes.explanation: Not one team at a time over months.

notes.front: Guiding coalition
notes.back: Influential, respected people who can secure resources and overcome resistance to the change.
notes.explanation: One coach is not enough.

sources.title: SAFe · Reaching the Tipping Point

notes.front: How does the Leading SAFe course page describe AI?
notes.back: As a powerful accelerant for organisational value and flow.
notes.explanation: It amplifies what is already there.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page

notes.front: Which AI assistant does the Leading SAFe course page name?
notes.back: SAFe CoPilot.
notes.explanation: For guidance, synthesising data and drafting artifacts.

sources.title: Scaled Agile · Leading SAFe certification page

notes.front: AI use on a train is uneven. What should a leader do?
notes.back: Create time, training and safe ways for everyone to experiment, and use AI openly themselves.
notes.explanation: Prompt quotas measure activity, not value.

notes.front: Who owns a change vision drafted with AI?
notes.back: The leader: accountability and authenticity cannot be handed to a tool.
notes.explanation: AI prepares, people decide.
